abstract: Intracellular recordings in spinal cord motoneurons and cerebral cortex neurons have provided new evidence on the correlational strength of monosynaptic connections, and the relation between the shapes of postsynaptic potentials and the associated increased firing probability. In these cells, excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) produce cross(cid:173) correlogram peaks which resemble in large part the derivative of the EPSP. Additional synaptic noise broadens the peak, but the peak area -- i.e., the number of above-chance firings triggered per EPSP -- remains proportional to the EPSP amplitude. A typical EPSP of 100 ~v triggers about .01 firings per EPSP. The consequences of these data for information processing by polysynaptic connections is discussed. The effects of sequential polysynaptic links can be calculated by convolving the effects of the underlying monosynaptic connections. The net effect of parallel pathways is the sum of the individual contributions.

paragraphs: The paper examines how a single synaptic connection changes the probability that a receiving neuron fires. Intracellular recordings from spinal motoneurons and cerebral cortex neurons connect the shape of an excitatory postsynaptic potential, or EPSP, with the timing of the extra spikes associated with that input.

The observed cross-correlogram peaks largely resemble the derivative of the EPSP: their shape reflects how the potential changes over time. Added synaptic noise broadens the peak, but its area remains proportional to EPSP amplitude. That area measures the number of firings above chance per input. A typical 100-microvolt EPSP produces about 0.01 such firings.

The authors then describe how these effects combine across pathways containing several synapses. Sequential connections are combined by convolution, which accounts for how their timing effects accumulate. Contributions from parallel pathways are added. This provides a computational account connecting measurements at individual synapses to the effects of larger pathways, while distinguishing the temporal spread of an influence from its overall contribution to firing.
summary.tldr: Recordings relate synaptic potentials to extra firing probability and support combining sequential pathway effects by convolution and parallel effects by addition.

title: Correlational Strength and Computational Algebra of Synaptic Connections Between Neurons

paragraphs: This study investigates what neuronal signals reveal about visual pattern recognition in monkeys performing a pattern-matching task. It focuses on neurons in inferior temporal cortex. The researchers use simple neural networks trained by backpropagation as tools for analyzing the relationship between the presented patterns, the behavioral situation, and the measured neural responses.

The analysis works in two directions. Some networks learn to distinguish stimulus conditions from recorded neuronal signals, testing which distinctions those signals carry. Other networks learn to predict the time-varying neuronal response from the spatial pattern of a stimulus. Together, these tasks examine both the information recoverable from neural activity and the relationship between visual structure and response waveforms.

The results indicate that the neurons carry temporally encoded information about currently visible patterns, remembered patterns, and behavioral context. The time course of a response therefore matters to its interpretation. The finding links visual processing with memory and task context in the measured signals, rather than treating the response solely as a description of the present image.
summary.tldr: Neural-network analyses indicate that inferior temporal responses encode current patterns, remembered patterns, and behavioral context over time.

title: Decoding of Neuronal Signals in Visual Pattern Recognition

abstract: A new neural network, the Binary Diamond, is presented and its use as a classifier is demonstrated and evaluated. The network is of the feed-forward type. It learns from examples in the 'one shot' mode, and recruits new neurons as needed. It was tested on the problem of pixel classification, and performed well. paragraphs: The paper introduces the Binary Diamond, a feed-forward neural network intended for classification. Its distinctive features are one-shot learning from examples and the ability to recruit additional neurons as needed. Learning and network growth are therefore connected parts of the proposed design, rather than requiring the entire network size to be settled in advance.

The approach is motivated by classification through clues. An item has basic features, and a clue can be any combination of those features. Such combinations are associated both with the items that contain them and with classes stored in memory. This gives the design a way to frame classification in terms of feature combinations that support particular category assignments.

The network is demonstrated and evaluated on pixel classification, where the authors report good performance. They also outline possible uses in associative memory. The contribution combines a proposed general-purpose classifier with a concrete application, emphasizing how examples, feature combinations, and the recruitment of neurons can work together in a classification system.
summary.tldr: The Binary Diamond network combines one-shot learning and neuron recruitment for classification, with a successful pixel-classification demonstration.

title: Classification of Multi-Spectral Pixels by the Binary Diamond Neural Network

abstract: In this paper we introduce a new class of image models, which we call dynamic trees or DTs. A dynamic tree model specifies a prior over a large number of trees, each one of which is a tree-structured belief net (TSBN). Experiments show that DTs are capable of generating images that are less blocky, and the models have better translation invariance properties than a fixed, "balanced" TSBN. We also show that Simulated Annealing is effective at finding trees which have high posterior probability.

paragraphs: Dynamic trees are image models that place a prior distribution over many possible tree structures. Each candidate structure is itself a tree-structured belief network. The model therefore includes uncertainty about the tree used to represent an image, giving it structural flexibility beyond a single fixed arrangement of connections.

The authors compare this approach with a fixed, balanced tree-structured belief network. Their experiments show that dynamic trees can generate images with less blockiness and have better translation-invariance properties. In plain language, the reported results suggest that allowing the structure to vary reduces visible artifacts associated with the fixed tree and improves how the model handles changes in image position.

The paper also investigates how to find useful tree structures. Simulated annealing is shown to locate trees with high posterior probability, meaning structures favored after the image evidence is taken into account. This provides an effective search method for the proposed model in the reported experiments. The combined contribution is a flexible family of image representations and evidence that useful members of that family can be found.
summary.tldr: Dynamic trees model images using many possible tree structures, producing less blocky images and better translation invariance in experiments.

title: DTs: Dynamic Trees

abstract: The performance of regular and irregular Gallager-type error(cid:173) correcting code is investigated via methods of statistical physics. The transmitted codeword comprises products of the original mes(cid:173) sage bits selected by two randomly-constructed sparse matrices; the number of non-zero row/column elements in these matrices constitutes a family of codes. We show that Shannon's channel capacity may be saturated in equilibrium for many of the regular codes while slightly lower performance is obtained for others which may be of higher practical relevance. Decoding aspects are con(cid:173) sidered by employing the TAP approach which is identical to the commonly used belief-propagation-based decoding. We show that irregular codes may saturate Shannon's capacity but with improved dynamical properties.

paragraphs: The paper uses statistical physics to investigate regular and irregular Gallager-type error-correcting codes. Codewords are built from products of message bits selected through two randomly constructed sparse matrices. The numbers of nonzero entries in the matrices' rows and columns define a family of codes whose performance can be compared within this framework.

The analysis shows that many regular codes may reach Shannon's channel capacity in equilibrium. Other regular codes have slightly lower performance but may be more practically relevant. This distinction separates the equilibrium performance available to a code from the considerations that determine whether it is useful in practice.

To examine decoding, the authors use the TAP approach, which they identify with the commonly used belief-propagation decoder. They show that irregular codes may also reach capacity while having improved dynamical properties. The significance is the connection between code structure, equilibrium limits, and decoding dynamics: capacity-level potential and favorable decoding behavior are both addressed, with the capacity statements retaining their qualified form.
summary.tldr: Statistical-physics analysis finds that irregular Gallager-type codes may reach Shannon capacity with improved decoding dynamics.

title: Regular and Irregular Gallager-zype Error-Correcting Codes

abstract: Over the last years signiﬁcant efforts have been made to develop kernels that can be applied to sequence data such as DNA, text, speech, video and images. The Fisher Kernel and similar variants have been suggested as good ways to combine an underlying generative model in the feature space and discriminant classiﬁers such as SVM’s. In this paper we sug- gest an alternative procedure to the Fisher kernel for systematically ﬁnd- ing kernel functions that naturally handle variable length sequence data in multimedia domains. In particular for domains such as speech and images we explore the use of kernel functions that take full advantage of well known probabilistic models such as Gaussian Mixtures and sin- gle full covariance Gaussian models. We derive a kernel distance based on the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between generative models. In effect our approach combines the best of both generative and discrim- inative methods and replaces the standard SVM kernels. We perform experiments on speaker identiﬁcation/veriﬁcation and image classiﬁca- tion tasks and show that these new kernels have the best performance in speaker veriﬁcation and mostly outperform the Fisher kernel based SVM’s and the generative classiﬁers in speaker identiﬁcation and image classiﬁcation.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to classify multimedia sequences whose lengths can vary. Its central idea is to describe the data with probabilistic models and then compare those models inside a support vector machine. This connects a generative description of the observations with a discriminative method for separating classes.

The authors derive a kernel distance using Kullback–Leibler divergence between generative models. They explore Gaussian mixtures and single Gaussian models with full covariance for speech and image applications. The resulting kernels replace standard SVM kernels and provide an alternative to the Fisher kernel. Comparing probabilistic descriptions gives the classifier a way to work with sequence data without requiring all sequences to have the same length.

Experiments cover speaker verification, speaker identification, and image classification. The proposed kernels achieve the best speaker-verification performance among the evaluated methods. For identification and image classification, they mostly outperform Fisher-kernel SVMs and generative classifiers. That distinction matters: the reported advantage is broad across the experiments, but is not described as an improvement in every comparison.
summary.tldr: Kernels built from KL divergence between probabilistic models improve several reported speech and image classification comparisons.

title: A Kullback-Leibler Divergence Based Kernel for SVM Classification in Multimedia Applications

abstract: During the last ten years there has been growing interest in the develop- ment of Brain Computer Interfaces (BCIs). The field has mainly been driven by the needs of completely paralyzed patients to communicate. With a few exceptions, most human BCIs are based on extracranial elec- troencephalography (EEG). However, reported bit rates are still low. One reason for this is the low signal-to-noise ratio of the EEG [16]. We are currently investigating if BCIs based on electrocorticography (ECoG) are a viable alternative. In this paper we present the method and examples of intracranial EEG recordings of three epilepsy patients with electrode grids placed on the motor cortex. The patients were asked to repeat- edly imagine movements of two kinds, e.g., tongue or finger movements. We analyze the classifiability of the data using Support Vector Machines (SVMs) [18, 21] and Recursive Channel Elimination (RCE) [11].

paragraphs: The paper investigates electrocorticography as a possible signal source for human brain-computer interfaces. Its motivation is communication for completely paralyzed people and the low reported information rates of interfaces based on EEG recorded outside the skull. The authors identify low EEG signal-to-noise ratio as one reason to investigate recordings made closer to the brain.

They present methods and example recordings from three epilepsy patients with electrode grids positioned over the motor cortex. The participants repeatedly imagined two kinds of movement, such as moving a tongue or a finger. The analysis asks whether these imagined actions produce signals that can be distinguished computationally.

Support vector machines and recursive channel elimination are used to assess how classifiable the recordings are. This makes the work an investigation of signal distinguishability relevant to an invasive interface. The stated scope is exploratory: the authors are examining whether electrocorticography is a viable alternative. The abstract reports the recording and analysis approach, rather than claiming a demonstrated communication-rate improvement or an established interface for paralyzed patients.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes motor-imagery recordings from three epilepsy patients to investigate electrocorticography as a possible basis for human brain-computer interfaces.

title: Methods Towards Invasive Human Brain Computer Interfaces

abstract: Angela J. Yu Center for Brain, Mind & Behavior Green Hall, Princeton University Princeton, NJ 08540, USA ajyu@princeton.edu Experimental data indicate that norepinephrine is critically involved in aspects of vigilance and attention. Previously, we considered the func- tion of this neuromodulatory system on a time scale of minutes and longer, and suggested that it signals global uncertainty arising from gross changes in environmental contingencies. However, norepinephrine is also known to be activated phasically by familiar stimuli in well- learned tasks. Here, we extend our uncertainty-based treatment of nore- pinephrine to this phasic mode, proposing that it is involved in the de- tection and reaction to state uncertainty within a task. This role of nore- pinephrine can be understood through the metaphor of neural interrupts.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an explanation for brief norepinephrine responses during familiar, well-learned tasks. Experimental evidence links norepinephrine to vigilance and attention, but a previous uncertainty-based account focused on longer timescales. That account associated the neuromodulatory system with broad uncertainty caused by major changes in environmental contingencies.

The new proposal extends this treatment to phasic activation: brief responses associated with stimuli. It suggests that norepinephrine participates in detecting and reacting to uncertainty about the current state within a task. A task can therefore be familiar overall while still presenting uncertainty about what is happening at a particular moment.

The authors describe this proposed role through the metaphor of neural interrupts. The metaphor connects a brief signal with the need to respond to uncertainty arising during ongoing task performance. The contribution is a conceptual extension linking longer-lasting environmental uncertainty and shorter-lived uncertainty within a task. It offers an interpretation of familiar-stimulus responses within the same uncertainty-based framework, while retaining the status of a proposed functional account.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes that brief norepinephrine responses act as neural interrupts for detecting and reacting to uncertainty within familiar tasks.

title: Norepinephrine and Neural Interrupts

abstract: CAP TCHAs are computer-generated tests that humans can pass but current computer systems cannot. CAP TCHAs provide a method for automatically distinguishing a human from a computer program, and therefore can protect Web services from abuse by so-called “bots.” Most CAP TCHAs consist of distorted images, usually text, for which a user must provide some description. Unfortunately, visual CAP TCHAs limit access to the millions of visually impaired people using the Web. Audio CAP TCHAs were created to solve this accessibility issue; however, the security of audio CAP TCHAs was never formally tested. Some visual CAP TCHAs have been broken using machine learning techniques, and we propose using similar ideas to test the security of audio CAP TCHAs. Audio CAP TCHAs are generally composed of a set of words to be identified, layered on top of noise. We analyzed the security of current audio CAP TCHAs from popular Web sites by using AdaBoost, SVM, and k-NN, and achieved correct solutions for test samples with accuracy up to 71%. Such accuracy is enough to consider these CAPTCHAs broken. Training several different machine learning algorithms on different types of audio CAP TCHAs allowed us to analyze the strengths and weaknesses of the algorithms so that we could suggest a design for a more robust audio CAPTCHA.

paragraphs: Audio CAPTCHAs address an accessibility problem created by visual challenges: people with visual impairments may be unable to read distorted images. Their protective role still depends on automated systems having difficulty solving them. This paper examines whether the audio challenges used by popular websites actually provide that separation between human and machine performance.

The challenges studied generally contain words layered over noise. The authors test their security using three machine learning approaches: AdaBoost, support vector machines, and nearest-neighbor classification. They train different algorithms on different types of audio CAPTCHA, allowing them to examine how recognition performance depends on both the learning method and the challenge format.

The experiments achieve correct solutions on test samples at rates as high as 71%, which the authors consider sufficient to regard the tested CAPTCHAs as broken. This is a result about the systems examined, rather than every possible audio challenge. The comparisons also inform a proposed design for a more robust audio CAPTCHA, connecting the security evaluation back to the accessibility problem that motivated these tests.
summary.tldr: Machine learning solved tested audio CAPTCHAs with accuracy up to 71%, exposing weaknesses and informing a proposed stronger design.

title: Breaking Audio CAPTCHAs

abstract: We consider the general problem of constructing nonparametric Bayesian models on infinite-dimensional random objects, such as functions, infinite graphs or infinite permutations. The problem has generated much interest in machine learning, where it is treated heuristically, but has not been studied in full generality in nonparametric Bayesian statistics, which tends to focus on models over probability distributions. Our approach applies a standard tool of stochastic process theory, the construction of stochastic processes from their finite-dimensional marginal distributions. The main contribution of the paper is a generalization of the classic Kolmogorov extension theorem to conditional probabilities. This extension allows a rigorous construction of nonparametric Bayesian models from systems of finite-dimensional, parametric Bayes equations. Using this approach, we show (i) how existence of a conjugate posterior for the nonparametric model can be guaranteed by choosing conjugate finite-dimensional models in the construction, (ii) how the mapping to the posterior parameters of the nonparametric model can be explicitly determined, and (iii) that the construction of conjugate models in essence requires the finite-dimensional models to be in the exponential family. As an application of our constructive framework, we derive a model on infinite permutations, the nonparametric Bayesian analogue of a model recently proposed for the analysis of rank data.

paragraphs: The paper develops a rigorous way to build Bayesian models for infinite-dimensional objects, including functions, infinite graphs, and infinite permutations. Such objects go beyond the probability distributions often emphasized in nonparametric Bayesian statistics. The construction starts with finite-dimensional models, providing a route from manageable Bayesian calculations to a model of an infinite object.

Its central contribution extends the Kolmogorov extension theorem to conditional probabilities. This allows systems of finite-dimensional Bayes equations to define nonparametric Bayesian models. The framework also explains how choosing conjugate finite-dimensional models can guarantee a conjugate posterior in the resulting nonparametric model and how to determine its posterior parameter update explicitly.

The authors further show that constructing conjugate models in this way essentially requires exponential-family finite-dimensional components. As an application, they derive a Bayesian model on infinite permutations that extends a model for rank data. The significance is a constructive connection between finite Bayesian specifications and infinite-dimensional inference, including conditions that support useful posterior structure.
summary.tldr: An extension theorem for conditional probabilities constructs infinite-dimensional Bayesian models from finite-dimensional Bayes equations.

title: Construction of Nonparametric Bayesian Models from Parametric Bayes Equations

abstract: Markov random fields (MRFs), or undirected graphical models, provide a powerful framework for modeling complex dependencies among random variables. Maximum likelihood learning in MRFs is hard due to the presence of the global normalizing constant. In this paper we consider a class of stochastic approximation algorithms of Robbins-Monro type that uses Markov chain Monte Carlo to do approximate maximum likelihood learning. We show that using MCMC operators based on tempered transitions enables the stochastic approximation algorithm to better explore highly multimodal distributions, which considerably improves parameter estimates in large densely-connected MRFs. Our results on MNIST and NORB datasets demonstrate that we can successfully learn good generative models of high-dimensional, richly structured data and perform well on digit and object recognition tasks.

paragraphs: Markov random fields represent dependencies among variables through an undirected graphical model. Learning their parameters by maximum likelihood is difficult because the probability model includes a global normalizing constant. This paper studies an approximate learning approach that combines Robbins-Monro stochastic approximation with Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling.

The proposed improvement concerns how the sampling component explores the model's distribution. The authors use operators based on tempered transitions to better explore distributions with many distinct modes. This matters because parameter learning depends on the information supplied by sampling; exploring the distribution more effectively can improve the estimates used during learning.

The authors report considerable improvements in parameter estimates for large, densely connected Markov random fields. Results on MNIST and NORB demonstrate learning of generative models for high-dimensional, structured data, along with good performance on digit and object recognition tasks. The contribution connects an improvement in sampling behavior to practical model learning: tempered transitions make the stochastic approximation procedure more effective in the multimodal settings examined.
summary.tldr: Tempered-transition sampling improves approximate maximum-likelihood learning in large Markov random fields by exploring multimodal distributions more effectively.

title: Learning in Markov Random Fields using Tempered Transitions

abstract: We define a data dependent permutation complexity for a hypothesis set \math{\hset}, which is similar to a Rademacher complexity or maximum discrepancy. The permutation complexity is based like the maximum discrepancy on (dependent) sampling. We prove a uniform bound on the generalization error, as well as a concentration result which means that the permutation estimate can be efficiently estimated.
originalAbstract: We define a data dependent permutation complexity for a hypothesis set \math{\hset}, which is similar to a Rademacher complexity or maximum discrepancy. The permutation complexity is based like the maximum discrepancy on (dependent) sampling. We prove a uniform bound on the generalization error, as well as a concentration result which means that the permutation estimate can be efficiently estimated.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a data-dependent way to measure the complexity of a hypothesis set. Its purpose is to connect the flexibility of candidate predictors with their behavior on unseen data. Because the quantity depends on the observed data, it supplies a sample-based ingredient for assessing generalization.

The proposed permutation complexity is related to Rademacher complexity and maximum discrepancy. Like maximum discrepancy, its construction uses dependent sampling. The authors prove a uniform generalization-error bound using this quantity. Uniformity means the guarantee applies across the hypothesis set, which makes the result relevant when a predictor is chosen from that set using the data.

A second result establishes concentration for the permutation estimate. The authors explain that this makes the complexity efficiently estimable. The two results address complementary needs: a complexity measure must support a useful generalization bound, and its value must be accessible enough to estimate. The paper supplies both a theoretical role and an estimation justification for the proposed measure.
summary.tldr: A data-dependent permutation complexity yields a uniform generalization bound and a concentration result supporting efficient estimation.

title: Permutation Complexity Bound on Out-Sample Error

abstract: We propose a new sparse Bayesian model for multi-task regression and classification. The model is able to capture correlations between tasks, or more specifically a low-rank approximation of the covariance matrix, while being sparse in the features. We introduce a general family of group sparsity inducing priors based on matrix-variate Gaussian scale mixtures. We show the amount of sparsity can be learnt from the data by combining an approximate inference approach with type II maximum likelihood estimation of the hyperparameters. Empirical evaluations on data sets from biology and vision demonstrate the applicability of the model, where on both regression and classification tasks it achieves competitive predictive performance compared to previously proposed methods.
originalAbstract: We propose a new sparse Bayesian model for multi-task regression and classification. The model is able to capture correlations between tasks, or more specifically a low-rank approximation of the covariance matrix, while being sparse in the features. We introduce a general family of group sparsity inducing priors based on matrix-variate Gaussian scale mixtures. We show the amount of sparsity can be learnt from the data by combining an approximate inference approach with type II maximum likelihood estimation of the hyperparameters. Empirical evaluations on data sets from biology and vision demonstrate the applicability of the model, where on both regression and classification tasks it achieves competitive predictive performance compared to previously proposed methods.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning considers several prediction tasks together so their relationships can inform learning. This paper proposes a sparse Bayesian model for both regression and classification. It captures correlations between tasks through a low-rank approximation of their covariance matrix while also encouraging sparsity in the features used for prediction.

The authors introduce a family of priors that encourage group sparsity, built from matrix-variate Gaussian scale mixtures. These priors provide the model’s mechanism for favoring sparse feature structure. The amount of sparsity can be learned from data by combining approximate inference with type II maximum likelihood estimation of the hyperparameters, making sparsity itself part of the estimation process.

Evaluations on biology and vision datasets demonstrate the model’s applicability to regression and classification. Its predictive performance is competitive with previously proposed methods in those experiments. The contribution combines two forms of structure in one Bayesian model: a compact account of task correlations and sparse feature use, with a data-driven procedure for setting the strength of sparsity.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian multi-task model jointly learns sparse feature use and low-rank task correlations, achieving competitive reported predictive performance.

title: Sparse Bayesian Multi-Task Learning

abstract: Components estimated by independent component analysis and related methods are typically not independent in real data. A very common form of nonlinear dependency between the components is correlations in their variances or ener- gies. Here, we propose a principled probabilistic model to model the energy- correlations between the latent variables. Our two-stage model includes a linear mixing of latent signals into the observed ones like in ICA. The main new fea- ture is a model of the energy-correlations based on the structural equation model (SEM), in particular, a Linear Non-Gaussian SEM. The SEM is closely related to divisive normalization which effectively reduces energy correlation. Our new two- stage model enables estimation of both the linear mixing and the interactions re- lated to energy-correlations, without resorting to approximations of the likelihood function or other non-principled approaches. We demonstrate the applicability of our method with synthetic dataset, natural images and brain signals.

paragraphs: The paper addresses dependencies that remain between components extracted from real data by independent component analysis and related methods. In particular, component variances or energies can be correlated even when the components are treated as independent. The authors build a probabilistic model that explicitly represents this form of nonlinear dependence among latent signals.

The model has two stages. One linearly mixes latent signals into the observations, as in independent component analysis. The other describes energy relationships through a linear non-Gaussian structural equation model. This second stage is closely related to divisive normalization, which reduces correlations between component energies. Together, the stages represent both how signals form observations and how their energies interact.

The formulation allows the linear mixing and energy-related interactions to be estimated without approximating the likelihood function or relying on the alternative non-principled approaches discussed by the authors. Demonstrations use synthetic data, natural images, and brain signals. These applications show the model’s applicability to several data types where energy dependence is relevant to component analysis.
summary.tldr: A two-stage probabilistic model combines linear signal mixing with structural equations for energy dependence, linking component analysis to divisive normalization.

title: Structural equations and divisive normalization for energy-dependent component analysis

abstract: We introduce a new notion of classification accuracy based on the top $\tau$-quantile values of a scoring function, a relevant criterion in a number of problems arising for search engines. We define an algorithm optimizing a convex surrogate of the corresponding loss, and show how its solution can be obtained by solving several convex optimization problems. We also present margin-based guarantees for this algorithm based on the $\tau$-quantile of the functions in the hypothesis set. Finally, we report the results of several experiments evaluating the performance of our algorithm. In a comparison in a bipartite setting with several algorithms seeking high precision at the top, our algorithm achieves a better performance in precision at the top.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a classification criterion focused on the highest scores produced by a model. A parameter specifies the upper fraction of scores that matters. This captures a concern arising in search engines: the quality of the items placed near the top deserves its own learning objective.

To make that objective tractable, the authors optimize a convex surrogate for the associated loss. A surrogate is an alternative objective used to guide learning when directly optimizing the desired criterion is difficult. They show that obtaining their algorithm's solution can be organized into several convex optimization problems. They also establish margin-based guarantees that incorporate the relevant score quantile of candidate functions.

Experiments evaluate the resulting algorithm, including comparisons with several methods designed for high precision at the top in a bipartite setting. The proposed method achieves better top precision in that comparison. The contribution therefore combines an explicit target for learning, an optimization procedure, and theoretical support tied to the same upper portion of the ranking.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a learning objective and algorithm for classification accuracy among the highest-scoring items.

title: Accuracy at the Top

abstract: A successful approach to structured learning is to write the learning objective as a joint function of linear parameters and inference messages, and iterate between updates to each. This paper observes that if the inference problem is “smoothed” through the addition of entropy terms, for fixed messages, the learning objective reduces to a traditional (non-structured) logistic regression problem with respect to parameters. In these logistic regression problems, each training example has a bias term determined by the current set of messages. Based on this insight, the structured energy function can be extended from linear factors to any function class where an “oracle” exists to minimize a logistic loss.

paragraphs: Structured learning involves models whose predictions have interacting parts. One approach writes the training objective jointly in terms of model parameters and inference messages, then alternates between updating these two sets of quantities. This paper identifies a useful simplification of the parameter-update step in that framework.

When entropy terms are added to smooth the inference problem, holding the messages fixed turns learning the parameters into an ordinary logistic regression problem. Each training example receives a bias determined by the current messages. The structured dependencies therefore still influence the update, but their effect enters the logistic regression subproblem through these message-dependent biases.

This observation opens a route beyond structured energy functions built only from linear factors. The factors can come from any function class for which an oracle is available to minimize logistic loss. That oracle requirement is the condition enabling the extension. The contribution is a reduction that connects structured training to familiar loss minimization, making a broader class of factor functions available within the alternating learning-and-inference approach.
summary.tldr: Entropy-smoothed structured learning reduces parameter updates to logistic regression, enabling richer factors when a logistic-loss minimization oracle exists.

title: Structured Learning via Logistic Regression

abstract: We propose a semi-parametric and dynamic rank factor model for topic modeling, capable of (1) discovering topic prevalence over time, and (2) learning contemporary multi-scale dependence structures, providing topic and word correlations as a byproduct. The high-dimensional and time-evolving ordinal/rank observations (such as word counts), after an arbitrary monotone transformation, are well accommodated through an underlying dynamic sparse factor model. The framework naturally admits heavy-tailed innovations, capable of inferring abrupt temporal jumps in the importance of topics. Posterior inference is performed through straightforward Gibbs sampling, based on the forward-filtering backward-sampling algorithm. Moreover, an efficient data subsampling scheme is leveraged to speed up inference on massive datasets. The modeling framework is illustrated on two real datasets: the US State of the Union Address and the JSTOR collection from Science.

paragraphs: Text collections change over time: topics become more or less prominent, and relationships among topics and words can also evolve. This paper proposes a dynamic rank factor model that addresses both aspects. It estimates topic prevalence over time while learning contemporary dependence structures at multiple scales, producing topic and word correlations as part of the model.

The approach connects high-dimensional ordinal or rank observations, including word counts, to an underlying sparse dynamic factor model after a monotone transformation. This semiparametric formulation allows flexibility in the relationship between observations and latent factors. Heavy-tailed innovations let the model accommodate abrupt changes in topic importance, rather than requiring every temporal change to be gradual.

Posterior inference uses Gibbs sampling built around forward filtering and backward sampling. An additional data subsampling scheme speeds inference on massive datasets. The authors illustrate the framework with State of the Union addresses and a JSTOR collection from Science. These applications demonstrate a way to examine changing topic prevalence and dependence within one probabilistic modeling framework.
summary.tldr: A dynamic rank factor model tracks topic prevalence and dependence over time while accommodating abrupt changes in topic importance.

title: Dynamic Rank Factor Model for Text Streams

abstract: Bayesian observer models are very effective in describing human performance in perceptual tasks, so much so that they are trusted to faithfully recover hidden mental representations of priors, likelihoods, or loss functions from the data. However, the intrinsic degeneracy of the Bayesian framework, as multiple combinations of elements can yield empirically indistinguishable results, prompts the question of model identifiability. We propose a novel framework for a systematic testing of the identifiability of a significant class of Bayesian observer models, with practical applications for improving experimental design. We examine the theoretical identifiability of the inferred internal representations in two case studies. First, we show which experimental designs work better to remove the underlying degeneracy in a time interval estimation task. Second, we find that the reconstructed representations in a speed perception task under a slow-speed prior are fairly robust.

paragraphs: Bayesian models can describe human perceptual behavior very well, but a good behavioral fit does not necessarily reveal a unique internal explanation. Different combinations of prior expectations, sensory likelihoods, and loss functions can produce indistinguishable observations. The paper studies identifiability: whether the available evidence can distinguish those underlying components.

The authors propose a framework for systematically testing identifiability across a substantial class of Bayesian observer models. This makes the question part of experimental design. Instead of interpreting a fitted internal representation solely through its agreement with behavior, researchers can examine whether their experiment separates it from alternative representations.

Two case studies illustrate the framework. For time interval estimation, the analysis identifies experimental designs that better resolve the ambiguity between model components. For speed perception with a slow-speed prior, the reconstructed representations are found to be fairly robust. Together, these findings show how identifiability analysis can both guide better experiments and strengthen confidence in particular interpretations, depending on the task and model.
summary.tldr: A framework tests whether Bayesian perception models uniquely identify internal representations and helps design experiments that resolve ambiguities.

title: A Framework for Testing Identifiability of Bayesian Models of Perception

abstract: We consider the problem of recovering the sparsest vector in a subspace $ \mathcal{S} \in \mathbb{R}^p $ with $ \text{dim}(\mathcal{S})=n$. This problem can be considered a homogeneous variant of the sparse recovery problem, and finds applications in sparse dictionary learning, sparse PCA, and other problems in signal processing and machine learning. Simple convex heuristics for this problem provably break down when the fraction of nonzero entries in the target sparse vector substantially exceeds $1/ \sqrt{n}$. In contrast, we exhibit a relatively simple nonconvex approach based on alternating directions, which provably succeeds even when the fraction of nonzero entries is $\Omega(1)$. To our knowledge, this is the first practical algorithm to achieve this linear scaling. This result assumes a planted sparse model, in which the target sparse vector is embedded in an otherwise random subspace. Empirically, our proposed algorithm also succeeds in more challenging data models arising, e.g., from sparse dictionary learning.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to recover the sparsest vector contained in a given subspace. Such a vector has relatively few nonzero entries, and finding it is relevant to sparse dictionary learning, sparse PCA, and other signal-processing problems. The challenge is to recover this structure from the subspace containing it.

For a subspace of dimension n, simple convex heuristics provably break down when the target's fraction of nonzero entries substantially exceeds 1 divided by the square root of n. The authors propose a relatively simple nonconvex method based on alternating directions. Their analysis establishes recovery with a constant-order fraction of nonzero entries, reaching the linear sparsity scaling emphasized in the title.

That guarantee assumes a planted sparse model: the desired sparse vector is embedded in an otherwise random subspace. The assumption is central to the theoretical result. Experiments also show success on more challenging data models arising from sparse dictionary learning. Together, the analysis and experiments identify a setting where a practical nonconvex method goes beyond the stated recovery range of simple convex heuristics.
summary.tldr: A nonconvex alternating-directions method provably recovers vectors with linear sparsity under a planted sparse-subspace model.

title: Finding a sparse vector in a subspace: Linear sparsity using alternating directions

abstract: In this paper, we propose a Sparse Random Feature algorithm, which learns a sparse non-linear predictor by minimizing an $\ell_1$-regularized objective function over the Hilbert Space induced from kernel function. By interpreting the algorithm as Randomized Coordinate Descent in the infinite-dimensional space, we show the proposed approach converges to a solution comparable within $\eps$-precision to exact kernel method by drawing $O(1/\eps)$ number of random features, contrasted to the $O(1/\eps^2)$-type convergence achieved by Monte-Carlo analysis in current Random Feature literature. In our experiments, the Sparse Random Feature algorithm obtains sparse solution that requires less memory and prediction time while maintains comparable performance on tasks of regression and classification. In the meantime, as an approximate solver for infinite-dimensional $\ell_1$-regularized problem, the randomized approach converges to better solution than Boosting approach when the greedy step of Boosting cannot be performed exactly.

paragraphs: Kernel methods can express nonlinear predictors through a feature space that may be infinite-dimensional. This paper proposes a Sparse Random Feature algorithm that minimizes an l1-regularized objective in the Hilbert space induced by a kernel. The goal is to learn a nonlinear predictor with a sparse representation.

The authors interpret random-feature learning as randomized coordinate descent in that infinite-dimensional space. Their analysis shows convergence to a solution comparable to the exact kernel method within epsilon precision using O(1/epsilon) random features. This contrasts with the O(1/epsilon²)-type dependence obtained through the Monte Carlo analyses discussed in the abstract, giving a different theoretical account of random-feature efficiency.

In regression and classification experiments, the algorithm produces sparse solutions that use less memory and prediction time while maintaining comparable performance. It also reaches better solutions than a boosting approach when boosting's greedy step cannot be performed exactly. That comparison is conditional on inexact greedy optimization. The paper thus combines a convergence argument with evidence that sparsity can improve the practical cost of prediction.
summary.tldr: Viewing sparse random-feature learning as coordinate descent yields improved feature-count bounds and compact predictors in experiments.

title: Sparse Random Feature Algorithm as Coordinate Descent in Hilbert Space

abstract: We propose a second-order (Hessian or Hessian-free) based optimization method for variational inference inspired by Gaussian backpropagation, and argue that quasi-Newton optimization can be developed as well. This is accomplished by generalizing the gradient computation in stochastic backpropagation via a reparametrization trick with lower complexity. As an illustrative example, we apply this approach to the problems of Bayesian logistic regression and variational auto-encoder (VAE). Additionally, we compute bounds on the estimator variance of intractable expectations for the family of Lipschitz continuous function. Our method is practical, scalable and model free. We demonstrate our method on several real-world datasets and provide comparisons with other stochastic gradient methods to show substantial enhancement in convergence rates.
originalAbstract: We propose a second-order (Hessian or Hessian-free) based optimization method for variational inference inspired by Gaussian backpropagation, and argue that quasi-Newton optimization can be developed as well. This is accomplished by generalizing the gradient computation in stochastic backpropagation via a reparametrization trick with lower complexity. As an illustrative example, we apply this approach to the problems of Bayesian logistic regression and variational auto-encoder (VAE). Additionally, we compute bounds on the estimator variance of intractable expectations for the family of Lipschitz continuous function. Our method is practical, scalable and model free. We demonstrate our method on several real-world datasets and provide comparisons with other stochastic gradient methods to show substantial enhancement in convergence rates.

paragraphs: Variational inference relies on optimization to fit an approximate probabilistic model. This paper develops a way to use second-order information in that optimization, drawing inspiration from Gaussian backpropagation. Second-order methods incorporate curvature information, giving the optimizer more information about the objective than a gradient direction alone.

The authors generalize gradient computation in stochastic backpropagation through a lower-complexity reparameterization trick. Their approach supports Hessian-based or Hessian-free optimization, and they argue that it can also support quasi-Newton methods. They additionally derive variance bounds for estimators of otherwise intractable expectations when the functions involved are Lipschitz continuous.

Bayesian logistic regression and variational autoencoders illustrate the approach. Experiments on several real-world datasets show substantially improved convergence rates compared with the stochastic gradient methods considered. The paper presents the method as practical, scalable, and model free. Its main contribution is to make curvature-aware optimization accessible within stochastic variational inference, alongside theoretical analysis of estimator variability for a specified function family.
summary.tldr: Generalized stochastic backpropagation enables second-order variational inference optimization, with reported convergence improvements over compared stochastic gradient methods.

title: Fast Second Order Stochastic Backpropagation for Variational Inference

abstract: By lifting the ReLU function into a higher dimensional space, we develop a smooth multi-convex formulation for training feed-forward deep neural networks (DNNs). This allows us to develop a block coordinate descent (BCD) training algorithm consisting of a sequence of numerically well-behaved convex optimizations. Using ideas from proximal point methods in convex analysis, we prove that this BCD algorithm will converge globally to a stationary point with R-linear convergence rate of order one. In experiments with the MNIST database, DNNs trained with this BCD algorithm consistently yielded better test-set error rates than identical DNN architectures trained via all the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) variants in the Caffe toolbox.
originalAbstract: By lifting the ReLU function into a higher dimensional space, we develop a smooth multi-convex formulation for training feed-forward deep neural networks (DNNs). This allows us to develop a block coordinate descent (BCD) training algorithm consisting of a sequence of numerically well-behaved convex optimizations. Using ideas from proximal point methods in convex analysis, we prove that this BCD algorithm will converge globally to a stationary point with R-linear convergence rate of order one. In experiments with the MNIST database, DNNs trained with this BCD algorithm consistently yielded better test-set error rates than identical DNN architectures trained via all the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) variants in the Caffe toolbox.

paragraphs: This paper develops a training method for Tikhonov-regularized feed-forward neural networks by reformulating their ReLU operations in a higher-dimensional space. The resulting objective is smooth and multi-convex. This means the formulation has convex structure when particular blocks of variables are optimized while the others are held fixed.

That structure enables block coordinate descent: training proceeds through a sequence of convex optimization problems. The authors describe these subproblems as numerically well behaved. Using ideas from proximal point methods, they establish global convergence of the algorithm to a stationary point and an R-linear convergence rate of order one.

The destination of that guarantee is a stationary point, which should not be confused with a globally optimal network. The empirical comparison uses MNIST and holds the network architecture fixed across training methods. Networks trained with the proposed procedure consistently achieve lower test error than identical architectures trained with the SGD variants available in Caffe. The results therefore combine an optimization guarantee with an observed predictive benefit in that comparison.
summary.tldr: A higher-dimensional ReLU reformulation enables block coordinate training with stationary-point convergence guarantees and improved MNIST test errors.

title: Convergent Block Coordinate Descent for Training Tikhonov Regularized Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Intracortical brain-computer interfaces (iBCIs) have allowed people with tetraplegia to control a computer cursor by imagining the movement of their paralyzed arm or hand. State-of-the-art decoders deployed in human iBCIs are derived from a Kalman filter that assumes Markov dynamics on the angle of intended movement, and a unimodal dependence on intended angle for each channel of neural activity. Due to errors made in the decoding of noisy neural data, as a user attempts to move the cursor to a goal, the angle between cursor and goal positions may change rapidly. We propose a dynamic Bayesian network that includes the on-screen goal position as part of its latent state, and thus allows the person’s intended angle of movement to be aggregated over a much longer history of neural activity. This multiscale model explicitly captures the relationship between instantaneous angles of motion and long-term goals, and incorporates semi-Markov dynamics for motion trajectories. We also introduce a multimodal likelihood model for recordings of neural populations which can be rapidly calibrated for clinical applications. In offline experiments with recorded neural data, we demonstrate significantly improved prediction of motion directions compared to the Kalman filter. We derive an efficient online inference algorithm, enabling a clinical trial participant with tetraplegia to control a computer cursor with neural activity in real time. The observed kinematics of cursor movement are objectively straighter and smoother than prior iBCI decoding models without loss of responsiveness.

paragraphs: Intracortical brain-computer interfaces can translate imagined arm or hand movements into cursor control. Noisy decoding can move the cursor away from its intended path, rapidly changing the direction toward the goal. This paper addresses that problem by modeling both immediate movement direction and the longer-term destination the user is trying to reach.

The proposed dynamic Bayesian network includes the on-screen goal as a latent variable, allowing intended direction to be inferred from a longer history of neural activity. It connects instantaneous motion to persistent goals through a multiscale model with semi-Markov trajectory dynamics. A multimodal neural-activity likelihood also replaces the unimodal dependence assumed by the described Kalman-filter decoders and supports rapid calibration.

Offline experiments improve motion-direction prediction over the Kalman filter. An efficient online inference algorithm also enables real-time cursor control by a clinical trial participant with tetraplegia. Observed cursor trajectories are straighter and smoother than with prior decoding models, without reduced responsiveness. The results connect richer temporal modeling with both predictive improvements and demonstrated interactive control.
summary.tldr: A decoder that jointly models movement direction and longer-term goals enables smoother, straighter neural cursor control.

title: Multiscale Semi-Markov Dynamics for Intracortical Brain-Computer Interfaces

abstract: We introduce the variational filtering EM algorithm, a simple, general-purpose method for performing variational inference in dynamical latent variable models using information from only past and present variables, i.e. filtering. The algorithm is derived from the variational objective in the filtering setting and consists of an optimization procedure at each time step. By performing each inference optimization procedure with an iterative amortized inference model, we obtain a computationally efficient implementation of the algorithm, which we call amortized variational filtering. We present experiments demonstrating that this general-purpose method improves inference performance across several recent deep dynamical latent variable models.
originalAbstract: We introduce the variational filtering EM algorithm, a simple, general-purpose method for performing variational inference in dynamical latent variable models using information from only past and present variables, i.e. filtering. The algorithm is derived from the variational objective in the filtering setting and consists of an optimization procedure at each time step. By performing each inference optimization procedure with an iterative amortized inference model, we obtain a computationally efficient implementation of the algorithm, which we call amortized variational filtering. We present experiments demonstrating that this general-purpose method improves inference performance across several recent deep dynamical latent variable models.

paragraphs: Dynamical latent variable models describe observations through hidden quantities that evolve over time. Filtering estimates those hidden quantities using only information available up to the current moment. The paper develops a general variational inference method for this setting, keeping future variables outside the information used for each inference step.

The proposed variational filtering EM algorithm follows from the variational objective under this information restriction. It performs an optimization procedure at every time step. This gives a common starting point for inference across dynamical models: determine the current hidden-state approximation by optimizing an objective that respects what is presently known.

To make that repeated optimization computationally efficient, the authors implement it with an iterative amortized inference model. A learned inference procedure carries out the successive updates, producing the method they call amortized variational filtering. Experiments show improved inference performance across several recent deep dynamical latent variable models. These findings support the usefulness of a shared inference approach across those models while retaining the past-and-present information requirement central to filtering.
summary.tldr: Amortized variational filtering uses learned iterative inference to efficiently estimate evolving hidden states from past and present information.

title: A General Method for Amortizing Variational Filtering

abstract: An important goal common to domain adaptation and causal inference is to make accurate predictions when the distributions for the source (or training) domain(s) and target (or test) domain(s) differ. In many cases, these different distributions can be modeled as different contexts of a single underlying system, in which each distribution corresponds to a different perturbation of the system, or in causal terms, an intervention. We focus on a class of such causal domain adaptation problems, where data for one or more source domains are given, and the task is to predict the distribution of a certain target variable from measurements of other variables in one or more target domains. We propose an approach for solving these problems that exploits causal inference and does not rely on prior knowledge of the causal graph, the type of interventions or the intervention targets. We demonstrate our approach by evaluating a possible implementation on simulated and real world data.
originalAbstract: An important goal common to domain adaptation and causal inference is to make accurate predictions when the distributions for the source (or training) domain(s) and target (or test) domain(s) differ. In many cases, these different distributions can be modeled as different contexts of a single underlying system, in which each distribution corresponds to a different perturbation of the system, or in causal terms, an intervention. We focus on a class of such causal domain adaptation problems, where data for one or more source domains are given, and the task is to predict the distribution of a certain target variable from measurements of other variables in one or more target domains. We propose an approach for solving these problems that exploits causal inference and does not rely on prior knowledge of the causal graph, the type of interventions or the intervention targets. We demonstrate our approach by evaluating a possible implementation on simulated and real world data.

paragraphs: A predictor trained in one setting may encounter a different distribution when deployed elsewhere. This paper studies cases where those settings can be understood as different contexts of the same underlying system. Their differences are modeled as perturbations, or interventions in causal language, providing a structured account of why the distributions change.

The task is to use data from one or more source domains to predict the distribution of a target variable from other measurements in one or more target domains. The proposed approach uses causal inference to address this transfer problem. It does not require prior knowledge of the causal graph, the kinds of interventions, or which variables the interventions affect.

This matters because those causal details may be unavailable even when several contexts share an underlying system. The approach applies to the class of causal domain adaptation problems studied, rather than establishing a solution for arbitrary distribution changes. The authors evaluate one possible implementation on simulated and real-world data, demonstrating how the proposed causal perspective can be put into practice.
summary.tldr: A causal approach transfers predictions across intervention-related domains without requiring prior knowledge of their causal graph or interventions.

title: Domain Adaptation by Using Causal Inference to Predict Invariant Conditional Distributions

abstract: Channel pruning is one of the predominant approaches for deep model compression. Existing pruning methods either train from scratch with sparsity constraints on channels, or minimize the reconstruction error between the pre-trained feature maps and the compressed ones. Both strategies suffer from some limitations: the former kind is computationally expensive and difficult to converge, whilst the latter kind optimizes the reconstruction error but ignores the discriminative power of channels. To overcome these drawbacks, we investigate a simple-yet-effective method, called discrimination-aware channel pruning, to choose those channels that really contribute to discriminative power. To this end, we introduce additional losses into the network to increase the discriminative power of intermediate layers and then select the most discriminative channels for each layer by considering the additional loss and the reconstruction error. Last, we propose a greedy algorithm to conduct channel selection and parameter optimization in an iterative way. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. For example, on ILSVRC-12, our pruned ResNet-50 with 30% reduction of channels even outperforms the original model by 0.39% in top-1 accuracy.

This example shows that their task-aware selection can remove substantial channel capacity while preserving, and in this case improving, measured classification performance.
summary.tldr: Discrimination-aware pruning selects channels for their contribution to classification as well as feature reconstruction, enabling effective network compression.

title: Discrimination-aware Channel Pruning for Deep Neural Networks

abstract: This paper presents the Poisson-randomized gamma dynamical system (PRGDS), a model for sequentially observed count tensors that encodes a strong inductive bias toward sparsity and burstiness. The PRGDS is based on a new motif in Bayesian latent variable modeling, an alternating chain of discrete Poisson and continuous gamma latent states that is analytically convenient and computationally tractable. This motif yields closed-form complete conditionals for all variables by way of the Bessel distribution and a novel discrete distribution that we call the shifted confluent hypergeometric distribution. We draw connections to closely related models and compare the PRGDS to these models in studies of real-world count data sets of text, international events, and neural spike trains. We find that a sparse variant of the PRGDS, which allows the continuous gamma latent states to take values of exactly zero, often obtains better predictive performance than other models and is uniquely capable of inferring latent structures that are highly localized in time.

The model represents evolving hidden structure through an alternating sequence of discrete Poisson states and continuous gamma states.

It yields closed-form conditional distributions for every variable using the Bessel distribution and a newly introduced shifted confluent hypergeometric distribution. Exact-zero states are thus tied to the model’s ability to represent sharply localized activity.
summary.tldr: Alternating Poisson and gamma hidden states provide tractable modeling of sparse, bursty count data and temporally localized structure.

title: Poisson-Randomized Gamma Dynamical Systems

abstract: Algorithmic machine teaching studies the interaction between a teacher and a learner where the teacher selects labeled examples aiming at teaching a target hypothesis. In a quest to lower teaching complexity and to achieve more natural teacher-learner interactions, several teaching models and complexity measures have been proposed for both the batch settings (e.g., worst-case, recursive, preference-based, and non-clashing models) as well as the sequential settings (e.g., local preference-based model). To better understand the connections between these different batch and sequential models, we develop a novel framework which captures the teaching process via preference functions $\Sigma$. In our framework, each function $\sigma \in \Sigma$ induces a teacher-learner pair with teaching complexity as $\TD(\sigma)$. We show that the above-mentioned teaching models are equivalent to specific types/families of preference functions in our framework. This equivalence, in turn, allows us to study the differences between two important teaching models, namely $\sigma$ functions inducing the strongest batch (i.e., non-clashing) model and $\sigma$ functions inducing a weak sequential (i.e., local preference-based) model. Finally, we identify preference functions inducing a novel family of sequential models with teaching complexity linear in the VC dimension of the hypothesis class: this is in contrast to the best known complexity result for the batch models which is quadratic in the VC dimension.

paragraphs: Algorithmic machine teaching asks how a teacher should select labeled examples to lead a learner toward a target hypothesis. Different models describe teaching through a batch of examples or through a sequence of interactions. This paper introduces a common language for comparing those models using functions that express learner preferences.

Each preference function determines a teacher–learner pair and an associated teaching complexity. The authors show that several established batch and sequential models correspond to particular families of these functions. This equivalence allows differences between models to be studied within one framework, including the strongest batch model considered and a weak sequential model based on local preferences.

The authors also identify a new family of sequential models whose teaching complexity grows linearly with the hypothesis class's VC dimension, a measure of its expressive capacity. They contrast this with the best known quadratic complexity result for batch models. The finding establishes a favorable bound for the identified sequential family; the comparison is with known batch results, rather than a proof that every batch model must require quadratic complexity.
summary.tldr: A preference-function framework unifies teaching models and identifies sequential models with teaching complexity linear in VC dimension.

title: Preference-Based Batch and Sequential Teaching: Towards a Unified View of Models

abstract: Belief propagation is a fundamental message-passing algorithm for probabilistic reasoning and inference in graphical models. While it is known to be exact on trees, in most applications belief propagation is run on graphs with cycles. Understanding the behavior of loopy'' belief propagation has been a major challenge for researchers in machine learning, and several positive convergence results for BP are known under strong assumptions which imply the underlying graphical model exhibits decay of correlations. We show that under a natural initialization, BP converges quickly to the global optimum of the Bethe free energy for Ising models on arbitrary graphs, as long as the Ising model is \emph{ferromagnetic} (i.e. neighbors prefer to be aligned). This holds even though such models can exhibit long range correlations and may have multiple suboptimal BP fixed points. We also show an analogous result for iterating the (naive) mean-field equations; perhaps surprisingly, both results are dimension-free'' in the sense that a constant number of iterations already provides a good estimate to the Bethe/mean-field free energy.

paragraphs: Belief propagation performs probabilistic inference by passing messages through a graph. Its behavior is well understood on trees, but cycles make convergence much harder to analyze. Earlier positive results often rely on assumptions ensuring that distant variables have progressively weaker influence on each other, a property called decay of correlations.

This paper proves fast convergence under a different set of conditions. For ferromagnetic Ising models, in which neighboring variables prefer alignment, belief propagation reaches the global optimum of the Bethe free energy from a natural initialization, even on arbitrary graphs. The result permits long-range correlations and the presence of other, suboptimal fixed points, so neither phenomenon by itself rules out the stated convergence.

The authors also establish an analogous result for iterative mean-field equations. Both results are dimension-free in the stated sense that a constant number of iterations gives a good estimate of the corresponding free energy. The guarantee concerns these variational objectives under the specified model and initialization conditions; it does not assert that loopy belief propagation becomes exact probabilistic inference on every graph.
summary.tldr: For ferromagnetic Ising models under a natural initialization, belief propagation quickly optimizes Bethe free energy even when long-range correlations persist.

title: Fast Convergence of Belief Propagation to Global Optima: Beyond Correlation Decay

abstract: We study quadrature rules for functions living in an RKHS, using nodes sampled from a projection determinantal point process (DPP). DPPs are parametrized by a kernel, and we use a truncated and saturated version of the RKHS kernel. This natural link between the two kernels, along with DPP machinery, leads to relatively tight bounds on the quadrature error, that depends on the spectrum of the RKHS kernel. Finally, we experimentally compare DPPs to existing kernel-based quadratures such as herding, Bayesian quadrature, or continuous leverage score sampling. Numerical results confirm the interest of DPPs, and even suggest faster rates than our bounds in particular cases.

paragraphs: Quadrature approximates an integral using function values at selected points. This paper studies that problem for functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, or RKHS, where a kernel specifies the function space’s structure. The main question is how to choose evaluation points and relate the resulting integration error to that structure.

The authors sample points using a projection determinantal point process, or DPP. They construct its kernel from a truncated and saturated version of the RKHS kernel. This connection between the sampling mechanism and the function space lets them derive relatively tight error bounds that depend on the spectrum of the original kernel.

The numerical results support the usefulness of DPP-based quadrature and suggest convergence faster than the theoretical bounds in some cases. That distinction matters: the bounds provide analytical guarantees, while the faster rates are observations from particular numerical settings.
summary.tldr: Sampling quadrature points with a DPP tied to the function-space kernel yields spectral error bounds and promising numerical performance.

title: Kernel quadrature with DPPs

abstract: We examine Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) through the lens of deep Energy Based Models (EBMs), with the goal of exploiting the density model that follows from this formulation. In contrast to a traditional view where the discriminator learns a constant function when reaching convergence, here we show that it can provide useful information for downstream tasks, e.g., feature extraction for classification. To be concrete, in the EBM formulation, the discriminator learns an unnormalized density function (i.e., the negative energy term) that characterizes the data manifold. We propose to evaluate both the generator and the discriminator by deriving corresponding Fisher Score and Fisher Information from the EBM. We show that by assuming that the generated examples form an estimate of the learned density, both the Fisher Information and the normalized Fisher Vectors are easy to compute. We also show that we are able to derive a distance metric between examples and between sets of examples. We conduct experiments showing that the GAN-induced Fisher Vectors demonstrate competitive performance as unsupervised feature extractors for classification and perceptual similarity tasks. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/apple/ml-afv}.

summary.tldr: An energy-based interpretation of GANs yields Fisher Vector features with competitive performance on classification and perceptual similarity tasks.

title: Adversarial Fisher Vectors for Unsupervised Representation Learning

abstract: Filter pruning is one of the most effective ways to accelerate and compress convolutional neural networks (CNNs). In this work, we propose a global filter pruning algorithm called Gate Decorator, which transforms a vanilla CNN module by multiplying its output by the channel-wise scaling factors (i.e. gate). When the scaling factor is set to zero, it is equivalent to removing the corresponding filter. We use Taylor expansion to estimate the change in the loss function caused by setting the scaling factor to zero and use the estimation for the global filter importance ranking. Then we prune the network by removing those unimportant filters. After pruning, we merge all the scaling factors into its original module, so no special operations or structures are introduced. Moreover, we propose an iterative pruning framework called Tick-Tock to improve pruning accuracy. The extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approaches. For example, we achieve the state-of-the-art pruning ratio on ResNet-56 by reducing 70% FLOPs without noticeable loss in accuracy. For ResNet-50 on ImageNet, our pruned model with 40% FLOPs reduction outperforms the baseline model by 0.31% in top-1 accuracy. Various datasets are used, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CUB-200, ImageNet ILSVRC-12 and PASCAL VOC 2011.

paragraphs: Gate Decorator reduces the computation and size of convolutional networks by identifying filters that can be removed. It attaches a scaling factor, or gate, to each output channel. Setting a gate to zero has the same effect as removing the corresponding filter, giving the method a direct way to estimate the consequences of pruning.

The algorithm uses a Taylor expansion to approximate how zeroing each gate would change the loss. These estimates form a global importance ranking, and filters judged unimportant are removed. An iterative framework called Tick-Tock improves pruning accuracy. Once pruning is complete, the remaining scaling factors are absorbed into the original modules, so the finished network needs no special gate operations or structures.

The reported experiments cover several datasets and network settings. On ResNet-56, the method reduces floating-point operations by 70% without a noticeable accuracy loss. On ImageNet with ResNet-50, a 40% reduction accompanies a reported 0.31% top-1 accuracy improvement over the baseline. These examples show substantial computational reductions while retaining or improving accuracy in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Gate Decorator ranks filters by estimated loss impact and removes low-importance filters, substantially reducing computation in the reported experiments.

title: Gate Decorator: Global Filter Pruning Method for Accelerating Deep Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: We propose a novel confidence metric, namely, attribution-based confidence (ABC) for deep neural networks (DNNs). ABC metric characterizes whether the output of a DNN on an input can be trusted. DNNs are known to be brittle on inputs outside the training distribution and are, hence, susceptible to adversarial attacks. This fragility is compounded by a lack of effectively computable measures of model confidence that correlate well with the accuracy of DNNs. These factors have impeded the adoption of DNNs in high-assurance systems. The proposed ABC metric addresses these challenges. It does not require access to the training data, the use of ensembles, or the need to train a calibration model on a held-out validation set. Hence, the new metric is usable even when only a trained model is available for inference. We mathematically motivate the proposed metric and evaluate its effectiveness with two sets of experiments. First, we study the change in accuracy and the associated confidence over out-of-distribution inputs. Second, we consider several digital and physically realizable attacks such as FGSM, CW, DeepFool, PGD, and adversarial patch generation methods. The ABC metric is low on out-of-distribution data and adversarial examples, where the accuracy of the model is also low. These experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the ABC metric to make DNNs more trustworthy and resilient.
