This paper proposes attribution-based confidence, or ABC, as a measure of whether a particular output should be trusted. The aim is to obtain a confidence signal that follows changes in prediction accuracy.

A practical feature is that ABC can be used when only the trained network is available. It requires neither the original training data nor an ensemble of models, and it does not require fitting a separate calibration model on validation examples. The authors give a mathematical motivation for the metric and evaluate its behavior in two groups of experiments.

The experiments examine inputs outside the training distribution and several digital or physically realizable adversarial attacks. In these evaluations, ABC is low where model accuracy is also low. This supports its use as an indicator of unreliable predictions in the studied settings, providing information about trustworthiness without the additional training resources required by some confidence-estimation approaches.
summary.tldr: ABC estimates prediction confidence from a trained network alone and shows low confidence on tested inputs where accuracy deteriorates.

title: Attribution-Based Confidence Metric For Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Learning meaningful and compact representations with disentangled semantic aspects is considered to be of key importance in representation learning. Since real-world data is notoriously costly to collect, many recent state-of-the-art disentanglement models have heavily relied on synthetic toy data-sets. In this paper, we propose a novel data-set which consists of over 1 million images of physical 3D objects with seven factors of variation, such as object color, shape, size and position. In order to be able to control all the factors of variation precisely, we built an experimental platform where the objects are being moved by a robotic arm. In addition, we provide two more datasets which consist of simulations of the experimental setup. These datasets provide for the first time the possibility to systematically investigate how well different disentanglement methods perform on real data in comparison to simulation, and how simulated data can be leveraged to build better representations of the real world. We provide a first experimental study of these questions and our results indicate that learned models transfer poorly, but that model and hyperparameter selection is an effective means of transferring information to the real world.

Much disentanglement research relies on synthetic toy datasets because collecting real observations is expensive. The authors create a controlled physical setting that allows the relationship between simulation and real-world representation learning to be examined systematically.

A robotic arm moves the objects so that the factors can be controlled precisely. The datasets make it possible to investigate both routes under controlled variation.
summary.tldr: Controlled real and simulated object datasets show poor direct model transfer but useful transfer through model and hyperparameter selection.

title: On the Transfer of Inductive Bias from Simulation to the Real World: a New Disentanglement Dataset

abstract: Model-agnostic meta-learners aim to acquire meta-learned parameters from similar tasks to adapt to novel tasks from the same distribution with few gradient updates. With the flexibility in the choice of models, those frameworks demonstrate appealing performance on a variety of domains such as few-shot image classification and reinforcement learning. However, one important limitation of such frameworks is that they seek a common initialization shared across the entire task distribution, substantially limiting the diversity of the task distributions that they are able to learn from. In this paper, we augment MAML with the capability to identify the mode of tasks sampled from a multimodal task distribution and adapt quickly through gradient updates. Specifically, we propose a multimodal MAML (MMAML) framework, which is able to modulate its meta-learned prior parameters according to the identified mode, allowing more efficient fast adaptation. We evaluate the proposed model on a diverse set of few-shot learning tasks, including regression, image classification, and reinforcement learning. The results not only demonstrate the effectiveness of our model in modulating the meta-learned prior in response to the characteristics of tasks but also show that training on a multimodal distribution can produce an improvement over unimodal training. The code for this project is publicly available at https://vuoristo.github.io/MMAML.

paragraphs: Model-agnostic meta-learning seeks parameters that can adapt to a new task after a few gradient updates. A shared initialization works toward that goal across related tasks, but a single starting point can restrict the diversity of tasks the method handles. This paper considers task distributions containing multiple modes, or different groups of task characteristics.

The proposed MMAML framework augments MAML by identifying the mode of a sampled task and modulating its meta-learned prior parameters accordingly. Gradient-based adaptation then proceeds from that adjusted starting point. The mechanism separates recognizing what kind of task is present from the subsequent rapid parameter updates, allowing the initial parameters to respond to task characteristics.

Evaluations cover few-shot regression, image classification, and reinforcement learning. The results support the effectiveness of the modulation mechanism and show that training across a multimodal task distribution can improve performance over unimodal training. This is an empirical possibility demonstrated by the study, rather than a guarantee that increasing task diversity always improves adaptation.
summary.tldr: MMAML adjusts meta-learned starting parameters to a task's identified mode, enabling effective few-shot adaptation across diverse task distributions.

title: Multimodal Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning via Task-Aware Modulation

abstract: Multi-agent Imitation learning (MAIL) refers to the problem that agents learn to perform a task interactively in a multi-agent system through observing and mimicking expert demonstrations, without any knowledge of a reward function from the environment. MAIL has received a lot of attention due to promising results achieved on synthesized tasks, with the potential to be applied to complex real-world multi-agent tasks. Key challenges for MAIL include sample efficiency and scalability. In this paper, we proposed Bayesian multi-type mean field multi-agent imitation learning (BM3IL). Our method improves sample efficiency through establishing a Bayesian formulation for MAIL, and enhances scalability through introducing a new multi-type mean field approximation. We demonstrate the performance of our algorithm through benchmarking with three state-of-the-art multi-agent imitation learning algorithms on several tasks, including solving a multi-agent traffic optimization problem in a real-world transportation network. Experimental results indicate that our algorithm significantly outperforms all other algorithms in all scenarios.

Experimental results indicate that our algorithm significantly outperforms all other algorithms in all scenarios.

paragraphs: Multi-agent imitation learning asks interacting agents to learn a task from expert demonstrations without receiving an environmental reward function. Learning becomes difficult when demonstrations must support many agents whose actions affect one another. This paper focuses on two linked challenges: using samples efficiently and keeping the learning approach scalable.

The proposed method, BM3IL, combines a Bayesian formulation of imitation learning with a multi-type mean field approximation. The Bayesian component is introduced to improve sample efficiency. The approximation addresses scalability by representing interactions through aggregate effects while distinguishing multiple agent types. Together, these components provide a framework for learning coordinated behavior from demonstrations.

The authors compare BM3IL with three leading multi-agent imitation learning algorithms across several tasks. These include traffic optimization on a real-world transportation network. They report significant improvements over every comparison method in all tested scenarios. These results support the combined approach in the evaluated settings, including a transportation application that goes beyond the synthesized tasks motivating much prior work.
summary.tldr: BM3IL combines Bayesian learning and multi-type mean field approximations to improve sample efficiency and scalability in multi-agent imitation.

title: Bayesian Multi-type Mean Field Multi-agent Imitation Learning

abstract: Much of the remarkable progress in computer vision has been focused around fully supervised learning mechanisms relying on highly curated datasets for a variety of tasks. In contrast, humans often learn about their world with little to no external supervision. Taking inspiration from infants learning from their environment through play and interaction, we present a computational framework to discover objects and learn their physical properties along this paradigm of Learning from Interaction. Our agent, when placed within the near photo-realistic and physics-enabled AI2-THOR environment, interacts with its world and learns about objects, their geometric extents and relative masses, without any external guidance. Our experiments reveal that this agent learns efficiently and effectively; not just for objects it has interacted with before, but also for novel instances from seen categories as well as novel object categories.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how an agent can learn about objects by acting in its environment. The proposed framework pursues object learning without external guidance, making interaction itself central to how the agent acquires knowledge.

The agent operates in AI2-THOR, an environment that combines near-photorealistic appearance with simulated physics. Through interaction, it learns to discover objects, identify their geometric extents, and estimate relative masses. These targets cover both where an object extends in space and how its physical properties compare with those of other objects.

The experiments report efficient and effective learning that extends beyond objects the agent has already encountered. The agent also learns about new instances from familiar categories and objects from unfamiliar categories. This generalization is central to the result: the learned knowledge is useful beyond the specific objects involved in earlier interactions. The demonstrated setting is a physics-enabled simulated environment, where the authors test whether interaction can support broader visual and physical understanding.
summary.tldr: An agent learns object boundaries and relative masses through unguided interaction, generalizing to unfamiliar objects in simulation.

title: Learning About Objects by Learning to Interact with Them

abstract: Navigation tasks in photorealistic 3D environments are challenging because they require perception and effective planning under partial observability. Recent work shows that map-like memory is useful for long-horizon navigation tasks. However, a focused investigation of the impact of maps on navigation tasks of varying complexity has not yet been performed. We propose the multiON task, which requires navigation to an episode-specific sequence of objects in a realistic environment. MultiON generalizes the ObjectGoal navigation task and explicitly tests the ability of navigation agents to locate previously observed goal objects. We perform a set of multiON experiments to examine how a variety of agent models perform across a spectrum of navigation task complexities. Our experiments show that: i) navigation performance degrades dramatically with escalating task complexity; ii) a simple semantic map agent performs surprisingly well relative to more complex neural image feature map agents; and iii) even oracle map agents achieve relatively low performance, indicating the potential for future work in training embodied navigation agents using maps.

paragraphs: An agent navigating a realistic environment sees only part of its surroundings at a time, making memory important for longer tasks. MultiON tests that memory by requiring navigation to a sequence of objects specified for each episode. It extends single-object navigation and explicitly asks agents to find goal objects they have previously observed.

The benchmark lets the authors compare agent models as navigation tasks become more complex. Its focus is the role of map-like memory: remembering what was seen and where it was located should help when a later goal refers to an earlier observation. The experiments compare several ways of representing that information.

Performance drops sharply as complexity increases. A simple semantic-map agent performs surprisingly well relative to more complex agents whose maps contain neural image features. Even agents with oracle maps achieve relatively low performance. Together, these findings show that richer map representations do not automatically produce better navigation, and that effectively using map information remains a substantial challenge in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: MultiON tests memory through sequential object navigation and finds that increasing complexity challenges even agents equipped with oracle maps.

title: MultiON: Benchmarking Semantic Map Memory using Multi-Object Navigation

abstract: We investigate the exploration of an unknown environment when no reward function is provided. Building on the incremental exploration setting introduced by Lim and Auer [1], we define the objective of learning the set of $\epsilon$-optimal goal-conditioned policies attaining all states that are incrementally reachable within $L$ steps (in expectation) from a reference state $s_0$. In this paper, we introduce a novel model-based approach that interleaves discovering new states from $s_0$ and improving the accuracy of a model estimate that is used to compute goal-conditioned policies to reach newly discovered states. The resulting algorithm, DisCo, achieves a sample complexity scaling as $\tilde{O}(L^5 S_{L+\epsilon} \Gamma_{L+\epsilon} A \epsilon^{-2})$, where $A$ is the number of actions, $S_{L+\epsilon}$ is the number of states that are incrementally reachable from $s_0$ in $L+\epsilon$ steps, and $\Gamma_{L+\epsilon}$ is the branching factor of the dynamics over such states. This improves over the algorithm proposed in [1] in both $\epsilon$ and $L$ at the cost of an extra $\Gamma_{L+\epsilon}$ factor, which is small in most environments of interest. Furthermore, DisCo is the first algorithm that can return an $\epsilon/c_{\min}$-optimal policy for any cost-sensitive shortest-path problem defined on the $L$-reachable states with minimum cost $c_{\min}$. Finally, we report preliminary empirical results confirming our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: An agent exploring without a reward function still needs a useful learning objective. This paper asks it to learn near-optimal policies for reaching every state that is incrementally reachable within an expected step budget from a reference state. The resulting knowledge describes where the agent can go and how to get there before a particular reward-driven task is supplied.

It uses that model to compute goal-conditioned policies for newly discovered destinations. Its sample-complexity bound improves the dependence on the step budget and accuracy requirement relative to the earlier incremental exploration algorithm, while adding a factor for the dynamics’ branching structure.

That tradeoff is favorable when the branching factor is small, as the authors say it is in many environments of interest. DisCo also supports cost-sensitive shortest-path tasks on the reachable states, with a policy optimality guarantee that depends on the minimum cost. Preliminary experiments support the theoretical findings, linking reward-free exploration to reusable knowledge for later navigation objectives.
summary.tldr: DisCo learns reusable goal-reaching policies without rewards, improving exploration bounds while introducing a dependence on the environment’s branching factor.

title: Improved Sample Complexity for Incremental Autonomous Exploration in MDPs

abstract: Recent Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms making use of Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization as a core component have shown outstanding performance. Yet, only little is understood theoretically about why KL regularization helps, so far. We study KL regularization within an approximate value iteration scheme and show that it implicitly averages q-values. Leveraging this insight, we provide a very strong performance bound, the very first to combine two desirable aspects: a linear dependency to the horizon (instead of quadratic) and an error propagation term involving an averaging effect of the estimation errors (instead of an accumulation effect). We also study the more general case of an additional entropy regularizer. The resulting abstract scheme encompasses many existing RL algorithms. Some of our assumptions do not hold with neural networks, so we complement this theoretical analysis with an extensive empirical study.

paragraphs: KL regularization is central to several successful reinforcement learning algorithms, but its theoretical benefits have been less clear. This paper studies it within approximate value iteration, where estimated action values guide learning. The main insight is that KL regularization implicitly averages q-values, revealing a mechanism behind its effect on the learning process.

Using that connection, the authors derive a performance bound combining two desirable properties. Its dependence on the horizon is linear instead of quadratic, and its error-propagation term averages estimation errors instead of accumulating them. Together, these features give a stronger account of how repeated estimation errors affect performance over a long decision horizon.

Some assumptions used in the theory do not hold for neural networks, so the authors complement the mathematical work with an extensive empirical study. The theoretical result therefore explains a benefit within its assumptions, while the experiments investigate the broader practical setting.
summary.tldr: KL regularization implicitly averages action values, yielding a performance bound with linear horizon dependence and averaged estimation errors.

title: Leverage the Average: an Analysis of KL Regularization in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Clustering ensemble is one of the most important problems in ensemble learning. Though it has been extensively studied in the past decades, the existing methods often suffer from the issues like high computational complexity and the difficulty on understanding the consensus. In this paper, we study the more general soft clustering ensemble problem where each individual solution is a soft clustering. We connect it to the well-known discrete Wasserstein barycenter problem in geometry. Based on some novel geometric insights in high dimensions, we propose the sampling-based algorithms with provable quality guarantees. We also provide the systematical analysis on the consensus of our model. Finally, we conduct the experiments to evaluate our proposed algorithms.

paragraphs: A clustering ensemble combines several clustering solutions into a shared consensus. This paper considers the more general case in which each input is a soft clustering, allowing graded membership rather than a single assignment for every item. Existing ensemble methods can be expensive to compute and can make the resulting consensus difficult to understand.

The authors connect this problem to a discrete Wasserstein barycenter, giving the combination of soft clusterings a geometric formulation. The title specifies a k-sparse barycenter formulation. Using insights about high-dimensional geometry, they develop sampling-based algorithms with provable quality guarantees. The approach therefore couples an interpretation of the consensus with a theoretically supported way to compute it.

The paper also provides a systematic analysis of the model's consensus and evaluates the algorithms experimentally. Its stated contribution is the connection between soft clustering ensembles and geometric averaging, together with algorithmic guarantees. This offers a framework for examining both the computational procedure and what agreement among multiple soft clustering solutions means.
summary.tldr: A Wasserstein-barycenter formulation supports sampling-based soft clustering ensemble algorithms with provable quality guarantees and an analysis of their consensus.

title: Solving Soft Clustering Ensemble via $k$-Sparse Discrete Wasserstein Barycenter

abstract: Temporal abstraction in reinforcement learning (RL), offers the promise of improving generalization and knowledge transfer in complex environments, by propagating information more efficiently over time. Although option learning was initially formulated in a way that allows updating many options simultaneously, using off-policy, intra-option learning (Sutton, Precup & Singh, 1999) , many of the recent hierarchical reinforcement learning approaches only update a single option at a time: the option currently executing. We revisit and extend intra-option learning in the context of deep reinforcement learning, in order to enable updating all options consistent with current primitive action choices, without introducing any additional estimates. Our method can therefore be naturally adopted in most hierarchical RL frameworks. When we combine our approach with the option-critic algorithm for option discovery, we obtain significant improvements in performance and data-efficiency across a wide variety of domains.

paragraphs: In hierarchical reinforcement learning, options represent behavior that unfolds over time rather than a single primitive action. Such temporal abstraction offers a way to propagate information more efficiently and potentially support generalization and transfer. Yet many recent methods update only the option currently being executed, leaving other options unable to learn from the same experience.

This paper revisits intra-option learning in deep reinforcement learning. Its approach updates every option consistent with the primitive action currently chosen, without introducing additional estimates. One interaction can therefore inform multiple compatible options. The authors describe the method as naturally usable within most hierarchical reinforcement-learning frameworks.

The authors combine the approach with option-critic, an algorithm for discovering options, and report significant improvements in performance and data efficiency across varied domains. The findings support the value of making broader use of existing experience during option learning. The reported gains concern this tested combination, while compatibility with other hierarchical frameworks motivates the method's wider usefulness.
summary.tldr: Updating all options compatible with an observed action improves performance and data efficiency when combined with option-critic.

title: Flexible Option Learning

abstract: In this work, we consider the problem of sequence-to-sequence alignment for signals containing outliers. Assuming the absence of outliers, the standard Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) algorithm efficiently computes the optimal alignment between two (generally) variable-length sequences. While DTW is robust to temporal shifts and dilations of the signal, it fails to align sequences in a meaningful way in the presence of outliers that can be arbitrarily interspersed in the sequences. To address this problem, we introduce Drop-DTW, a novel algorithm that aligns the common signal between the sequences while automatically dropping the outlier elements from the matching. The entire procedure is implemented as a single dynamic program that is efficient and fully differentiable. In our experiments, we show that Drop-DTW is a robust similarity measure for sequence retrieval and demonstrate its effectiveness as a training loss on diverse applications. With Drop-DTW, we address temporal step localization on instructional videos, representation learning from noisy videos, and cross-modal representation learning for audio-visual retrieval and localization. In all applications, we take a weakly- or unsupervised approach and demonstrate state-of-the-art results under these settings.

paragraphs: Aligning two sequences means determining which elements correspond, even when the sequences have different lengths or unfold at different speeds. Dynamic Time Warping handles timing shifts and stretching, but unrelated elements scattered through either sequence can undermine the resulting alignment. This paper addresses that problem directly.

Drop-DTW jointly aligns the shared signal and excludes elements treated as outliers. Both decisions are handled within one efficient dynamic program, so dropping elements is part of finding the alignment. The procedure is also fully differentiable, allowing it to serve as a training loss as well as a measure of similarity between sequences.

These include locating instructional steps in videos, learning representations from noisy videos, and connecting audio with visual content for retrieval and localization. The reported state-of-the-art results apply to the weakly supervised or unsupervised settings studied. They show how handling unmatched content within alignment can benefit both comparison and representation learning.
summary.tldr: Drop-DTW aligns shared sequence content while excluding outliers, providing a differentiable similarity measure and training loss.

title: Drop-DTW: Aligning Common Signal Between Sequences While Dropping Outliers

abstract: We study the Riemannian gradient method for PCA on which a crucial fact is that despite the simplicity of the considered setting, i.e., deterministic version of Krasulina's method, the convergence rate has not been well-understood yet. In this work, we provide a general tight analysis for the gap-dependent rate at $O(\frac{1}{\Delta}\log\frac{1}{\epsilon})$ that holds for any real symmetric matrix. More importantly, when the gap $\Delta$ is significantly smaller than the target accuracy $\epsilon$ on the objective sub-optimality of the final solution, the rate of this type is actually not tight any more, which calls for a worst-case rate. We further give the first worst-case analysis that achieves a rate of convergence at $O(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\log\frac{1}{\epsilon})$. The two analyses naturally roll out a comprehensively tight convergence rate at $O(\frac{1}{\max\{\Delta,\epsilon\}}\hskip-.3em\log\frac{1}{\epsilon})$. Particularly, our gap-dependent analysis suggests a new promising learning rate for stochastic variance reduced PCA algorithms. Experiments are conducted to confirm our findings as well.

paragraphs: This paper studies how quickly a Riemannian gradient method solves principal component analysis. The algorithm is a deterministic version of Krasulina’s method. Although the setting is relatively simple, its convergence rate had remained incompletely understood. The authors analyze how the required optimization effort depends jointly on the spectral gap and the desired accuracy.

Their gap-dependent bound scales as O((1/Δ) log(1/ε)), where Δ is the gap and ε measures objective suboptimality. The analysis applies to any real symmetric matrix. However, when the gap is much smaller than the requested accuracy, this expression no longer gives a tight description. The authors therefore also establish a worst-case rate of O((1/ε) log(1/ε)).

Together, these results yield a tight combined rate of O((1/max{Δ, ε}) log(1/ε)). This explains why an extremely small gap need not dictate the convergence cost at a coarser target accuracy. The analysis also suggests a promising learning-rate choice for stochastic variance-reduced PCA algorithms, and the reported experiments support the theoretical findings.
summary.tldr: A tight analysis shows how the spectral gap and target accuracy jointly govern gradient descent convergence for PCA.

title: A Comprehensively Tight Analysis of Gradient Descent for PCA

abstract: Learning disentangled representations for user intentions from multi-feedback (i.e., positive and negative feedback) can enhance the accuracy and explainability of recommendation algorithms. However, learning such disentangled representations from multi-feedback data is challenging because i) multi-feedback is complex: there exist complex relations among different types of feedback (e.g., click, unclick, and dislike, etc) as well as various user intentions, and ii) multi-feedback is noisy: there exists noisy (useless) information both in features and labels, which may deteriorate the recommendation performance. Existing works on disentangled representation learning only focus on positive feedback, failing to handle the complex relations and noise hidden in multi-feedback data. To solve this problem, in this work we propose a Curriculum Disentangled Recommendation (CDR) model that is capable of efficiently learning disentangled representations from complex and noisy multi-feedback for better recommendation. Concretely, we design a co-filtering dynamic routing mechanism that simultaneously captures the complex relations among different behavioral feedback and user intentions as well as denoise the representations in the feature level. We then present an adjustable self-evaluating curriculum that is able to evaluate sample difficulties for better model training and conduct denoising in the label level via disregarding useless information. Our extensive experiments on several real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed CDR model can significantly outperform several state-of-the-art methods in terms of recommendation accuracy.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems can receive several kinds of feedback, including clicks, missing clicks, and dislikes. These signals have complex relationships with the intentions behind a user's behavior. The paper studies how to learn representations that separate those intentions while handling noise in both input features and feedback labels. Methods focused only on positive feedback leave these additional relationships and noise sources unaddressed.

The proposed Curriculum Disentangled Recommendation model combines two mechanisms. A co-filtering dynamic routing mechanism learns relationships among feedback types and user intentions while removing noise from feature representations. An adjustable, self-evaluating curriculum estimates the difficulty of training examples and disregards useless information at the label level. The two components therefore address different places where noise enters learning.

Experiments on several real-world datasets show significant recommendation-accuracy improvements over several state-of-the-art methods. The findings support treating varied feedback as structured evidence about user intentions while also filtering unreliable information. Although separating intentions motivates potential explainability benefits, the stated experimental finding concerns improved recommendation accuracy.
summary.tldr: CDR learns separate user intentions from varied feedback by combining feature denoising with a curriculum that filters noisy labels.

title: Curriculum Disentangled Recommendation with Noisy Multi-feedback

abstract: Normalizing flows are invertible neural networks with tractable change-of-volume terms, which allow optimization of their parameters to be efficiently performed via maximum likelihood. However, data of interest are typically assumed to live in some (often unknown) low-dimensional manifold embedded in a high-dimensional ambient space. The result is a modelling mismatch since -- by construction -- the invertibility requirement implies high-dimensional support of the learned distribution. Injective flows, mappings from low- to high-dimensional spaces, aim to fix this discrepancy by learning distributions on manifolds, but the resulting volume-change term becomes more challenging to evaluate. Current approaches either avoid computing this term entirely using various heuristics, or assume the manifold is known beforehand and therefore are not widely applicable. Instead, we propose two methods to tractably calculate the gradient of this term with respect to the parameters of the model, relying on careful use of automatic differentiation and techniques from numerical linear algebra. Both approaches perform end-to-end nonlinear manifold learning and density estimation for data projected onto this manifold. We study the trade-offs between our proposed methods, empirically verify that we outperform approaches ignoring the volume-change term by more accurately learning manifolds and the corresponding distributions on them, and show promising results on out-of-distribution detection. Our code is available at https://github.com/layer6ai-labs/rectangular-flows.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows make likelihood-based learning tractable through invertible transformations. However, their full-dimensional distributions can mismatch data assumed to lie on a lower-dimensional manifold within the observation space. Injective flows address that mismatch by mapping a lower-dimensional space into a higher-dimensional one, but their volume-change term is harder to evaluate.

The paper proposes two methods for computing gradients of that volume-change term with respect to model parameters. Both use automatic differentiation and numerical linear algebra. This enables end-to-end learning of a nonlinear manifold together with a density for data projected onto it. Accounting for volume change is central because the geometry of the mapping affects the resulting density.

The authors study the trade-offs between their two methods and compare them with approaches that ignore the volume-change term. Experiments show more accurate learning of both manifolds and their associated distributions. Results on out-of-distribution detection are described as promising. The contribution is a tractable route to jointly learning geometry and density without assuming the manifold is already known.
summary.tldr: Rectangular flows make volume-change gradients tractable for jointly learning low-dimensional manifolds and probability distributions on them.

title: Rectangular Flows for Manifold Learning

abstract: Lipschitz constants are connected to many properties of neural networks, such as robustness, fairness, and generalization. Existing methods for computing Lipschitz constants either produce relatively loose upper bounds or are limited to small networks. In this paper, we develop an efficient framework for computing the $\ell_\infty$ local Lipschitz constant of a neural network by tightly upper bounding the norm of Clarke Jacobian via linear bound propagation. We formulate the computation of local Lipschitz constants with a linear bound propagation process on a high-order backward graph induced by the chain rule of Clarke Jacobian. To enable linear bound propagation, we derive tight linear relaxations for specific nonlinearities in Clarke Jacobian. This formulate unifies existing ad-hoc approaches such as RecurJac, which can be seen as a special case of ours with weaker relaxations. The bound propagation framework also allows us to easily borrow the popular Branch-and-Bound (BaB) approach from neural network verification to further tighten Lipschitz constants. Experiments show that on tiny models, our method produces comparable bounds compared to exact methods that cannot scale to slightly larger models; on larger models, our method efficiently produces tighter results than existing relaxed or naive methods, and our method scales to much larger practical models that previous works could not handle. We also demonstrate an application on provable monotonicity analysis. Code is available at https://github.com/shizhouxing/Local-Lipschitz-Constants.
originalAbstract: Lipschitz constants are connected to many properties of neural networks, such as robustness, fairness, and generalization. Existing methods for computing Lipschitz constants either produce relatively loose upper bounds or are limited to small networks. In this paper, we develop an efficient framework for computing the $\ell_\infty$ local Lipschitz constant of a neural network by tightly upper bounding the norm of Clarke Jacobian via linear bound propagation. We formulate the computation of local Lipschitz constants with a linear bound propagation process on a high-order backward graph induced by the chain rule of Clarke Jacobian. To enable linear bound propagation, we derive tight linear relaxations for specific nonlinearities in Clarke Jacobian. This formulate unifies existing ad-hoc approaches such as RecurJac, which can be seen as a special case of ours with weaker relaxations. The bound propagation framework also allows us to easily borrow the popular Branch-and-Bound (BaB) approach from neural network verification to further tighten Lipschitz constants. Experiments show that on tiny models, our method produces comparable bounds compared to exact methods that cannot scale to slightly larger models; on larger models, our method efficiently produces tighter results than existing relaxed or naive methods, and our method scales to much larger practical models that previous works could not handle. We also demonstrate an application on provable monotonicity analysis. Code is available at https://github.com/shizhouxing/Local-Lipschitz-Constants.

paragraphs: A local Lipschitz constant describes how strongly a neural network's output can change as its input changes within a local region. Such quantities connect to robustness, fairness, and generalization. This paper develops an efficient way to obtain tight upper bounds for the local constant measured using the infinity norm.

The method bounds the norm of a Clarke Jacobian, a generalized derivative suitable for the network operations considered. It turns the calculation into linear bound propagation over a backward graph derived from the chain rule. New linear relaxations handle nonlinear terms in that graph. The framework includes RecurJac as a special case with weaker relaxations and can use branch-and-bound to tighten its results further.

On tiny networks, experiments obtain bounds comparable to exact methods. On larger networks, the method gives tighter bounds than existing relaxed or naive approaches and handles practical models beyond the reach of previous work. The authors also demonstrate provable monotonicity analysis. These results concern efficient certification through upper bounds, rather than exact computation for every network.
summary.tldr: A bound-propagation framework computes tight local Lipschitz upper bounds and scales to networks that earlier methods could not handle.

title: Efficiently Computing Local Lipschitz Constants of Neural Networks via Bound Propagation

abstract: When answering a question, humans utilize the information available across different modalities to synthesize a consistent and complete chain of thought (CoT). This process is normally a black box in the case of deep learning models like large-scale language models. Recently, science question benchmarks have been used to diagnose the multi-hop reasoning ability and interpretability of an AI system. However, existing datasets fail to provide annotations for the answers, or are restricted to the textual-only modality, small scales, and limited domain diversity. To this end, we present Science Question Answering (ScienceQA), a new benchmark that consists of ~21k multimodal multiple choice questions with a diverse set of science topics and annotations of their answers with corresponding lectures and explanations. We further design language models to learn to generate lectures and explanations as the chain of thought (CoT) to mimic the multi-hop reasoning process when answering ScienceQA questions. ScienceQA demonstrates the utility of CoT in language models, as CoT improves the question answering performance by 1.20% in few-shot GPT-3 and 3.99% in fine-tuned UnifiedQA. We also explore the upper bound for models to leverage explanations by feeding those in the input; we observe that it improves the few-shot performance of GPT-3 by 18.96%. Our analysis further shows that language models, similar to humans, benefit from explanations to learn from fewer data and achieve the same performance with just 40% of the data. The data and code are available at https://scienceqa.github.io.

Answers are accompanied by lectures and explanations, giving models material for learning an explanatory sequence as well as selecting the correct answer.

On ScienceQA, this improves question-answering performance by a reported 1.20% for few-shot GPT-3 and 3.99% for fine-tuned UnifiedQA. Together, the results support explanations as useful learning information for this benchmark.
summary.tldr: ScienceQA supplies multimodal science questions and explanations, showing that explanation-based learning can improve answer accuracy and data efficiency.

title: Learn to Explain: Multimodal Reasoning via Thought Chains for Science Question Answering

abstract: Automatic differentiation (autodiff) has revolutionized machine learning. Itallows to express complex computations by composing elementary ones in creativeways and removes the burden of computing their derivatives by hand. Morerecently, differentiation of optimization problem solutions has attractedwidespread attention with applications such as optimization layers, and inbi-level problems such as hyper-parameter optimization and meta-learning.However, so far, implicit differentiation remained difficult to use forpractitioners, as it often required case-by-case tedious mathematicalderivations and implementations. In this paper, we proposeautomatic implicit differentiation, an efficientand modular approach for implicit differentiation of optimization problems. Inour approach, the user defines directly in Python a function $F$ capturing theoptimality conditions of the problem to be differentiated. Once this is done, weleverage autodiff of $F$ and the implicit function theorem to automaticallydifferentiate the optimization problem. Our approach thus combines the benefitsof implicit differentiation and autodiff. It is efficient as it can be added ontop of any state-of-the-art solver and modular as the optimality conditionspecification is decoupled from the implicit differentiation mechanism. We showthat seemingly simple principles allow to recover many existing implicitdifferentiation methods and create new ones easily. We demonstrate the ease offormulating and solving bi-level optimization problems using our framework. Wealso showcase an application to the sensitivity analysis of molecular dynamics.

paragraphs: Machine learning systems sometimes need derivatives of an optimization problem's solution, as in optimization layers, hyperparameter tuning, and meta-learning. Computing these derivatives through implicit differentiation has often required mathematical derivations and specialized implementations for each problem. This paper proposes a reusable way to automate that work.

The user writes a Python function describing the problem's optimality conditions: the relationships that characterize a solution. The framework applies automatic differentiation to this function and uses the implicit function theorem to obtain derivatives of the optimization problem. This separates the specification of what makes a solution optimal from the machinery that computes its derivatives.

That separation also allows the differentiation mechanism to be added on top of an existing solver. The authors show how the framework recovers many established implicit differentiation methods and makes new ones easier to formulate. They demonstrate its use for bilevel optimization and sensitivity analysis in molecular dynamics. The practical contribution is a modular interface that brings solver-based computations into differentiable workflows.
summary.tldr: Automatic implicit differentiation computes derivatives of optimization solutions from user-written optimality conditions, separating differentiation from the choice of solver.

title: Efficient and Modular Implicit Differentiation

abstract: Humans communicate with graphical sketches apart from symbolic languages. Primarily focusing on the latter, recent studies of emergent communication overlook the sketches; they do not account for the evolution process through which symbolic sign systems emerge in the trade-off between iconicity and symbolicity. In this work, we take the very first step to model and simulate this process via two neural agents playing a visual communication game; the sender communicates with the receiver by sketching on a canvas. We devise a novel reinforcement learning method such that agents are evolved jointly towards successful communication and abstract graphical conventions. To inspect the emerged conventions, we define three key properties -- iconicity, symbolicity, and semanticity -- and design evaluation methods accordingly. Our experimental results under different controls are consistent with the observation in studies of human graphical conventions. Of note, we find that evolved sketches can preserve the continuum of semantics under proper environmental pressures. More interestingly, co-evolved agents can switch between conventionalized and iconic communication based on their familiarity with referents. We hope the present research can pave the path for studying emergent communication with the modality of sketches.

paragraphs: A drawing can communicate by resembling its subject or by functioning as a learned convention. The paper studies how these forms of communication can emerge together, addressing a gap in work that primarily examines symbolic language. It sets up a visual communication game in which one neural agent draws on a canvas and another interprets the sketch.

A new reinforcement learning method trains the agents jointly toward successful communication and abstract graphical conventions. To examine the resulting sketches, the authors define and evaluate iconicity, symbolicity, and semanticity. These properties let them investigate resemblance, conventional meaning, and the semantic structure preserved by the drawings, rather than judging the agents only by communication success.

Experiments under different controls produce results consistent with observations from studies of human graphical conventions. Under appropriate environmental pressures, sketches can preserve a continuum of semantics. The jointly trained agents can also switch between conventionalized and iconic communication depending on their familiarity with the referents. The work offers an initial simulation framework for studying how graphical communication develops.
summary.tldr: Two agents learn to communicate through sketches, developing conventions that can shift with environmental pressure and familiarity.

title: Emergent Graphical Conventions in a Visual Communication Game

abstract: Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) has emerged as a compelling method to represent 3D objects and scenes for photo-realistic rendering. However, its implicit representation causes difficulty in manipulating the models like the explicit mesh representation.Several recent advances in NeRF manipulation are usually restricted by a shared renderer network, or suffer from large model size. To circumvent the hurdle, in this paper, we present a neural field representation that enables efficient and convenient manipulation of models.To achieve this goal, we learn a hybrid tensor rank decomposition of the scene without neural networks. Motivated by the low-rank approximation property of the SVD algorithm, we propose a rank-residual learning strategy to encourage the preservation of primary information in lower ranks. The model size can then be dynamically adjusted by rank truncation to control the levels of detail, achieving near-optimal compression without extra optimization.Furthermore, different models can be arbitrarily transformed and composed into one scene by concatenating along the rank dimension.The growth of storage cost can also be mitigated by compressing the unimportant objects in the composed scene. We demonstrate that our method is able to achieve comparable rendering quality to state-of-the-art methods, while enabling extra capability of compression and composition.Code is available at https://github.com/ashawkey/CCNeRF.

paragraphs: Neural radiance fields can represent scenes for realistic rendering, but their implicit structure makes editing and combining objects difficult. This paper introduces a representation designed to support those operations while also allowing flexible compression. It represents the scene through a hybrid tensor rank decomposition learned without neural networks.

The central training idea is to concentrate the most important scene information in lower ranks of the decomposition. Inspired by low-rank approximation in singular value decomposition, the rank-residual strategy makes later rank truncation useful: removing components reduces storage and detail without requiring another optimization stage. The authors describe the resulting compression as near-optimal.

The same representation supports composition by concatenating models along the rank dimension after transforming them. Objects that matter less in the combined scene can receive stronger compression, limiting storage growth. The reported rendering quality is comparable to state-of-the-art methods. The practical contribution is therefore a scene representation whose structure supports a controllable tradeoff between detail and size, together with convenient assembly of multiple models.
summary.tldr: A rank-based scene representation enables compression and composition while maintaining rendering quality comparable to state-of-the-art methods.

title: Compressible-composable NeRF via Rank-residual Decomposition

abstract: Policy Optimization (PO) algorithms have been proven particularly suited to handle the high-dimensionality of real-world continuous control tasks. In this context, Trust Region Policy Optimization methods represent a popular approach to stabilize the policy updates. These usually rely on the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence to limit the change in the policy. The Wasserstein distance represents a natural alternative, in place of the KL divergence, to define trust regions or to regularize the objective function. However, state-of-the-art works either resort to its approximations or do not provide an algorithm for continuous state-action spaces, reducing the applicability of the method.In this paper, we explore optimal transport discrepancies (which include the Wasserstein distance) to define trust regions, and we propose a novel algorithm - Optimal Transport Trust Region Policy Optimization (OT-TRPO) - for continuous state-action spaces. We circumvent the infinite-dimensional optimization problem for PO by providing a one-dimensional dual reformulation for which strong duality holds.We then analytically derive the optimal policy update given the solution of the dual problem. This way, we bypass the computation of optimal transport costs and of optimal transport maps, which we implicitly characterize by solving the dual formulation.Finally, we provide an experimental evaluation of our approach across various control tasks. Our results show that optimal transport discrepancies can offer an advantage over state-of-the-art approaches.

paragraphs: Trust-region policy optimization stabilizes reinforcement learning by limiting how much a policy changes in one update. These limits commonly use KL divergence. This paper instead considers optimal transport discrepancies, including Wasserstein distance, and develops a method that applies to continuous state and action spaces.

The central challenge is an infinite-dimensional policy optimization problem. The authors derive a one-dimensional dual reformulation and establish strong duality, connecting its solution to that of the original problem. Once the dual problem is solved, they analytically derive the optimal policy update. This supplies a concrete computational route for the proposed Optimal Transport Trust Region Policy Optimization algorithm, OT-TRPO.

The formulation avoids explicitly computing optimal transport costs or maps; those are characterized implicitly through the dual solution. Experimental evaluations across several control tasks show that optimal transport discrepancies can provide an advantage over the state-of-the-art approaches compared. The contribution combines a mathematical reformulation with an algorithm for continuous control, making this alternative way of constraining policy changes more directly usable in the setting studied.
summary.tldr: OT-TRPO uses a one-dimensional dual problem to implement optimal-transport trust regions for continuous-control policy updates.

title: Trust Region Policy Optimization with Optimal Transport Discrepancies: Duality and Algorithm for Continuous Actions

abstract: Homophily is a graph property describing the tendency of edges to connect similar nodes; the opposite is called heterophily. It is often believed that heterophilous graphs are challenging for standard message-passing graph neural networks (GNNs), and much effort has been put into developing efficient methods for this setting. However, there is no universally agreed-upon measure of homophily in the literature. In this work, we show that commonly used homophily measures have critical drawbacks preventing the comparison of homophily levels across different datasets. For this, we formalize desirable properties for a proper homophily measure and verify which measures satisfy which properties. In particular, we show that a measure that we call adjusted homophily satisfies more desirable properties than other popular homophily measures while being rarely used in graph machine learning literature. Then, we go beyond the homophily-heterophily dichotomy and propose a new characteristic that allows one to further distinguish different sorts of heterophily. The proposed label informativeness (LI) characterizes how much information a neighbor's label provides about a node's label. We prove that this measure satisfies important desirable properties. We also observe empirically that LI better agrees with GNN performance compared to homophily measures, which confirms that it is a useful characteristic of the graph structure.

paragraphs: Homophily describes a tendency for connected nodes to be similar, while heterophily describes the opposite tendency. These concepts often guide judgments about whether a graph will suit a message-passing neural network. The paper questions how reliably existing homophily measures support those judgments, especially when researchers compare datasets with different characteristics.

The authors formalize desirable properties for a homophily measure and examine which established measures satisfy them. They find critical drawbacks in commonly used choices that prevent meaningful comparisons across datasets. A measure they call adjusted homophily satisfies more of the desired properties than other popular measures, despite receiving relatively little use in graph machine learning.

The paper then introduces label informativeness, which asks how much a neighbor's label reveals about a node's label. This distinguishes different forms of heterophily: different labels can still have an informative relationship. The authors prove desirable properties of this measure and find that it agrees better with observed graph neural network performance than homophily measures do. That empirical result supports a richer characterization of graph structure.
summary.tldr: Label informativeness captures useful relationships between neighboring labels and empirically tracks graph neural network performance better than homophily measures.

title: Characterizing Graph Datasets for Node Classification: Homophily-Heterophily Dichotomy and Beyond

abstract: This paper investigates fairness and bias in Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA), a widely used statistical technique for examining the relationship between two sets of variables. We present a framework that alleviates unfairness by minimizing the correlation disparity error associated with protected attributes. Our approach enables CCA to learn global projection matrices from all data points while ensuring that these matrices yield comparable correlation levels to group-specific projection matrices. Experimental evaluation on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrates the efficacy of our method in reducing correlation disparity error without compromising CCA accuracy.

paragraphs: Canonical correlation analysis, or CCA, studies relationships between two sets of variables by finding projections that reveal their correlation. This paper asks whether projections learned across an entire dataset serve groups associated with protected attributes comparably. Its focus is fairness in the correlations captured by the statistical representation.

The proposed framework minimizes correlation disparity error. It learns global projection matrices from all data points while requiring the resulting correlation levels to be comparable to those obtained from group-specific projection matrices. The group-specific results therefore provide a reference for assessing how well the shared projections represent each group's relationships.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show reduced correlation disparity without compromising CCA accuracy in the reported evaluation. The result matters because a shared representation can be assessed for more than its overall statistical fit: its behavior across protected groups also enters the learning objective. The paper demonstrates a concrete way to address this particular form of unfairness while retaining CCA's purpose of measuring relationships between variable sets.
summary.tldr: Fair CCA learns shared projections that reduce group correlation disparities while preserving accuracy in the reported experiments.

title: Fair Canonical Correlation Analysis

abstract: We study the problem of experiment planning with function approximation in contextual bandit problems. In settings where there is a significant overhead to deploying adaptive algorithms---for example, when the execution of the data collection policies is required to be distributed, or a human in the loop is needed to implement these policies---producing in advance a set of policies for data collection is paramount. We study the setting where a large dataset of contexts but not rewards is available and may be used by the learner to design an effective data collection strategy. Although when rewards are linear this problem has been well studied, results are still missing for more complex reward models. In this work we propose two experiment planning strategies compatible with function approximation. The first is an eluder planning and sampling procedure that can recover optimality guarantees depending on the eluder dimension of the reward function class. For the second, we show that a uniform sampler achieves competitive optimality rates in the setting where the number of actions is small. We finalize our results introducing a statistical gap fleshing out the fundamental differences between planning and adaptive learning and provide results for planning with model selection.

paragraphs: In contextual bandit problems, data collection can adapt as rewards arrive. That flexibility becomes costly when policies must be deployed across distributed systems or implemented by people. This paper asks how to plan data collection policies in advance, using a large collection of contexts for which rewards have not yet been observed.

The authors extend experiment planning beyond the well-studied case of linear rewards to settings using function approximation. They propose an eluder planning and sampling procedure whose optimality guarantees depend on the eluder dimension of the reward function class. They also analyze a simpler alternative: uniform sampling achieves competitive optimality rates when the number of available actions is small.

The paper additionally identifies a statistical gap between planning in advance and adaptive learning, and provides results for planning with model selection. Together, these contributions clarify what advance planning can achieve and how its guarantees depend on the reward class or action count. The practical motivation is to obtain useful collection strategies when repeatedly changing a deployed policy carries substantial overhead.
summary.tldr: The paper develops advance data-collection strategies for contextual bandits with function approximation and characterizes their guarantees and differences from adaptive learning.

title: Experiment Planning with Function Approximation

abstract: In human-AI collaboration systems for critical applications, in order to ensure minimal error, users should set an operating point based on model confidence to determine when the decision should be delegated to human experts. Samples for which model confidence is lower than the operating point would be manually analysed by experts to avoid mistakes.Such systems can become truly useful only if they consider two aspects: models should be confident only for samples for which they are accurate, and the number of samples delegated to experts should be minimized.The latter aspect is especially crucial for applications where available expert time is limited and expensive, such as healthcare. The trade-off between the model accuracy and the number of samples delegated to experts can be represented by a curve that is similar to an ROC curve, which we refer to as confidence operating characteristic (COC) curve. In this paper, we argue that deep neural networks should be trained by taking into account both accuracy and expert load and, to that end, propose a new complementary loss function for classification that maximizes the area under this COC curve.This promotes simultaneously the increase in network accuracy and the reduction in number of samples delegated to humans.We perform experiments on multiple computer vision and medical image datasets for classification.Our results demonstrate that the proposed loss improves classification accuracy and delegates less number of decisions to experts, achieves better out-of-distribution samples detection and on par calibration performance compared to existing loss functions.

paragraphs: A human-AI classification system can refer low-confidence cases to experts while letting the model handle more confident predictions. Its usefulness depends on both prediction accuracy and how much work reaches the experts. This paper argues that training should account for both objectives, especially when expert time is scarce or expensive.

The authors describe their relationship using a confidence operating characteristic curve. Changing the confidence threshold changes the balance between accuracy and the number of delegated cases. They propose a complementary classification loss that maximizes the area under this curve. The training objective therefore encourages the network to improve its decisions while reducing the need for manual review across operating points.

Experiments on computer vision and medical-image classification datasets show higher classification accuracy and fewer delegated decisions compared with existing losses. The authors also report better detection of out-of-distribution samples and comparable calibration. These results indicate that confidence-based delegation can be considered during learning itself, with expert workload serving as an explicit part of the objective.
summary.tldr: A classification loss that accounts for confidence-based delegation improves accuracy and reduces expert workload in the reported experiments.

title: Expert load matters: operating networks at high accuracy and low manual effort

abstract: While distant supervision has been extensively explored and exploited in NLP tasks like named entity recognition, a major obstacle stems from the inevitable noisy distant labels tagged unsupervisedly. A few past works approach this problem by adopting a self-training framework with a sample-selection mechanism. In this work, we innovatively identify two types of biases that were omitted by prior work, and these biases lead to inferior performance of the distant-supervised NER setup. First, we characterize the noise concealed in the distant labels as highly structural rather than fully randomized. Second, the self-training framework would ubiquitously introduce an inherent bias that causes erroneous behavior in both sample selection and eventually prediction. To cope with these problems, we propose a novel self-training framework, dubbed DesERT. This framework augments the conventional NER predicative pathway to a dual form that effectively adapts the sample-selection process to conform to its innate distributional-bias structure. The other crucial component of DesERT composes a debiased module aiming to enhance the token representations, hence the quality of the pseudo-labels. Extensive experiments are conducted to validate the DesERT. The results show that our framework establishes a new state-of-art performance, it achieves a +2.22% average F1 score improvement on five standardized benchmarking datasets. Lastly, DesERT demonstrates its effectiveness under a new DSNER benchmark where additional distant supervision comes from the ChatGPT model.
originalAbstract: While distant supervision has been extensively explored and exploited in NLP tasks like named entity recognition, a major obstacle stems from the inevitable noisy distant labels tagged unsupervisedly. A few past works approach this problem by adopting a self-training framework with a sample-selection mechanism. In this work, we innovatively identify two types of biases that were omitted by prior work, and these biases lead to inferior performance of the distant-supervised NER setup. First, we characterize the noise concealed in the distant labels as highly structural rather than fully randomized. Second, the self-training framework would ubiquitously introduce an inherent bias that causes erroneous behavior in both sample selection and eventually prediction. To cope with these problems, we propose a novel self-training framework, dubbed DesERT. This framework augments the conventional NER predicative pathway to a dual form that effectively adapts the sample-selection process to conform to its innate distributional-bias structure. The other crucial component of DesERT composes a debiased module aiming to enhance the token representations, hence the quality of the pseudo-labels. Extensive experiments are conducted to validate the DesERT. The results show that our framework establishes a new state-of-art performance, it achieves a +2.22% average F1 score improvement on five standardized benchmarking datasets. Lastly, DesERT demonstrates its effectiveness under a new DSNER benchmark where additional distant supervision comes from the ChatGPT model.

paragraphs: Distantly supervised named entity recognition learns from automatically supplied labels that can contain errors. Self-training methods attempt to improve these labels by selecting examples and producing new predictions for further learning. This paper argues that two overlooked biases interfere with that process: distant-label errors have structure, and self-training itself introduces bias into selection and prediction.

The proposed framework, DesERT, addresses both sources. It expands the usual prediction pathway into a dual form so that sample selection can account for the distributional structure of the bias. A separate debiasing module improves token representations, with the aim of producing better pseudo-labels. The method thus changes both which training signals are selected and the representations used to generate them.

Across five standardized datasets, the authors report a new state of the art and an average F1 improvement of +2.22%. They also demonstrate effectiveness on a benchmark incorporating additional distant supervision from ChatGPT. These findings support treating label noise and self-training bias as distinct, interacting problems rather than relying on sample selection alone.
summary.tldr: DesERT improves distantly supervised entity recognition by addressing structured label noise and bias introduced during self-training.

title: Debiased and Denoised Entity Recognition from Distant Supervision

abstract: Graph models based on factorization of the adjacency matrix often fail to capture network structures related to links between dissimilar nodes (heterophily). We introduce a novel graph factorization model that leverages two nonnegative vectors per node to interpretably account for links between both similar and dissimilar nodes. We prove that our model can exactly represent any graph with low *arboricity*, a property that many real-world networks satisfy; our proof also applies to related models but has much greater scope than the closest prior bound, which is based on low *max degree*. Our factorization also has compelling properties besides expressiveness: due to its symmetric structure and nonnegativity, fitting the model inherently finds node communities, and the model's link predictions can be interpreted in terms of these communities. In experiments on real-world networks, we demonstrate our factorization's effectiveness on a variety of tasks, including community detection and link prediction.

paragraphs: Representing a graph by factorizing its adjacency matrix can struggle with heterophily: connections between nodes that are dissimilar. This paper introduces a factorization that assigns two nonnegative vectors to each node. The representation is designed to account interpretably for both similarity-based connections and links across differences.

The authors prove that the model can exactly represent graphs with low arboricity, a sparsity property satisfied by many real-world networks. This guarantee has broader scope than the closest previous bound based on low maximum degree. The proof also applies to related models, extending the theoretical contribution beyond the proposed factorization.

Symmetry and nonnegativity give the representation another useful property: fitting it inherently discovers node communities. Predicted links can then be explained through those communities, connecting expressiveness with interpretation. Experiments on real-world networks demonstrate effectiveness for community detection and link prediction. The central result is therefore both representational and practical: a condition for exact graph representation accompanies a model whose fitted structure helps explain its predictions.
summary.tldr: A symmetric factorization with two nonnegative vectors per node captures heterophily and exactly represents graphs with low arboricity.

title: Exact Representation of Sparse Networks with Symmetric Nonnegative Embeddings

abstract: We propose a post hoc saliency-based explanation framework for counterfactual reasoning in probabilistic multivariate time-series forecasting (regression) settings. Building upon Miller's framework of explanations derived from research in multiple social science disciplines, we establish a conceptual link between counterfactual reasoning and saliency-based explanation techniques. To address the lack of a principled notion of saliency, we leverage a unifying definition of information-theoretic saliency grounded in preattentive human visual cognition and extend it to forecasting settings. Specifically, we obtain a closed-form expression for commonly used density functions to identify which observed timesteps appear salient to an underlying model in making its probabilistic forecasts. We empirically validate our framework in a principled manner using synthetic data to establish ground-truth saliency that is unavailable for real-world data. Finally, using real-world data and forecasting models, we demonstrate how our framework can assist domain experts in forming new data-driven hypotheses about the causal relationships between features in the wild.

paragraphs: Probabilistic time-series models predict distributions over future outcomes, making explanation more involved than identifying the inputs behind a single number. This paper develops a post hoc framework for identifying observed timesteps that appear salient to such a model. It connects those explanations to counterfactual reasoning about why a particular future was forecast.

The framework draws on a social-science account of explanation and an information-theoretic definition of saliency grounded in preattentive visual cognition. The authors extend that definition to multivariate forecasting and derive closed-form expressions for commonly used probability densities. This provides a principled basis for highlighting past observations associated with the model's probabilistic predictions.

The authors validate the method using synthetic data, where ground-truth saliency can be established. They then demonstrate applications with real-world data and forecasting models. Those examples show how the explanations can help domain experts formulate new hypotheses about causal relationships between features. The role is to support hypothesis formation; the stated real-world findings do not establish that salient observations are themselves proven causes.
summary.tldr: An information-theoretic saliency framework identifies past timesteps relevant to probabilistic forecasts and helps experts formulate counterfactual and causal hypotheses.

title: Why Did This Model Forecast This Future? Information-Theoretic Saliency for Counterfactual Explanations of Probabilistic Regression Models

abstract: We present a new method that includes three key components of distributed optimization and federated learning: variance reduction of stochastic gradients, partial participation, and compressed communication. We prove that the new method has optimal oracle complexity and state-of-the-art communication complexity in the partial participation setting. Regardless of the communication compression feature, our method successfully combines variance reduction and partial participation: we get the optimal oracle complexity, never need the participation of all nodes, and do not require the bounded gradients (dissimilarity) assumption.
originalAbstract: We present a new method that includes three key components of distributed optimization and federated learning: variance reduction of stochastic gradients, partial participation, and compressed communication. We prove that the new method has optimal oracle complexity and state-of-the-art communication complexity in the partial participation setting. Regardless of the communication compression feature, our method successfully combines variance reduction and partial participation: we get the optimal oracle complexity, never need the participation of all nodes, and do not require the bounded gradients (dissimilarity) assumption.

paragraphs: Distributed optimization divides learning work among multiple computing nodes. Two costs matter: the calculations needed to improve the model and the messages exchanged between nodes. Partial participation adds another challenge because an update uses only some nodes. This paper presents a method that addresses computation, communication, and participation together for nonconvex optimization.

The method combines variance reduction, partial participation, and compressed communication. Variance reduction reduces the variability in stochastic gradient estimates, while compression reduces the information transmitted. The authors prove optimal oracle complexity, which concerns the number of optimization queries required, and communication complexity that matches the stated state of the art in the partial participation setting.

A central result remains relevant even without compression: the method combines variance reduction with partial participation while retaining optimal oracle complexity. It never requires every node to participate and does not need the bounded gradients or dissimilarity assumption identified in the abstract. These properties matter because the computation guarantee does not depend on occasional rounds of universal participation or that particular restriction on gradients.
summary.tldr: A distributed optimization method combines variance reduction, partial participation, and compression with optimal oracle complexity and strong communication guarantees.

title: A Computation and Communication Efficient Method for Distributed Nonconvex Problems in the Partial Participation Setting

abstract: Making good decisions in partially observable and non-deterministic scenarios is a crucial capability for robots. A Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) is a general framework for the above problem. Despite advances in POMDP solving, problems with long planning horizons and evolving environments remain difficult to solve even by the best approximate solvers today. To alleviate this difficulty, we propose a slightly modified POMDP problem, called a Reference-Based POMDP, where the objective is to balance between maximizing the expected total reward and being close to a given reference (stochastic) policy. The optimal policy of a Reference-Based POMDP can be computed via iterative expectations using the given reference policy, thereby avoiding exhaustive enumeration of actions at each belief node of the search tree. We demonstrate theoretically that the standard POMDP under stochastic policies is related to the Reference-Based POMDP. To demonstrate the feasibility of exploiting the formulation, we present a basic algorithm RefSolver. Results from experiments on long-horizon navigation problems indicate that this basic algorithm substantially outperforms POMCP.
