paragraphs: Causal Bayesian networks describe relationships among variables, but calculating probabilities for statements involving interventions can be difficult. This paper examines when such probabilities can be uniquely estimated. Its scope includes probabilities of sufficiency and necessity, which concern whether a cause can produce an outcome or was needed for it.

The authors show that relatively simple independence assumptions can make these estimates unique. They describe the assumptions as often realistic and discuss circumstances in which they are appropriate. These assumptions are a substantive part of the result: the claimed ability to determine intervention-related probabilities depends on their suitability for the problem being studied.

In many cases of interest, when those assumptions hold appropriately, the resulting estimates can be evaluated from observational data. This offers a route to answering certain causal questions in settings where experiments are impractical or impossible. The contribution is therefore a conditional identification result, connecting explicit assumptions about independence to the possibility of calculating otherwise challenging intervention probabilities.
summary.tldr: Appropriate independence assumptions can uniquely determine intervention probabilities, with observational data sufficient to evaluate them in many cases.

title: Intervention and Conditioning in Causal Bayesian Networks

abstract: In this work, we offer a theoretical analysis of two modern optimization techniques for training large and complex models: (i) adaptive optimization algorithms, such as Adam, and (ii) the model exponential moving average (EMA). Specifically, we demonstrate that a clipped version of Adam with model EMA achieves the optimal convergence rates in various nonconvex optimization settings, both smooth and nonsmooth. Moreover, when the scale varies significantly across different coordinates, we demonstrate that the coordinate-wise adaptivity of Adam is provably advantageous. Notably, unlike previous analyses of Adam, our analysis crucially relies on its core elements---momentum and discounting factors---as well as model EMA, motivating their wide applications in practice.
originalAbstract: In this work, we offer a theoretical analysis of two modern optimization techniques for training large and complex models: (i) adaptive optimization algorithms, such as Adam, and (ii) the model exponential moving average (EMA). Specifically, we demonstrate that a clipped version of Adam with model EMA achieves the optimal convergence rates in various nonconvex optimization settings, both smooth and nonsmooth. Moreover, when the scale varies significantly across different coordinates, we demonstrate that the coordinate-wise adaptivity of Adam is provably advantageous. Notably, unlike previous analyses of Adam, our analysis crucially relies on its core elements---momentum and discounting factors---as well as model EMA, motivating their wide applications in practice.

paragraphs: Adam and exponential moving averages of model parameters are common ingredients in training large models. This paper studies their combination theoretically. Its focus is nonconvex optimization, where the objective can have a complicated landscape, and it considers both smooth objectives and objectives that are nonsmooth. The analysis concerns a clipped version of Adam combined with model averaging.

The authors prove that this combination achieves optimal convergence rates in several such settings. They also examine what happens when different parameter coordinates have substantially different scales. In that situation, they establish a benefit from Adam's coordinate-wise adaptation, which allows its updates to respond differently across coordinates.

A distinctive feature of the analysis is that it depends on momentum, discounting factors, and model exponential moving averaging. These are central parts of the analyzed method, rather than incidental implementation choices. The results therefore provide theoretical support for using these components together. The optimal-rate claim applies to the specified clipped algorithm and the optimization settings studied, while the advantage of coordinate adaptation is tied to pronounced differences in scale.
summary.tldr: Clipped Adam with model exponential averaging achieves optimal rates in several nonconvex settings, with provable benefits from coordinate adaptation when scales differ substantially.

title: Adam with model exponential moving average is effective for nonconvex optimization

abstract: Neural embedding models have become a fundamental component of modern information retrieval (IR) pipelines. These models produce a single embedding $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ per data-point, allowing for fast retrieval via highly optimized maximum inner product search (MIPS) algorithms. Recently, beginning with the landmark ColBERT paper, multi-vector models, which produce a set of embedding per data point, have achieved markedly superior performance for IR tasks. Unfortunately, using these models for IR is computationally expensive due to the increased complexity of multi-vector retrieval and scoring. In this paper, we introduce MUVERA (MUlti-VEctor Retrieval Algorithm), a retrieval mechanism which reduces multi-vector similarity search to single-vector similarity search. This enables the usage of off-the-shelf MIPS solvers for multi-vector retrieval. MUVERA asymmetrically generates Fixed Dimensional Encodings (FDEs) of queries and documents, which are vectors whose inner product approximates multi-vector similarity. We prove that FDEs give high-quality $\epsilon$-approximations, thus providing the first single-vector proxy for multi-vector similarity with theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we find that FDEs achieve the same recall as prior state-of-the-art heuristics while retrieving 2-5$\times$ fewer candidates. Compared to prior state of the art implementations, MUVERA achieves consistently good end-to-end recall and latency across a diverse set of the BEIR retrieval datasets, achieving an average of 10% improved recall with 90% lower latency.

paragraphs: Representing a query or document with several vectors can improve information retrieval, but comparing sets of vectors is expensive. Single-vector search has highly optimized algorithms, creating a practical gap between representation quality and retrieval speed. MUVERA bridges that gap by converting multi-vector similarity search into a form that existing single-vector search systems can handle.

The method constructs fixed-dimensional encodings for queries and documents using different encoding procedures for the two sides. The inner product between these encodings approximates the original multi-vector similarity. The authors prove approximation guarantees, providing a theoretically supported single-vector proxy that can be used with off-the-shelf maximum inner product search solvers.

Across the evaluated BEIR datasets, MUVERA reports average recall improvement of 10% with 90% lower latency relative to prior state-of-the-art implementations. The results connect the mathematical approximation to practical gains in retrieval quality and speed.
summary.tldr: MUVERA approximates multi-vector similarity with fixed-dimensional vectors, enabling fast standard retrieval with theoretical guarantees.

title: MUVERA: Multi-Vector Retrieval via Fixed Dimensional Encoding

abstract: Forecasting a typical object's future motion is a critical task for interpreting and interacting with dynamic environments in computer vision. Event-based sensors, which could capture changes in the scene with exceptional temporal granularity, may potentially offer a unique opportunity to predict future motion with a level of detail and precision previously unachievable. Inspired by that, we propose to integrate the strong learning capacity of the video diffusion model with the rich motion information of an event camera as a motion simulation framework. Specifically, we initially employ pre-trained stable video diffusion models to adapt the event sequence dataset. This process facilitates the transfer of extensive knowledge from RGB videos to an event-centric domain. Moreover, we introduce an alignment mechanism that utilizes reinforcement learning techniques to enhance the reverse generation trajectory of the diffusion model, ensuring improved performance and accuracy. Through extensive testing and validation, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in various complex scenarios, showcasing its potential to revolutionize motion flow prediction in computer vision applications such as autonomous vehicle guidance, robotic navigation, and interactive media. Our findings suggest a promising direction for future research in enhancing the interpretative power and predictive accuracy of computer vision systems. The source code ispublicly available at https://github.com/p4r4mount/E-Motion.

paragraphs: E-Motion investigates future-motion prediction using event-camera data. These sensors capture changes in a scene with very fine timing, potentially supplying motion information that is valuable for forecasting. The paper combines this information with video diffusion models, aiming to bring a strong learned video-generation capability into an event-based motion simulation framework.

The method adapts pretrained stable video diffusion models to an event-sequence dataset. This transfers knowledge learned from RGB videos into a domain organized around scene-change events. An additional alignment mechanism uses reinforcement learning techniques to improve the diffusion model's reverse generation trajectory. Both stages contribute to the intended forecasting behavior: transferring useful visual knowledge and refining how predictions are generated.

The authors report that extensive testing demonstrates effectiveness across complex scenarios. They describe autonomous vehicle guidance, robotic navigation, and interactive media as potential applications of improved motion-flow prediction. The findings support the framework as a promising research direction; the abstract presents the broader application impact as potential rather than establishing deployment outcomes in those settings.
summary.tldr: E-Motion adapts video diffusion to event-camera sequences and refines generation through reinforcement learning to predict future motion.

title: E-Motion: Future Motion Simulation via Event Sequence Diffusion

abstract: Sample efficiency in Reinforcement Learning (RL) has traditionally been driven by algorithmic enhancements. In this work, we demonstrate that scaling can also lead to substantial improvements. We conduct a thorough investigation into the interplay of scaling model capacity and domain-specific RL enhancements. These empirical findings inform the design choices underlying our proposed BRO (Bigger, Regularized, Optimistic) algorithm. The key innovation behind BRO is that strong regularization allows for effective scaling of the critic networks, which, paired with optimistic exploration, leads to superior performance. BRO achieves state-of-the-art results, significantly outperforming the leading model-based and model-free algorithms across 40 complex tasks from the DeepMind Control, MetaWorld, and MyoSuite benchmarks. BRO is the first model-free algorithm to achieve near-optimal policies in the notoriously challenging Dog and Humanoid tasks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning systems often improve their use of training experience through changes to the learning algorithm. This paper investigates another route: increasing model capacity. It studies how larger networks interact with techniques designed specifically for reinforcement learning, using the empirical findings to develop BRO, short for Bigger, Regularized, Optimistic.

The central design choice is to scale the critic networks, which provide evaluations used in learning, while applying strong regularization. The authors find that regularization enables this increase in capacity to work effectively. BRO combines these larger critics with optimistic exploration, bringing together model scale, constraints on learning, and an exploration strategy.

Across 40 tasks from DeepMind Control, MetaWorld, and MyoSuite, BRO reportedly outperforms leading model-based and model-free algorithms. The authors also report the first model-free achievement of near-optimal policies on the challenging Dog and Humanoid tasks. These findings support scaling as a useful source of sample-efficiency improvements when paired with the right reinforcement-learning design choices.
summary.tldr: BRO combines larger, strongly regularized critics with optimistic exploration to improve continuous-control reinforcement learning.

title: Bigger, Regularized, Optimistic: scaling for compute and sample efficient continuous control

abstract: The quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) is a well-known NP-hard problem that takes an $n\times n$ matrix $Q$ as input and decides an $n$-dimensional 0-1 vector $x$, to optimize a quadratic function. Existing learning-based models that always formulate the solution process as sequential decisions suffer from high computational overload. To overcome this issue, we propose a neural solver called the Value Classification Model (VCM) that formulates the solution process from a classification perspective. It applies a Depth Value Network (DVN) based on graph convolution that exploits the symmetry property in $Q$ to auto-grasp value features. These features are then fed into a Value Classification Network (VCN) which directly generates classification solutions. Trained by a highly efficient model-tailored Greedy-guided Self Trainer (GST) which does not require any priori optimal labels, VCM significantly outperforms competitors in both computational efficiency and solution quality with a remarkable generalization ability. It can achieve near-optimal solutions in milliseconds with an average optimality gap of just 0.362\% on benchmarks with up to 2500 variables. Notably, a VCM trained at a specific DVN depth can steadily find better solutions by simply extending the testing depth, which narrows the gap to 0.034\% on benchmarks. To our knowledge, this is the first learning-based model to reach such a performance.

paragraphs: Quadratic unconstrained binary optimization asks for a vector of zeros and ones that optimizes a quadratic objective defined by a matrix. The problem is NP-hard. This paper targets the computational overhead of learning-based solvers that build an answer through sequential decisions, proposing instead to generate the binary assignment through classification.

The Value Classification Model uses a graph-convolution-based Depth Value Network to extract features by exploiting symmetry in the input matrix. A Value Classification Network then directly produces a candidate solution. Training uses a specialized Greedy-guided Self Trainer that does not require previously supplied optimal solutions as labels.

On benchmarks with up to 2,500 variables, the model produces near-optimal solutions in milliseconds, with a reported average optimality gap of 0.362%. Increasing the feature network’s depth at test time improves solutions further and reduces the reported gap to 0.034%. The results support both computational efficiency and solution quality in the evaluated settings. The additional test-time depth finding suggests that the learned solver can benefit from more processing without retraining at that depth.
summary.tldr: VCM treats binary optimization as classification, producing near-optimal benchmark solutions quickly without requiring optimal training labels.

title: Learning to Solve Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization in a Classification Way

abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in producing images based on textual prompts. Numerous methods have been proposed to ensure these models generate safe images. Early methods attempt to incorporate safety filters into models to mitigate the risk of generating harmful images but such external filters do not inherently detoxify the model and can be easily bypassed. Hence, model unlearning and data cleaning are the most essential methods for maintaining the safety of models, given their impact on model parameters.However, malicious fine-tuning can still make models prone to generating harmful or undesirable images even with these methods.Inspired by the phenomenon of catastrophic forgetting, we propose a training policy using contrastive learning to increase the latent space distance between clean and harmful data distribution, thereby protecting models from being fine-tuned to generate harmful images due to forgetting.The experimental results demonstrate that our methods not only maintain clean image generation capabilities before malicious fine-tuning but also effectively prevent DMs from producing harmful images after malicious fine-tuning. Our method can also be combined with other safety methods to maintain their safety against malicious fine-tuning further.

Hence, model unlearning and data cleaning are the most essential methods for maintaining the safety of models, given their impact on model parameters.However, malicious fine-tuning can still make models prone to generating harmful or undesirable images even with these methods.Inspired by the phenomenon of catastrophic forgetting, we propose a training policy using contrastive learning to increase the latent space distance between clean and harmful data distribution, thereby protecting models from being fine-tuned to generate harmful images due to forgetting.The experimental results demonstrate that our methods not only maintain clean image generation capabilities before malicious fine-tuning but also effectively prevent DMs from producing harmful images after malicious fine-tuning. paragraphs: This paper studies diffusion-model safety after malicious fine-tuning. External filters can be bypassed, while model unlearning and data cleaning affect the model more directly. Even those approaches can leave a model vulnerable to subsequent training that restores harmful image generation. The research therefore targets the durability of safety under such later modifications.

The proposed training policy draws on catastrophic forgetting and uses contrastive learning to increase the distance between clean and harmful data distributions in latent space. Its aim is to make the model resist being fine-tuned into producing harmful images. This connects the safety intervention to the model's internal representation and to how that representation behaves during additional training.

Experiments report that the method preserves clean image generation before malicious fine-tuning and effectively prevents harmful generation after the tested malicious fine-tuning. The authors also describe combining it with other safety methods to strengthen their resistance. The findings support this training policy as an additional defense whose effectiveness is demonstrated in the reported experimental settings.
summary.tldr: A contrastive training policy separates clean and harmful latent distributions to improve diffusion-model safety against malicious fine-tuning.

title: Leveraging Catastrophic Forgetting to Develop Safe Diffusion Models against Malicious Finetuning

abstract: The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) in the real world has come with a rise in copyright cases against companies for training their models on unlicensed data from the internet. Recent works have presented methods to identify if individual text sequences were members of the model's training data, known as membership inference attacks (MIAs). We demonstrate that the apparent success of these MIAs is confounded by selecting non-members (text sequences not used for training) belonging to a different distribution from the members (e.g., temporally shifted recent Wikipedia articles compared with ones used to train the model). This distribution shift makes membership inference appear successful. However, most MIA methods perform no better than random guessing when discriminating between members and non-members from the same distribution (e.g., in this case, the same period of time).Even when MIAs work, we find that different MIAs succeed at inferring membership of samples from different distributions.Instead, we propose a new dataset inference method to accurately identify the datasets used to train large language models. This paradigm sits realistically in the modern-day copyright landscape, where authors claim that an LLM is trained over multiple documents (such as a book) written by them, rather than one particular paragraph.While dataset inference shares many of the challenges of membership inference, we solve it by selectively combining the MIAs that provide positive signal for a given distribution, and aggregating them to perform a statistical test on a given dataset. Our approach successfully distinguishes the train and test sets of different subsets of the Pile with statistically significant p-values $< 0.1$, without any false positives.

paragraphs: Determining whether a language model trained on a particular text is difficult when apparent evidence of memorization can instead reflect differences between data distributions. This paper shows that membership inference can look successful when training examples are compared with nonmembers from a different distribution, such as more recent articles. Most tested methods fall to chance-level performance when that mismatch is removed.

The authors shift the question from individual passages to collections of documents. Their dataset inference method selects membership-inference techniques that provide useful signals for the distribution being examined, then aggregates those signals into a statistical test. This accommodates the finding that different techniques work on different kinds of text.

On different subsets of the Pile, the method distinguishes training and test sets with reported p-values below 0.1 and no false positives in those evaluations. The result supports assessing evidence across a dataset rather than relying on a single passage. It also highlights that distribution matching is essential to interpreting whether a detected signal actually concerns training membership.
summary.tldr: Dataset inference combines distribution-specific membership signals to test whether a collection of texts was used in language-model training.

title: LLM Dataset Inference: Did you train on my dataset?

abstract: Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) formalizes the problem of autocurricula through interactive training between a teacher agent and a student agent. The teacher generates new training environments with high learning potential, curating an adaptive curriculum that strengthens the student's ability to handle unseen scenarios. Existing UED methods mainly rely on *regret*, a metric that measures the difference between the agent's optimal and actual performance, to guide curriculum design. Regret-driven methods generate curricula that progressively increase environment complexity for the student but overlook environment *novelty* — a critical element for enhancing an agent's generalizability. Measuring environment novelty is especially challenging due to the underspecified nature of environment parameters in UED, and existing approaches face significant limitations. To address this, this paper introduces the *Coverage-based Evaluation of Novelty In Environment* (CENIE) framework. CENIE proposes a scalable, domain-agnostic, and curriculum-aware approach to quantifying environment novelty by leveraging the student's state-action space coverage from previous curriculum experiences. We then propose an implementation of CENIE that models this coverage and measures environment novelty using Gaussian Mixture Models. By integrating both regret and novelty as complementary objectives for curriculum design, CENIE facilitates effective exploration across the state-action space while progressively increasing curriculum complexity. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that augmenting existing regret-based UED algorithms with CENIE achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks, underscoring the effectiveness of novelty-driven autocurricula for robust generalization.

paragraphs: Unsupervised environment design trains a teacher to create environments that help a student agent learn. Existing approaches often use regret, the gap between optimal and actual performance, to select increasingly challenging experiences. The paper argues that this overlooks novelty: an environment can be challenging without expanding what the student has encountered.

CENIE measures novelty through the student's previous coverage of state-action space. This makes novelty depend on the curriculum experienced so far, rather than only on environment parameters, whose meaning can be underspecified. The authors implement the idea using Gaussian mixture models to represent coverage and assess how novel a candidate environment is.

The framework combines novelty and regret as complementary curriculum objectives. One encourages broader exploration, while the other supports increasing complexity. Adding CENIE to existing regret-based environment-design algorithms produces state-of-the-art performance across multiple evaluated benchmarks. These empirical results support the value of accounting for prior experience when creating curricula intended to improve generalization to unseen environments.
summary.tldr: CENIE improves automated curricula by combining regret with novelty measured from the student's previous state-action coverage.

title: Improving Environment Novelty Quantification for Effective Unsupervised Environment Design

abstract: Prompt-based models have demonstrated impressive prompt-following capability at image editing tasks. However, the models still struggle with following detailed editing prompts or performing local edits. Specifically, global image quality often deteriorates immediately after a single editing step. To address these challenges, we introduce SPICE, a training-free workflow that accepts arbitrary resolutions and aspect ratios, accurately follows user requirements, and consistently improves image quality during more than 100 editing steps, while keeping the unedited regions intact. By synergizing the strengths of a base diffusion model and a Canny edge ControlNet model, SPICE robustly handles free-form editing instructions from the user. On a challenging realistic image-editing dataset, SPICE quantitatively outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and is consistently preferred by human annotators. We release the workflow implementation for popular diffusion model Web UIs to support further research and artistic exploration.

paragraphs: SPICE addresses a practical problem in prompt-based image editing: detailed or local changes can damage the overall picture, sometimes after a single step. The paper introduces a training-free workflow intended to follow editing instructions while preserving regions the user has not asked to change. It also accepts arbitrary image resolutions and aspect ratios.

The workflow combines a base diffusion model with a Canny edge ControlNet model. This pairing brings the two models’ strengths together to handle free-form instructions. The authors report that SPICE can consistently improve image quality through more than one hundred editing steps while keeping unedited regions intact, making repeated refinement a central feature of the approach.

On a challenging dataset of realistic image-editing tasks, SPICE quantitatively outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and is consistently preferred by human annotators. These results support its usefulness for iterative editing that must balance requested changes with image preservation. The authors also release an implementation for popular diffusion-model web interfaces, making the workflow available for further research and artistic use.
summary.tldr: SPICE combines diffusion and edge-based control for precise, repeated image editing while preserving unedited regions.

title: SPICE: A Synergistic, Precise, Iterative, and Customizable Image Editing Workflow

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently refuse to respond to pseudo-malicious instructions: semantically harmless input queries triggering unnecessary LLM refusals due to conservative safety alignment, significantly impairing user experience. Collecting such instructions is crucial for evaluating and mitigating over-refusals, but existing instruction curation methods, like manual creation or instruction rewriting, either lack scalability or fail to produce sufficiently diverse and effective refusal-inducing prompts. To address these limitations, we introduce EVOREFUSE, a prompt optimization approach that generates diverse pseudo-malicious instructions consistently eliciting confident refusals across LLMs. EVOREFUSE employs an evolutionary algorithm exploring the instruction space in more diverse directions than existing methods via mutation strategies and recombination, and iteratively evolves seed instructions to maximize evidence lower bound on LLM refusal probability. Using EVOREFUSE, we create two novel datasets: EVOREFUSE-TEST, a benchmark of 582 pseudo-malicious instructions that outperforms the next-best benchmark with 85.34% higher average refusal triggering rate across 9 LLMs, 34.86% greater lexical diversity, and 40.03% improved LLM response confidence scores; and EVOREFUSE-ALIGN, which provides 3,000 pseudo-malicious instructions with responses for supervised and preference-based alignment training. LLAMA3.1-8B-INSTRUCT supervisedly fine-tuned on EVOREFUSE-ALIGN achieves up to 29.85% fewer over-refusals than models trained on the second-best alignment dataset, without compromising safety. Our analysis with EVOREFUSE-TEST reveals models trigger over-refusals by overly focusing on sensitive keywords while ignoring broader context. Our code and datasets are available at https://github.com/FishT0ucher/EVOREFUSE.

paragraphs: Language models sometimes reject harmless requests because their wording resembles unsafe content. EVOREFUSE generates these pseudo-malicious instructions to evaluate and reduce unnecessary refusals. It addresses the difficulty of collecting examples that are simultaneously diverse, scalable to produce, and effective at exposing overly conservative model behavior.

The method evolves seed instructions using mutations and recombination. Its optimization objective increases a lower bound on refusal probability, guiding the search toward prompts that elicit confident refusals. The authors create EVOREFUSE-TEST with 582 instructions and EVOREFUSE-ALIGN with 3,000 instruction-response examples for supervised and preference-based alignment. The evaluation set improves refusal triggering, lexical diversity, and response confidence over the next-best benchmark in the reported comparisons.

Analysis suggests that models can overemphasize sensitive keywords while overlooking broader context. The work connects that observed failure pattern to both evaluation data and corrective training.
summary.tldr: EVOREFUSE evolves harmless refusal-triggering prompts into evaluation and alignment datasets, helping reduce measured over-refusal without sacrificing evaluated safety.

title: EVOREFUSE: Evolutionary Prompt Optimization for Evaluation and Mitigation of LLM Over-Refusal to Pseudo-Malicious Instructions

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many generation tasks. Nevertheless, effectively aligning them with desired behaviors remains a significant challenge. Activation steering is an effective and cost-efficient approach that directly modifies the activations of LLMs during the inference stage, aligning their responses with the desired behaviors and avoiding the high cost of fine-tuning. Existing methods typically indiscriminately intervene to all generations or rely solely on the question to determine intervention, which limits the accurate assessment of the intervention strength. To this end, we propose the **F**lexible **A**ctivation **S**teering with **B**acktracking (**FASB**) framework, which dynamically determines both the necessity and strength of intervention by tracking the internal states of the LLMs during generation, considering both the question and the generated content. Since intervening after detecting a deviation from the desired behavior is often too late, we further propose the backtracking mechanism to correct the deviated tokens and steer the LLMs toward the desired behavior. Extensive experiments on the TruthfulQA dataset and six multiple-choice datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms baselines. Our code will be released at https://github.com/gjw185/FASB.

paragraphs: Activation steering changes a language model's internal activations during generation to encourage desired behavior without fine-tuning. Existing approaches often intervene on every generation or decide how to intervene using only the question. FASB instead monitors the model as its answer develops, using both the question and generated content.

This monitoring determines whether intervention is needed and how strong it should be. The framework also includes backtracking because detecting a behavioral deviation may occur after problematic tokens have already been generated. Backtracking lets the system correct those tokens and redirect generation, connecting detection with revision of the output already produced.

Experiments on TruthfulQA and six multiple-choice datasets show improvements over the evaluated baselines. The contribution is a more responsive use of activation steering: intervention depends on the ongoing generation process, and correction can reach back to where the answer deviated. These findings support assessing internal state throughout generation when deciding when and how strongly to steer a model.
summary.tldr: FASB monitors generation to adjust activation steering and backtracks to correct tokens produced before a deviation was detected.

title: Steering When Necessary: Flexible Steering Large Language Models with Backtracking

abstract: Sample-wise learning curves plot performance versus training set size. They are useful for studying scaling laws and speeding up hyperparameter tuning and model selection. Learning curves are often assumed to be well-behaved: monotone (i.e. improving with more data) and convex. By constructing the Learning Curves Database 1.1 (LCDB 1.1), a large-scale database with high-resolution learning curves including more modern learners (CatBoost, TabNet, RealMLP, and TabPFN), we show that learning curves are less often well-behaved than previously thought. Using statistically rigorous methods, we observe significant ill-behavior in approximately 15% of the learning curves, almost twice as much as in previous estimates. We also identify which learners are to blame and show that specific learners are more ill-behaved than others. Additionally, we demonstrate that different feature scalings rarely resolve ill-behavior. We evaluate the impact of ill-behavior on downstream tasks, such as learning curve fitting and model selection, and find it poses significant challenges, underscoring the relevance and potential of LCDB 1.1 as a challenging benchmark for future research.

paragraphs: Learning curves describe how a model's performance changes as its training set grows. They help researchers study scaling and make faster choices among models or hyperparameters. These uses often assume curves are monotone and convex: performance improves with more data and follows a regular shape. LCDB 1.1 examines how often those assumptions hold.

The authors build a large database of densely measured learning curves, including modern learners such as CatBoost, TabNet, RealMLP, and TabPFN. Statistical analysis finds significant departures from the expected behavior in approximately 15% of curves, nearly twice the frequency of earlier estimates. The tendency varies across learners, and changing feature scaling rarely resolves it.

The paper also evaluates how these irregularities affect curve fitting and model selection, finding substantial challenges for both. This matters because methods that rely on a regular curve can encounter behavior their assumptions do not capture. LCDB 1.1 supplies a benchmark for studying those cases and improving methods that make decisions from learning curves.
summary.tldr: LCDB 1.1 finds statistically significant irregular behavior in approximately 15% of learning curves, challenging assumptions used in curve fitting and model selection.

title: LCDB 1.1: A Database Illustrating Learning Curves Are More Ill-Behaved Than Previously Thought

abstract: Attention with bias, which extends standard attention by introducing prior knowledge as an additive bias matrix to the query-key scores, has been widely deployed in vision, language, protein-folding and other advanced scientific models, underscoring its status as a key evolution of this foundational module. However, introducing bias terms creates a severe efficiency bottleneck in attention computation. It disrupts the tightly fused memory-compute pipeline that underlies the speed of accelerators like FlashAttention, thereby stripping away most of their performance gains and leaving biased attention computationally expensive. Surprisingly, despite its common usage, targeted efficiency optimization for attention with bias remains absent, which seriously hinders its application in complex tasks. Diving into the computation of FlashAttention, we prove that its optimal efficiency is determined by the rank of the attention weight matrix. Inspired by this theoretical result, this paper presents FlashBias based on the low-rank compressed sensing theory, which can provide fast-exact computation for many widely used attention biases and a fast-accurate approximation for biases in general formalizations. FlashBias can fully take advantage of the extremely optimized matrix multiplication operation in modern GPUs, achieving 1.5$\times$ speedup for Pairformer in AlphaFold 3, and over 2$\times$ speedup for attention with bias in vision and language models without loss of accuracy. Code is available at this repository: https://github.com/thuml/FlashBias.

paragraphs: Attention with bias adds prior information to the scores that determine which inputs attend to one another. Although this is widely used in language, vision, and scientific models, the additional bias can disrupt the tightly coordinated memory access and computation that make FlashAttention fast. The paper targets that specific source of computational expense.

The authors establish a theoretical connection between FlashAttention’s optimal efficiency and the rank of the attention weight matrix. Building on that result, FlashBias uses low-rank compressed sensing theory to reorganize biased attention computation. It supports fast exact computation for many commonly used biases and fast, accurate approximation for more general bias formulations.

This distinction matters because the method does not claim exactness for every possible bias. Its implementation makes use of highly optimized GPU matrix multiplication. The reported results include a 1.5-fold speedup for AlphaFold 3’s Pairformer and more than a twofold speedup for biased attention in vision and language models without loss of accuracy. These findings show that incorporating prior information into attention need not forfeit the reported acceleration benefits.
summary.tldr: FlashBias accelerates attention with additive biases through exact computation for many common biases and accurate approximation for general ones.

title: FlashBias: Fast Computation of Attention with Bias

abstract: Gradient clipping is increasingly important in centralized learning (CL) and federated learning (FL). Many works focus on its optimization properties under strong assumptions involving Gaussian noise and standard smoothness. However, practical machine learning tasks often only satisfy weaker conditions, such as heavy-tailed noise and $(L_0, L_1)$-smoothness. To bridge this gap, we propose a high-probability analysis for clipped Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) under these weaker assumptions. Our findings show a better convergence rate than existing ones can be achieved, and our high-probability analysis does not rely on the bounded gradient assumption. Moreover, we extend our analysis to FL, where a gap remains between expected and high-probability convergence, which the naive clipped SGD cannot bridge. Thus, we design a new \underline{Fed}erated \underline{C}lipped \underline{B}atched \underline{G}radient (FedCBG) algorithm, and prove the convergence and generalization bounds with high probability for the first time. Our analysis reveals the trade-offs between the optimization and generalization performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that \methodname{} can generalize better to unseen client distributions than state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Gradient clipping is widely used in centralized and federated learning, but its theoretical analysis often assumes Gaussian noise and standard smoothness. This paper studies weaker conditions: heavy-tailed noise and a generalized smoothness condition called (L0, L1)-smoothness. It seeks convergence guarantees that hold with high probability, providing control beyond statements about performance averaged over randomness.

For clipped stochastic gradient descent, the analysis establishes a better convergence rate than existing results and does not require bounded gradients. The authors then examine federated learning, where simply applying clipped SGD does not close the gap between expected and high-probability convergence. They introduce Federated Clipped Batched Gradient, or FedCBG, to address that problem.

The paper proves high-probability convergence and generalization bounds for the proposed federated algorithm and exposes trade-offs between optimization and generalization. Experiments report better generalization to unseen client distributions than state-of-the-art baselines. Together, the results connect weaker noise and smoothness assumptions with guarantees and empirical behavior relevant to heterogeneous federated data.
summary.tldr: The paper strengthens high-probability guarantees for clipped SGD under weaker assumptions and introduces FedCBG for federated optimization and generalization.

title: Tight High-Probability Bounds for Nonconvex Heavy-Tailed Scenario under Weaker Assumptions

abstract: Meta-learning has been demonstrated to be useful to improve the sampling efficiency of Bayesian optimization (BO) and surrogate-assisted evolutionary algorithms (SAEAs) when solving expensive optimization problems (EOPs). Existing studies mainly focus on either combinations of existing meta-learning modeling methods with optimization algorithms, or the development of meta-learning acquisition functions for specific meta BO. However, the meta-learning models used in the literature are not designed for optimization purpose, and the generalization ability of meta-learning acquisition functions is limited. In this work, we develop a novel architecture of meta-learning model for optimization purpose and propose a generalized few-shot evolutionary optimization (FSEO) framework to solve EOPs. We focus on the scenario of expensive multi-objective EOPs (EMOPs) in the context of few-shot optimization as there are few studies on it and its high requirement on surrogate modeling performance. The surrogates in FSEO framework combines neural network with Gaussian Processes (GPs), their network parameters and some parameters of GPs represent task-independent experience and are meta-learned across related optimization tasks, the remaining GPs parameters are task-specific parameters that represent unique features of the target task. We demonstrate that our FSEO framework is able to improve the sampling efficiency of existing SAEAs on EMOPs.

paragraphs: When evaluating a candidate solution is expensive, optimization must make productive use of a small number of evaluations. FSEO addresses this challenge for problems with multiple objectives. It uses experience from related optimization tasks to improve surrogate models, which help evolutionary algorithms decide how to search without evaluating every candidate directly.

The proposed surrogate combines a neural network with Gaussian processes. Network parameters and some Gaussian-process parameters represent experience shared across tasks and are meta-learned from related problems. Other Gaussian-process parameters remain specific to the target task. This division gives the model both reusable optimization knowledge and a way to represent features unique to the current problem.

The paper develops this architecture specifically for optimization and incorporates it into a generalized few-shot evolutionary framework. Its results demonstrate improved sampling efficiency for existing surrogate-assisted evolutionary algorithms on expensive multi-objective problems. The stated gain concerns using costly evaluations more effectively, with transfer from related tasks and target-specific modeling working together within the surrogate.
summary.tldr: FSEO meta-learns neural-network and Gaussian-process surrogates to improve evaluation efficiency in expensive multi-objective evolutionary optimization.

title: FSEO: Few-Shot Evolutionary Optimization via Meta-Learning for Expensive Multi-Objective Optimization

abstract: Reference-driven image completion, which restores missing regions in a target view using additional images, is particularly challenging when the target view differs significantly from the references. Existing generative methods rely solely on diffusion priors and, without geometric cues such as camera pose or depth, often produce misaligned or implausible content. We propose GeoComplete, a novel framework that incorporates explicit 3D structural guidance to enforce geometric consistency in the completed regions, setting it apart from prior image-only approaches. GeoComplete introduces two key ideas: conditioning the diffusion process on projected point clouds to infuse geometric information, and applying target-aware masking to guide the model toward relevant reference cues. The framework features a dual-branch diffusion architecture. One branch synthesizes the missing regions from the masked target, while the other extracts geometric features from the projected point cloud. Joint self-attention across branches ensures coherent and accurate completion. To address regions visible in references but absent in the target, we project the target view into each reference to detect occluded areas, which are then masked during training. This target-aware masking directs the model to focus on useful cues, enhancing performance in difficult scenarios. By integrating a geometry-aware dual-branch diffusion architecture with a target-aware masking strategy, GeoComplete offers a unified and robust solution for geometry-conditioned image completion. Experiments show that GeoComplete achieves a 17.1% PSNR improvement over state-of-the-art methods, significantly boosting geometric accuracy while maintaining high visual quality.

paragraphs: Reference-driven image completion fills missing regions in a target image using other views. Large viewpoint differences make this difficult because visually plausible content can still be geometrically misaligned. GeoComplete introduces explicit three-dimensional structural guidance so that completion can account for how the scene should appear from the target viewpoint.

Its diffusion architecture has two branches. One generates the missing image regions from the masked target, while the other extracts geometric features from a projected point cloud. Joint self-attention lets the branches exchange information during completion. This couples image synthesis with a geometric representation, giving the generator structural cues beyond those available from image appearance alone.

GeoComplete also projects the target view into reference images to identify occluded regions and masks those areas during training. This target-aware masking directs learning toward reference cues useful for the target view. Experiments report a 17.1% improvement in PSNR over state-of-the-art methods, together with improved geometric accuracy and high visual quality. The results support combining explicit geometry with selective use of reference information.
summary.tldr: GeoComplete combines projected 3D geometry and target-aware reference masking to improve image completion across differing viewpoints.

title: GeoComplete: Geometry-Aware Diffusion for Reference-Driven Image Completion

abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables distributed devices to collaboratively train machine learning (ML) models while maintaining data privacy. However, the heterogeneous hardware capabilities of participating devices often result in significant training delays, as straggler clients with limited resources prolong the aggregation process. Existing solutions such as client selection, asynchronous FL, and partial training partially address these challenges but encounter issues such as reduced accuracy, stale updates, and compromised model performance due to inconsistent training contributions. To overcome these limitations, we propose FedEL, a federated elastic learning framework that enhances training efficiency while maintaining model accuracy. FedEL introduces a novel window-based training process, sliding the window to locate the training part of the model and dynamically selecting important tensors for training within a coordinated runtime budget. This approach ensures progressive and balanced training across all clients, including stragglers. Additionally, FedEL employs a tensor importance adjustment module, harmonizing local and global tensor importance to mitigate biases caused by data heterogeneity. The experiment results shows that FedEL achieves up to 3.87× improvement in time-to-accuracy compared to baselines while maintaining or exceeding final test accuracy.
originalAbstract: Federated learning (FL) enables distributed devices to collaboratively train machine learning (ML) models while maintaining data privacy. However, the heterogeneous hardware capabilities of participating devices often result in significant training delays, as straggler clients with limited resources prolong the aggregation process. Existing solutions such as client selection, asynchronous FL, and partial training partially address these challenges but encounter issues such as reduced accuracy, stale updates, and compromised model performance due to inconsistent training contributions. To overcome these limitations, we propose FedEL, a federated elastic learning framework that enhances training efficiency while maintaining model accuracy. FedEL introduces a novel window-based training process, sliding the window to locate the training part of the model and dynamically selecting important tensors for training within a coordinated runtime budget. This approach ensures progressive and balanced training across all clients, including stragglers. Additionally, FedEL employs a tensor importance adjustment module, harmonizing local and global tensor importance to mitigate biases caused by data heterogeneity. The experiment results shows that FedEL achieves up to 3.87× improvement in time-to-accuracy compared to baselines while maintaining or exceeding final test accuracy.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets distributed devices contribute to shared model training while keeping their data local. Differences in hardware can make this process slow because resource-limited clients delay aggregation. FedEL aims to improve training speed while preserving accuracy and keeping slower devices involved in a coordinated learning process.

Its main mechanism is a sliding training window that determines which portion of the model a client trains. Within a coordinated runtime budget, FedEL dynamically selects important tensors from that portion. Moving the window supports progressive, balanced training across clients. A separate adjustment module reconciles local and global tensor importance to reduce biases associated with differences in client data.

Experiments report up to a 3.87-fold improvement in time-to-accuracy over the evaluated baselines, while matching or exceeding their final test accuracy. This is a reported maximum improvement, rather than a uniform gain for every setting. The results support adapting the amount and location of training work to device capabilities while coordinating contributions across the model.
summary.tldr: FedEL coordinates selective model training across unequal devices, reporting up to 3.87× better time-to-accuracy while preserving final accuracy.

title: FedEL: Federated Elastic Learning for Heterogeneous Devices

abstract: Heterophilous graphs, where dissimilar nodes tend to connect, pose a challenge for graph neural networks (GNNs). Increasing the GNN depth can expand the scope (i.e., receptive field), potentially finding homophily from the higher-order neighborhoods. However, GNNs suffer from performance degradation as depth increases. Despite having better expressivity, state-of-the-art deeper GNNs achieve only marginal improvements compared to their shallow variants. Through theoretical and empirical analysis, we systematically demonstrate a shift in GNN generalization preferences across nodes with different homophily levels as depth increases. This creates a disparity in generalization patterns between GNN models with varying depth. Based on these findings, we propose to improve deeper GNN generalization while maintaining high expressivity by Mixture of scope experts at test (Moscat). Experimental results show that Moscat works flexibly with various GNN architectures across a wide range of datasets while significantly improving accuracy.

paragraphs: In heterophilous graphs, connected nodes often differ from one another, making immediate neighbors potentially difficult sources of predictive information. A deeper graph neural network can inspect more distant neighborhoods, where similar nodes may become accessible. Yet increasing depth can also degrade performance, so a larger information-gathering scope does not automatically translate into better predictions.

The paper studies this tension theoretically and empirically. It finds that changing depth shifts generalization preferences across nodes with different levels of homophily. Consequently, shallow and deep versions of a network can have different patterns of strengths across nodes. This provides a reason to consider their scopes jointly rather than treating depth as a uniformly beneficial choice.

Based on that analysis, Moscat combines scope experts at test time to improve deeper networks’ generalization while retaining their expressivity. Experiments show significant accuracy improvements across a wide range of datasets and compatibility with various graph neural network architectures. The findings support using the complementary generalization patterns of shallow and deep variants.
summary.tldr: Moscat improves deeper graph networks by combining experts with different neighborhood scopes at test time.

title: Mixture of Scope Experts at Test: Generalizing Deeper Graph Neural Networks with Shallow Variants

abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has emerged as a powerful framework for modeling autonomous agents that independently optimize their individual objectives. However, in mixed-motive MARL environments, rational self-interested behaviors often lead to collectively suboptimal outcomes situations commonly referred to as social dilemmas. A key challenge in addressing social dilemmas lies in accurately quantifying and representing them in a numerical form that captures how self-interested agent behaviors impact social welfare. To address this challenge, \textit{externalities} in the economic concept is adopted and extended to denote the unaccounted-for impact of one agent's actions on others, as a means to rigorously quantify social dilemmas. Based on this measurement, a novel method, \textbf{L}earning \textbf{O}ptimal \textbf{P}igovian \textbf{T}ax (\textbf{LOPT}) is proposed. Inspired by Pigovian taxes, which are designed to internalize externalities by imposing cost on negative societal impacts, LOPT employs an auxiliary tax agent that learns an optimal Pigovian tax policy to reshape individual rewards aligned with social welfare, thereby promoting agent coordination and mitigating social dilemmas. We support LOPT with theoretical analysis and validate it on standard MARL benchmarks, including Escape Room and Cleanup. Results show that by effectively internalizing externalities that quantify social dilemmas, LOPT aligns individual objectives with collective goals, significantly improving social welfare over state-of-the-art baselines.

This paper uses the economic concept of externalities to quantify those unaccounted-for effects, giving social dilemmas a numerical representation tied to social welfare.

LOPT introduces an auxiliary tax agent that learns a Pigovian tax policy. Its role is to reshape individual rewards so that the consequences of an agent’s behavior for others enter its own incentives. By internalizing these externalities, the method aims to make self-interested learning more compatible with coordination and collective goals.

The authors support the approach with theoretical analysis and experiments on standard multi-agent benchmarks, including Escape Room and Cleanup. They report significantly higher social welfare than state-of-the-art baselines. The findings connect measurement and intervention: quantifying the external effects of behavior provides a basis for learning reward adjustments that improve group outcomes in the evaluated environments, rather than relying solely on agents’ original individual rewards.
summary.tldr: LOPT learns tax-based reward adjustments that account for agents’ effects on others and improve collective welfare in tested social dilemmas.

title: LOPT: Learning Optimal Pigovian Tax in Sequential Social Dilemmas

abstract: Learning shared representations is a primary area of multimodal representation learning. The current approaches to achieve a shared embedding space rely heavily on paired samples from each modality, which are significantly harder to obtain than unpaired ones. In this work, we demonstrate that shared representations can be learned almost exclusively from unpaired data. Our arguments are grounded in the spectral embeddings of the random walk matrices constructed independently from each unimodal representation. Empirical results in computer vision and natural language processing domains support its potential, revealing the effectiveness of unpaired data in capturing meaningful cross-modal relations, demonstrating high capabilities in retrieval tasks, generation, arithmetics, zero-shot, and cross-domain classification. This work, to the best of our knowledge, is the first to demonstrate these capabilities almost exclusively from unpaired samples, giving rise to a cross-modal embedding that could be viewed as universal, i.e., independent of the specific modalities of the data. Our project page: https://shaham-lab.github.io/SUE_page.

paragraphs: Shared representations place different kinds of data into a common embedding space so that relationships can be expressed across modalities. Training such spaces usually relies heavily on paired examples, which are harder to obtain than independent collections. This paper demonstrates that useful shared representations can be learned almost exclusively from unpaired data.

The argument draws on spectral embeddings of random-walk matrices constructed separately from each modality's representations. Rather than making paired observations the main foundation, it uses structure available within the individual modalities. The central question is whether those independently constructed structures can support a common representation that captures meaningful cross-modal relationships.

Experiments in computer vision and natural language processing support that possibility across retrieval, generation, representation arithmetic, zero-shot classification, and cross-domain classification. The authors suggest that the resulting embedding could be regarded as universal in the sense of being independent of particular modalities. That remains a proposed interpretation of the findings; the demonstrated training regime is almost entirely unpaired, rather than asserted to require no paired data whatsoever.
summary.tldr: The paper shows that spectral structure within separate modalities can support useful shared embeddings learned almost entirely from unpaired data.

title: Learning Shared Representations from Unpaired Data

abstract: The recently proposed optimization algorithm for deep neural networks Sharpness Aware Minimization (SAM) suggests perturbing parameters before gradient calculation by a gradient ascent step to guide the optimization into parameter space regions of flat loss. While significant generalization improvements and thus reduction of overfitting could be demonstrated, the computational costs are doubled due to the additionally needed gradient calculation, making SAM unfeasible in case of limited computationally capacities. Motivated by Nesterov Accelerated Gradient (NAG) we propose Momentum-SAM (MSAM), which perturbs parameters in the direction of the accumulated momentum vector to achieve low sharpness without significant computational overhead or memory demands over SGD or Adam. We evaluate MSAM in detail and reveal insights on separable mechanisms of NAG, SAM and MSAM regarding training optimization and generalization.

While significant generalization improvements and thus reduction of overfitting could be demonstrated, the computational costs are doubled due to the additionally needed gradient calculation, making SAM unfeasible in case of limited computationally capacities. Motivated by Nesterov Accelerated Gradient (NAG) we propose Momentum-SAM (MSAM), which perturbs parameters in the direction of the accumulated momentum vector to achieve low sharpness without significant computational overhead or memory demands over SGD or Adam. We evaluate MSAM in detail and reveal insights on separable mechanisms of NAG, SAM and MSAM regarding training optimization and generalization.

paragraphs: Sharpness Aware Minimization, or SAM, trains neural networks by perturbing their parameters before calculating the gradient used for optimization. The aim is to reach regions where the loss changes less sharply with parameter changes. SAM has shown generalization benefits, but obtaining its perturbation requires an additional gradient calculation that doubles computational cost.

Momentum-SAM replaces that gradient-based perturbation direction with the accumulated momentum vector. Inspired by Nesterov Accelerated Gradient, it uses information accumulated during optimization to guide the parameter perturbation. The authors propose this as a way to obtain low sharpness without significant additional computation or memory compared with SGD or Adam.

The paper evaluates Momentum-SAM in detail and examines separable mechanisms behind Nesterov acceleration, SAM, and the proposed method. This analysis distinguishes effects on training optimization from effects on generalization. The approach matters because it targets the extra work that makes SAM difficult to use with limited computational capacity, while investigating how momentum-based perturbations relate to the benefits of sharpness-aware training.
summary.tldr: Momentum-SAM uses accumulated momentum to guide sharpness-aware parameter perturbations without significant overhead over SGD or Adam.

title: Momentum-SAM: Sharpness Aware Minimization without Computational Overhead

abstract: What does it truly mean for a language model to “reason” strategically, and can scaling up alone guarantee intelligent, context-aware decisions? Strategic decision-making requires adaptive reasoning, where agents anticipate and respond to others’ actions under uncertainty. Yet, most evaluations of large language models (LLMs) for strategic decision-making often rely heavily on Nash Equilibrium (NE) benchmarks, overlook reasoning depth, and fail to reveal the mechanisms behind model behavior. To address this gap, we introduce a behavioral game-theoretic evaluation framework that disentangles intrinsic reasoning from contextual influence. Using this framework, we evaluate 22 state-of-the-art LLMs across diverse strategic scenarios. We find models like GPT-o3-mini, GPT-o1, and DeepSeek-R1 lead in reasoning depth. Through thinking chain analysis, we identify distinct reasoning styles—such as maximin or belief-based strategies—and show that longer reasoning chains do not consistently yield better decisions. Furthermore, embedding demographic personas reveals context-sensitive shifts: some models (e.g., GPT-4o, Claude-3-Opus) improve when assigned female identities, while others (e.g., Gemini 2.0) show diminished reasoning under minority sexuality personas. These findings underscore that technical sophistication alone is insufficient; alignment with ethical standards, human expectations, and situational nuance is essential for the responsible deployment of LLMs in interactive settings.

paragraphs: Strategic reasoning involves anticipating other participants’ actions and adapting decisions under uncertainty. The paper argues that evaluations centered on Nash equilibrium benchmarks can overlook how deeply language models reason and what drives their choices. It introduces a behavioral game theory framework designed to separate intrinsic reasoning from contextual influences, then evaluates 22 models across varied strategic scenarios.

GPT-o3-mini, GPT-o1, and DeepSeek-R1 are among the leaders in reasoning depth. Examining models’ thinking chains also reveals different strategic styles, including maximin and belief-based approaches. Longer chains do not consistently produce better decisions. This finding makes reasoning length an unreliable stand-in for decision quality in these evaluations and highlights the value of examining how models approach a strategic problem.

Some, including GPT-4o and Claude-3-Opus, improve when given female identities, while Gemini 2.0 shows reduced reasoning under minority sexuality personas. These results describe model responses to assigned identities, rather than properties of those demographic groups. The authors connect this context sensitivity to responsible deployment: technical sophistication alone is insufficient, and interactive systems must also account for ethical standards, human expectations, and situational nuance.
summary.tldr: An evaluation of 22 language models reveals differences in strategic reasoning depth, finds that longer reasoning does not consistently improve decisions, and shows sensitivity to assigned demographic personas.

title: LLM Strategic Reasoning: Agentic Study through Behavioral Game Theory

abstract: Motivated by applications for set containment problems, we consider the following fundamental problem: can we design set-to-vector functions so that the natural partial order on sets is preserved, namely $S\subseteq T \text{ if and only if } F(S)\leq F(T) $. We call functions satisfying this property \emph{Monotone and Separating (MAS)} set functions. We establish lower and upper bounds for the vector dimension necessary to obtain MAS functions, as a function of the cardinality of the multisets and the underlying ground set. In the important case of an infinite ground set, we show that MAS functions do not exist, but provide a model called \our\ which provably enjoys a relaxed MAS property we name 'weakly MAS' and is stable in the sense of Holder continuity. We also show that MAS functions can be used to construct universal models which are monotone by construction, and can approximate all monotone set functions. Experimentally, we consider a variety of set containtment tasks. The experiments show the benefit of using our \our\ model, in comparsion with standard set models which do not incorporate set containment as an inductive bias.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether sets can be represented as vectors that preserve containment exactly. The desired rule works in both directions: one set is contained in another precisely when its representation is no larger in every coordinate. The authors call representations with this property monotone and separating, or MAS.

They establish bounds on the vector dimension required, depending on multiset size and the underlying collection of possible elements. For an infinite underlying set, they show that MAS functions do not exist. They therefore introduce a neural model with a relaxed property called weakly MAS and prove stability through Hölder continuity.

The work also shows how MAS functions can construct universal models that preserve monotonicity by design while approximating all monotone set functions. Experiments on containment tasks demonstrate benefits over standard set models without a containment-based inductive bias. The theoretical results clarify both the representational requirements of exact containment and why a principled relaxation is needed in the infinite-ground-set case.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes vector representations that preserve set containment and develops a stable relaxation for settings where exact preservation is impossible.

title: Monotone and Separable Set Functions: Characterizations and Neural Models

abstract: Abstract Visual Reasoning (AVR) entails discerning latent patterns in visual data and inferring underlying rules. Existing solutions often lack scalability and adaptability, as deep architectures tend to overfit training data, and static neural networks fail to dynamically capture diverse rules. To tackle the challenges, we propose a Dynamic and Scalable Reasoning Framework (DSRF) that greatly enhances the reasoning ability by widening the network instead of deepening it, and dynamically adjusting the reasoning network to better fit novel samples instead of a static network. Specifically, we design a Multi-View Reasoning Pyramid (MVRP) to capture complex rules through layered reasoning to focus features at each view on distinct combinations of attributes, widening the reasoning network to cover more attribute combinations analogous to complex reasoning rules. Additionally, we propose a Dynamic Domain-Contrast Prediction (DDCP) block to handle varying task-specific relationships dynamically by introducing a Gram matrix to model feature distributions, and a gate matrix to capture subtle domain differences between context and target features. Extensive experiments on six AVR tasks demonstrate DSRF’s superior performance, achieving state-of-the-art results under various settings. Code is available here: https://github.com/UNNCRoxLi/DSRF.

paragraphs: Abstract visual reasoning requires finding hidden patterns and inferring the rules that connect visual examples. DSRF addresses two difficulties identified in existing approaches: deeper models can overfit, and fixed networks can struggle to accommodate different rules. Its design expands the range of reasoning pathways and adjusts processing to individual samples.

The Multi-View Reasoning Pyramid organizes features around different combinations of attributes. This widens the network's coverage of possible rule combinations while retaining layered reasoning within each view. A Dynamic Domain-Contrast Prediction block then models relationships that vary across tasks. It uses a Gram matrix to represent feature distributions and a gate matrix to capture differences between context and target features.

The two components address complementary needs: representing a wider variety of patterns and adapting comparisons to the current problem. Experiments across six abstract visual reasoning tasks report state-of-the-art performance under multiple settings. These results support the framework's combination of broader attribute coverage and sample-dependent reasoning in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: DSRF improves abstract visual reasoning by expanding attribute-combination pathways and dynamically adapting relationships to each problem.

title: DSRF: A Dynamic and Scalable Reasoning Framework for Solving RPMs

abstract: Recent advancements in video generation models have enabled the creation of diverse and realistic videos, with promising applications in advertising and film production. However, as one of the essential tasks of video generation models, video concept transfer remains significantly challenging. Existing methods generally model video as an entirety, leading to limited flexibility and precision when solely editing specific regions or concepts. To mitigate this dilemma, we propose a novel architecture UniTransfer, which introduces both spatial and diffusion timestep decomposition in a progressive paradigm, achieving precise and controllable video concept transfer. Specifically, in terms of spatial decomposition, we decouple videos into three key components: the foreground subject, the background, and the motion flow. Building upon this decomposed formulation, we further introduce a dual-to-single-stream DiT-based architecture for supporting fine-grained control over different components in the videos. We also introduce a self-supervised pretraining strategy based on random masking to enhance the decomposed representation learning from large-scale unlabeled video data. Inspired by the Chain-of-Thought reasoning paradigm, we further revisit the denoising diffusion process and propose a Chain-of-Prompt (CoP) mechanism to achieve the timestep decomposition. We decompose the denoising process into three stages of different granularity and leverage large language models (LLMs) for stage-specific instructions to guide the generation progressively. We also curate an animal-centric video dataset called OpenAnimal to facilitate the advancement and benchmarking of research in video concept transfer. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves high-quality and controllable video concept transfer across diverse reference images and scenes, surpassing existing baselines in both visual fidelity and editability.

paragraphs: UniTransfer makes video concept transfer more controllable by separating elements that are often modeled together. It divides a video into foreground subject, background, and motion flow. This decomposition addresses the difficulty of changing a specific concept or region precisely when the entire video is treated as a single unit.

A dual-to-single-stream diffusion-transformer architecture supports control over these components. Random-masking pretraining helps learn their representations from large amounts of unlabeled video. The method also divides diffusion denoising into three stages with different levels of granularity. Their experiments report high-quality, controllable transfer across varied reference images and scenes, outperforming existing baselines in visual fidelity and editability. The combined finding is that separating both video components and denoising stages can improve control while retaining visual quality in the evaluated transfer tasks.
summary.tldr: UniTransfer separates video components and stages diffusion guidance to improve the visual quality and controllability of concept transfer.

title: UniTransfer: Video Concept Transfer via Progressive Spatio-Temporal Decomposition

abstract: Model pruning has gained traction as a promising defense strategy against backdoor attacks in deep learning. However, existing pruning-based approaches often fall short in accurately identifying and removing the specific parameters responsible for inducing backdoor behaviors. Despite the dominance of fine-tuning-based defenses in recent literature, largely due to their superior performance, pruning remains a compelling alternative, offering greater interpretability and improved robustness in low-data regimes. In this paper, we propose a novel pruning approach featuring a learned \emph{selection} mechanism to identify parameters critical to both main and backdoor tasks, along with an \emph{invertible} pruning mask designed to simultaneously achieve two complementary goals: eliminating the backdoor task while preserving it through the inverse mask. We formulate this as a bi-level optimization problem that jointly learns selection variables, a sparse invertible mask, and sample-specific backdoor perturbations derived from clean data. The inner problem synthesizes candidate triggers using the inverse mask, while the outer problem refines the mask to suppress backdoor behavior without impairing clean-task accuracy. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing pruning-based backdoor mitigation approaches, maintains strong performance under limited data conditions, and achieves competitive results compared to state-of-the-art fine-tuning approaches. Notably, the proposed approach is particularly effective in restoring correct predictions for compromised samples after successful backdoor mitigation.
