paragraphs: Online learning requires decisions as data arrive, including decisions about the learning system's own configuration. ChaCha addresses this problem by choosing hyperparameters during the online learning process. It organizes the search around a current champion and a changing group of live challengers, making configuration selection an ongoing part of learning.

The algorithm determines which configuration should be champion and schedules challengers using sample complexity bounds. These bounds inform how candidates are evaluated over time. An application-dependent oracle proposes configurations based on the champions, so the candidate-generation mechanism is an explicit part of the setup rather than something the algorithm's guarantee makes unnecessary.

The theoretical result guarantees sublinear regret after the optimal configuration enters consideration through that oracle. This means the cumulative performance gap grows more slowly than the learning duration under the stated condition. Experiments report good performance across a wide range of datasets while optimizing both feature-construction choices and hyperparameters, supporting the practical usefulness of the champion–challenger organization.
summary.tldr: ChaCha manages competing online learning configurations and guarantees sublinear regret once an application-dependent oracle introduces the optimal configuration.

title: ChaCha for Online AutoML

abstract: Sparse coding strategies have been lauded for their parsimonious representations of data that leverage low dimensional structure. However, inference of these codes typically relies on an optimization procedure with poor computational scaling in high-dimensional problems. For example, sparse inference in the representations learned in the high-dimensional intermediary layers of deep neural networks (DNNs) requires an iterative minimization to be performed at each training step. As such, recent, quick methods in variational inference have been proposed to infer sparse codes by learning a distribution over the codes with a DNN. In this work, we propose a new approach to variational sparse coding that allows us to learn sparse distributions by thresholding samples, avoiding the use of problematic relaxations. We first evaluate and analyze our method by training a linear generator, showing that it has superior performance, statistical efficiency, and gradient estimation compared to other sparse distributions. We then compare to a standard variational autoencoder using a DNN generator on the CelebA dataset.

paragraphs: Sparse coding represents data using relatively few active components, taking advantage of low-dimensional structure. Inferring those codes can be expensive in high-dimensional problems. In deep-network intermediate representations, it can require an iterative optimization at every training step. Variational approaches instead learn a distribution over codes using a neural network.

This paper proposes learning sparse distributions by thresholding samples. The thresholding mechanism provides sparsity while avoiding problematic relaxations used to make the learning process tractable. The approach fits within variational sparse coding, targeting the distribution of codes rather than repeatedly solving a separate optimization problem for each inference.

The authors first study the method with a linear generator. In that setting, they report better performance, statistical efficiency, and gradient estimation than alternative sparse distributions. They then compare a version with a deep neural generator against a standard variational autoencoder on CelebA. The stated positive findings concern the linear-generator analysis, while the additional comparison examines the method in a more complex image-generation setting.
summary.tldr: Learned sample thresholding enables variational sparse coding without problematic relaxations, improving several measures in the paper's linear-generator evaluation.

title: Variational Sparse Coding with Learned Thresholding

abstract: Linear contextual bandits and their variants are usually solved using algorithms guided by parameter estimation. Cauchy-Schwartz inequality established that estimation errors dominate algorithm regrets, and thus, accurate estimators suffice to guarantee algorithms with low regrets. In this paper, we complete the reverse direction by establishing the necessity. In particular, we provide a generic transformation from algorithms for linear contextual bandits to estimators for linear models, and show that algorithm regrets dominate estimation errors of their induced estimators, i.e., low-regret algorithms must imply accurate estimators. Moreover, our analysis reduces the regret lower bound to an estimation error, bridging the lower bound analysis in linear contextual bandit problems and linear regression.

paragraphs: Linear contextual bandit algorithms make decisions while learning how observed features relate to rewards. Many approaches rely on estimating the parameters of a linear model. A familiar theoretical argument establishes that sufficiently accurate estimates can produce low regret, meaning a small cumulative shortfall relative to better decisions. This paper investigates the reverse relationship: what does successful decision-making imply about estimation?

The authors construct a general transformation that turns a linear contextual bandit algorithm into an estimator for a linear model. They show that the resulting estimator’s error is controlled by the algorithm’s regret. Consequently, a low-regret algorithm must yield an accurate estimator through this transformation, even if parameter estimation is not the algorithm’s explicit organizing principle.

This relationship provides a route to proving limits on bandit performance. Estimation lower bounds can help establish regret lower bounds, connecting the analysis of sequential decisions to linear regression. The contribution therefore complements existing sufficiency arguments with a necessity result and a reusable analytical reduction.
summary.tldr: A general reduction shows that low-regret linear contextual bandit algorithms must induce accurate linear-model estimators.

title: A Reduction from Linear Contextual Bandits Lower Bounds to Estimations Lower Bounds

abstract: Graph learning (GL) aims to infer the topology of an unknown graph from a set of observations on its nodes, i.e., graph signals. While most of the existing GL approaches focus on homogeneous datasets, in many real world applications, data is heterogeneous, where graph signals are clustered and each cluster is associated with a different graph. In this paper, we address the problem of learning multiple graphs from heterogeneous data by formulating an optimization problem for joint graph signal clustering and graph topology inference. In particular, our approach extends spectral clustering by partitioning the graph signals not only based on their pairwise similarities but also their smoothness with respect to the graphs associated with the clusters. The proposed method also learns the representative graph for each cluster using the smoothness of the graph signals with respect to the graph topology. The resulting optimization problem is solved with an efficient block-coordinate descent algorithm and results on simulated and real data indicate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Graph learning infers connections between nodes from measurements taken at those nodes. Many methods assume that all observations share one underlying graph. This paper addresses heterogeneous data, where different groups of observations may instead correspond to different graph structures, requiring both the groups and their graphs to be discovered.

The authors formulate clustering and graph inference as a joint optimization problem. Their method extends spectral clustering by considering not only pairwise similarities between graph signals but also how smoothly those signals vary over a candidate cluster graph. It learns a representative graph for each cluster using the same relationship between signal smoothness and graph topology.

This coupling allows the inferred graph structure to inform the grouping of observations, while each group’s signals inform its graph. The resulting problem is solved using an efficient block-coordinate descent algorithm. Results on simulated and real data indicate that the method is effective. The contribution is a unified treatment of two interdependent tasks that arise when a single graph cannot adequately represent all the observations.
summary.tldr: The method jointly clusters heterogeneous graph signals and learns a representative graph for each cluster using similarity and signal smoothness.

title: Simultaneous Graph Signal Clustering and Graph Learning

abstract: We study the entropic Gromov-Wasserstein and its unbalanced version between (unbalanced) Gaussian distributions with different dimensions. When the metric is the inner product, which we refer to as inner product Gromov-Wasserstein (IGW), we demonstrate that the optimal transportation plans of entropic IGW and its unbalanced variant are (unbalanced) Gaussian distributions. Via an application of von Neumann’s trace inequality, we obtain closed-form expressions for the entropic IGW between these Gaussian distributions. Finally, we consider an entropic inner product Gromov-Wasserstein barycenter of multiple Gaussian distributions. We prove that the barycenter is a Gaussian distribution when the entropic regularization parameter is small. We further derive a closed-form expression for the covariance matrix of the barycenter.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to compare Gaussian distributions that may occupy spaces of different dimensions. It considers entropy-regularized Gromov–Wasserstein transport and an unbalanced variant. The analysis focuses on the inner-product formulation, called IGW, so its conclusions concern that particular way of comparing the internal structure of distributions.

The authors show that optimal transport plans for entropic IGW between Gaussian distributions are themselves Gaussian, with an analogous result for the unbalanced version. This identifies the form of the optimal solution. Using von Neumann’s trace inequality, they then obtain closed-form expressions for the entropic IGW comparison between the distributions.

The paper also studies a barycenter, a representative distribution for several Gaussian inputs under this transport criterion. It proves that this barycenter is Gaussian when the entropy-regularization parameter is small, and derives an explicit formula for its covariance matrix. Together, the results turn these transport and averaging questions into analytically characterized problems within the stated Gaussian and inner-product setting.
summary.tldr: For Gaussian inputs, entropic inner-product Gromov–Wasserstein transport has Gaussian optimal plans and closed-form expressions.

title: Entropic Gromov-Wasserstein between Gaussian Distributions

abstract: We consider the linear contextual multi-class multi-period packing problem (LMMP) where the goal is to pack items such that the total vector of consumption is below a given budget vector and the total value is as large as possible. We consider the setting where the reward and the consumption vector associated with each action is a class-dependent linear function of the context, and the decision-maker receives bandit feedback. LMMP includes linear contextual bandits with knapsacks and online revenue management as special cases. We establish a new estimator which guarantees a faster convergence rate, and consequently, a lower regret in LMMP. We propose a bandit policy that is a closed-form function of said estimated parameters. When the contexts are non-degenerate, the regret of the proposed policy is sublinear in the context dimension, the number of classes, and the time horizon $T$ when the budget grows at least as $\sqrt{T}$. We also resolve an open problem posed in Agrawal & Devanur (2016) and extend the result to a multi-class setting. Our numerical experiments clearly demonstrate that the performance of our policy is superior to other benchmarks in the literature.

Items belong to different classes, and each action’s reward and resource consumption are class-dependent linear functions of its context. The decision-maker receives bandit feedback, learning from selected actions while trying to keep total consumption within a vector of budgets.

The authors introduce an estimator with a faster convergence rate and use its parameter estimates in a closed-form decision policy. More accurate estimation leads to lower regret, the performance shortfall used to assess the policy. The formulation covers both linear contextual bandits with knapsack constraints and online revenue management, connecting several resource-allocation settings.

Under those conditions, regret is sublinear in context dimension, class count, and time horizon. The paper also resolves a previously posed open problem and extends the result to multiple classes. Numerical experiments report better performance than the literature benchmarks considered.
summary.tldr: A faster estimator supports a closed-form resource-allocation policy with improved regret under stated context and budget conditions.

title: Improved Algorithms for Multi-period Multi-class Packing Problems with Bandit Feedback

abstract: Learning to Optimize (L2O), a technique that utilizes machine learning to learn an optimization algorithm automatically from data, has gained arising attention in recent years. A generic L2O approach parameterizes the iterative update rule and learns the update direction as a black-box network. While the generic approach is widely applicable, the learned model can overfit and may not generalize well to out-of-distribution test sets. In this paper, we derive the basic mathematical conditions that successful update rules commonly satisfy. Consequently, we propose a novel L2O model with a mathematics-inspired structure that is broadly applicable and generalized well to out-of-distribution problems. Numerical simulations validate our theoretical findings and demonstrate the superior empirical performance of the proposed L2O model.

Consequently, we propose a novel L2O model with a mathematics-inspired structure that is broadly applicable and generalized well to out-of-distribution problems. paragraphs: Learning to optimize uses machine learning to construct an optimization algorithm from data. A common approach learns the direction of each iterative update with a black-box network. Although broadly applicable, this flexibility can lead to overfitting and weak performance on problems outside the training distribution.

The paper derives basic mathematical conditions commonly satisfied by successful update rules. Those conditions guide the structure of a new learned optimizer. The approach places mathematical organization inside the model that learns the update rule, connecting the design of the learned algorithm to properties associated with effective optimization. Its goal is to retain broad applicability while improving behavior on unfamiliar problems.

Numerical simulations support the theoretical findings and show superior empirical performance for the proposed model. The authors also report good generalization to out-of-distribution problems. These results support using mathematical structure as a design principle for learned optimizers, with the observed generalization gains demonstrated in the evaluated problems rather than asserted as universal behavior.
summary.tldr: Mathematical conditions on update rules guide a learned optimizer that generalizes well to out-of-distribution problems in experiments.

title: Towards Constituting Mathematical Structures for Learning to Optimize

abstract: We propose a new method for count-based exploration in high-dimensional state spaces. Unlike previous work which relies on density models, we show that counts can be derived by averaging samples from the Rademacher distribution (or coin flips). This insight is used to set up a simple supervised learning objective which, when optimized, yields a state’s visitation count. We show that our method is significantly more effective at deducing ground-truth visitation counts than previous work; when used as an exploration bonus for a model-free reinforcement learning algorithm, it outperforms existing approaches on most of 9 challenging exploration tasks, including the Atari game Montezuma’s Revenge.

paragraphs: Count-based exploration encourages a reinforcement learning agent to investigate states it has visited less often. The paper addresses this idea in high-dimensional state spaces, where obtaining useful visitation counts is difficult. Its central contribution is a way to estimate those counts through a simple supervised learning problem, avoiding the density models used by previous approaches.

The key observation connects visitation counts to averages of samples from a Rademacher distribution, which can be understood as signed coin flips. The authors use this connection to construct a learning objective whose optimized predictions yield a state’s visitation count. Random coin outcomes therefore provide a route to estimating how familiar a state is to the agent.

The method is reported to recover ground-truth visitation counts substantially more effectively than previous work. When its estimates supply an exploration bonus to a model-free reinforcement learning algorithm, it outperforms existing approaches on most of nine challenging exploration tasks, including Montezuma’s Revenge. The findings link improved count estimation to better exploration in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: A supervised objective built from coin flips estimates state visitation counts and improves exploration on most of the evaluated tasks.

title: Flipping Coins to Estimate Pseudocounts for Exploration in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Diffusion models are a class of generative models that learn to synthesize samples by inverting a diffusion process that gradually maps data into noise. While these models have enjoyed great success recently, a full theoretical understanding of their observed properties is still lacking, in particular, their weak sensitivity to the choice of noise family and the role of adequate scheduling of noise levels for good synthesis. By identifying a correspondence between diffusion models and a well-known paradigm in cognitive science known as serial reproduction, whereby human agents iteratively observe and reproduce stimuli from memory, we show how the aforementioned properties of diffusion models can be explained as a natural consequence of this correspondence. We then complement our theoretical analysis with simulations that exhibit these key features. Our work highlights how classic paradigms in cognitive science can shed light on state-of-the-art machine learning problems.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate samples by learning to reverse a process that gradually turns data into noise. Their practical success leaves theoretical questions about why some design choices matter more than others. This paper focuses on their relatively weak sensitivity to the chosen noise family and the importance of scheduling noise levels appropriately.

The authors connect diffusion to serial reproduction, a cognitive science paradigm in which people repeatedly observe stimuli and reproduce them from memory. They identify a correspondence between this repeated reconstruction process and diffusion models. Through that connection, the two properties become understandable consequences of a shared structure, rather than isolated observations about generative modeling.

Simulations complement the theoretical analysis by exhibiting the same key features. The contribution is an explanation of observed behavior through a connection to an established cognitive paradigm. It clarifies why noise-family choice can have limited influence while the progression of noise levels remains consequential for synthesis, without claiming that every noise choice or schedule works equally well.
summary.tldr: A connection to serial reproduction in cognitive science explains diffusion models’ weak sensitivity to noise families and their need for suitable noise schedules.

title: Analyzing Diffusion as Serial Reproduction

abstract: We develop a variant of the stochastic prox-linear method for minimizing the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) objective. CVaR is a risk measure focused on minimizing worst-case performance, defined as the average of the top quantile of the losses. In machine learning, such a risk measure is useful to train more robust models. Although the stochastic subgradient method (SGM) is a natural choice for minimizing the CVaR objective, we show that our stochastic prox-linear (SPL+) algorithm can better exploit the structure of the objective, while still providing a convenient closed form update. Our SPL+ method also adapts to the scaling of the loss function, which allows for easier tuning. We then specialize a general convergence theorem for SPL+ to our setting, and show that it allows for a wider selection of step sizes compared to SGM. We support this theoretical finding experimentally.

CVaR is a risk measure focused on minimizing worst-case performance, defined as the average of the top quantile of the losses. In machine learning, such a risk measure is useful to train more robust models. Although the stochastic subgradient method (SGM) is a natural choice for minimizing the CVaR objective, we show that our stochastic prox-linear (SPL+) algorithm can better exploit the structure of the objective, while still providing a convenient closed form update. Our SPL+ method also adapts to the scaling of the loss function, which allows for easier tuning. We then specialize a general convergence theorem for SPL+ to our setting, and show that it allows for a wider selection of step sizes compared to SGM. paragraphs: Training against average loss can leave the most difficult outcomes insufficiently addressed. Conditional Value-at-Risk, or CVaR, instead averages losses within the worst-performing portion of outcomes. Minimizing this quantity directs training toward the high-loss tail, making it useful for developing more robust models.

The paper introduces SPL+, a variant of stochastic prox-linear optimization designed around the structure of the CVaR objective. Stochastic subgradient descent is a natural alternative, but the authors show that SPL+ can use that structure more effectively while retaining an update with a closed-form expression. The method also adapts to changes in the scale of the loss, which makes tuning easier.

The theoretical contribution specializes a general convergence result to this setting. It permits a wider range of step sizes than the corresponding result for stochastic subgradient descent, and experiments support this finding. The practical significance is greater flexibility in choosing how aggressively to update the model while retaining the stated convergence guarantee.
summary.tldr: SPL+ exploits the structure of CVaR to support easier tuning and a wider theoretically justified range of step sizes.

title: A Model-Based Method for Minimizing CVaR and Beyond

abstract: One of the key capabilities of intelligent agents is the ability to discover useful skills without external supervision. However, the current unsupervised skill discovery methods are often limited to acquiring simple, easy-to-learn skills due to the lack of incentives to discover more complex, challenging behaviors. We introduce a novel unsupervised skill discovery method, Controllability-aware Skill Discovery (CSD), which actively seeks complex, hard-to-control skills without supervision. The key component of CSD is a controllability-aware distance function, which assigns larger values to state transitions that are harder to achieve with the current skills. Combined with distance-maximizing skill discovery, CSD progressively learns more challenging skills over the course of training as our jointly trained distance function reduces rewards for easy-to-achieve skills. Our experimental results in six robotic manipulation and locomotion environments demonstrate that CSD can discover diverse complex skills including object manipulation and locomotion skills with no supervision, significantly outperforming prior unsupervised skill discovery methods. Videos and code are available at https://seohong.me/projects/csd/

paragraphs: An agent learning without external supervision needs a reason to discover behaviors beyond those it already finds easy. Existing unsupervised skill discovery methods often settle on simple skills because they lack an incentive to pursue more challenging ones. This paper introduces Controllability-aware Skill Discovery, or CSD, to make that incentive depend on the agent’s evolving abilities.

CSD learns a distance function that gives larger values to state transitions that are difficult to achieve with the current skills. The skill-learning process seeks to maximize this distance. Because the distance function is trained jointly with the skills, transitions that become easy receive less reward, directing learning toward progressively harder behaviors.

The authors evaluate CSD in six robotic manipulation and locomotion environments. They report diverse, complex skills learned without supervision, including object manipulation and locomotion, and significant improvements over prior unsupervised skill discovery methods. The findings support an adaptive approach to exploration: what counts as a rewarding discovery changes as the agent becomes more capable, helping it move beyond repeatedly practicing easy behaviors.
summary.tldr: CSD rewards transitions that current skills find difficult, enabling progressively more complex unsupervised behaviors in robotic environments.

title: Controllability-Aware Unsupervised Skill Discovery

abstract: While Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have long been investigated and applied, as well as theorized, we aim to provide a slightly different perspective into their nature — through the perspective of their Hessian maps. The reason is that the loss Hessian captures the pairwise interaction of parameters and therefore forms a natural ground to probe how the architectural aspects of CNNs get manifested in their structure and properties. We develop a framework relying on Toeplitz representation of CNNs, and then utilize it to reveal the Hessian structure and, in particular, its rank. We prove tight upper bounds (with linear activations), which closely follow the empirical trend of the Hessian rank and in practice also hold for more general settings. Overall, our work generalizes and further establishes the key insight that the Hessian rank grows as the square root of the number of parameters, even in CNNs.

paragraphs: This paper studies convolutional neural networks through the Hessian of their loss. The Hessian describes pairwise interactions between parameters in the local curvature of the loss function. Examining it offers a way to ask how architectural choices appear in the structure of the optimization problem, beyond simply counting the network’s parameters.

The authors build a framework based on a Toeplitz representation of convolutional networks and use it to analyze Hessian structure, especially rank. They prove tight upper bounds for networks with linear activations. These bounds closely track observed Hessian-rank trends and are also found to hold empirically in more general settings.

The work extends the insight that Hessian rank grows with the square root of the number of parameters to convolutional networks. This relates the size of a model to the number of independent curvature directions captured by its Hessian. The formal bounds apply to the stated linear-activation setting, while experiments provide evidence that the perspective remains useful beyond that setting.
summary.tldr: A Toeplitz-based analysis yields tight Hessian-rank bounds for linear-activation CNNs and supports square-root scaling with parameter count.

title: The Hessian perspective into the Nature of Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: Robust Markov decision processes (RMDPs) provide a promising framework for computing reliable policies in the face of model errors. Many successful reinforcement learning algorithms build on variations of policy-gradient methods, but adapting these methods to RMDPs has been challenging. As a result, the applicability of RMDPs to large, practical domains remains limited. This paper proposes a new Double-Loop Robust Policy Gradient (DRPG), the first generic policy gradient method for RMDPs. In contrast with prior robust policy gradient algorithms, DRPG monotonically reduces approximation errors to guarantee convergence to a globally optimal policy in tabular RMDPs. We introduce a novel parametric transition kernel and solve the inner loop robust policy via a gradient-based method. Finally, our numerical results demonstrate the utility of our new algorithm and confirm its global convergence properties.

paragraphs: Robust Markov decision processes seek reliable policies when the environment model contains errors. Policy-gradient methods are widely useful in reinforcement learning, but adapting them to robust decision processes has proved difficult. This paper introduces Double-Loop Robust Policy Gradient, or DRPG, described as the first generic policy-gradient method for this setting.

A central feature is that DRPG steadily reduces approximation errors during optimization. The authors use that property to guarantee convergence to a globally optimal policy in tabular robust Markov decision processes. The tabular scope is part of the guarantee: it specifies the setting in which the claimed global result holds.

The method introduces a new parameterized transition kernel and uses a gradient-based procedure to solve the robust policy problem in its inner loop. Numerical experiments demonstrate the algorithm’s utility and support its global convergence properties. The work connects a practical family of policy optimization methods to robust decision-making, with explicit control of approximation errors providing the basis for the theoretical convergence result.
summary.tldr: DRPG controls approximation errors to guarantee convergence to a globally optimal policy in tabular robust Markov decision processes.

title: Policy Gradient in Robust MDPs with Global Convergence Guarantee

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a vast amount of world knowledge, often extractable via question-answering (e.g., "What is Abraham Lincoln’s birthday?”). However, do they answer such questions based on exposure to similar questions during training (i.e., cheating), or by genuinely learning to extract knowledge from sources like Wikipedia? In this paper, we investigate this issue using a controlled biography dataset. We find a strong correlation between the model’s ability to extract knowledge and various diversity measures of the training data. Essentially, for knowledge to be reliably extracted, it must be sufficiently augmented (e.g., through paraphrasing, sentence shuffling) during pretraining. Without such augmentation, knowledge may be memorized but not extractable, leading to 0% accuracy, regardless of subsequent instruction fine-tuning. To understand why this occurs, we employ (nearly) linear probing to demonstrate a strong connection between the observed correlation and how the model internally encodes knowledge — whether it is linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names or distributed across other token embeddings in the training text. This paper provides several key recommendations for LLM pretraining in the industry: (1) rewrite the pretraining data — using small, auxiliary models — to provide knowledge augmentation, and (2) incorporate more instruction-finetuning data into the pretraining stage before it becomes too late.

paragraphs: A language model may encounter a fact during training yet fail to retrieve it when asked a question. Using a controlled biography dataset, this paper studies the distinction between storing knowledge and making it accessible through question answering. It asks how training-text diversity affects extraction from factual sources, beyond exposure to similar questions.

The experiments find a strong relationship between knowledge extraction and diversity in pretraining data. Augmentations such as paraphrasing and sentence shuffling are needed for reliable extraction in the studied setting. Without such augmentation, knowledge may be memorized yet yield zero question-answering accuracy, even after instruction fine-tuning. This makes the form of exposure during pretraining central to the reported result.

Nearly linear probes connect these outcomes to where knowledge is represented internally: in entity-name embeddings or distributed across other text tokens. The authors recommend rewriting pretraining material with auxiliary models and including more instruction-fine-tuning data during pretraining. These recommendations follow from the controlled finding that later instruction tuning may fail to make already memorized knowledge retrievable.
summary.tldr: Controlled biography experiments show that pretraining diversity strongly affects whether memorized facts can later be extracted through question answering.

title: Physics of Language Models: Part 3.1, Knowledge Storage and Extraction

abstract: Effective resistance is a distance between vertices of a graph that is both theoretically interesting and useful in applications. We study a variant of effective resistance called the biharmonic distance. While the effective resistance measures how well-connected two vertices are, we prove several theoretical results supporting the idea that the biharmonic distance measures how important an edge is to the global topology of the graph. Our theoretical results connect the biharmonic distance to well-known measures of connectivity of a graph like its total resistance and sparsity. Based on these results, we introduce two clustering algorithms using the biharmonic distance. Finally, we introduce a further generalization of the biharmonic distance that we call the $k$-harmonic distance. We empirically study the utility of biharmonic and $k$-harmonic distance for edge centrality and graph clustering.

paragraphs: Graph distances can describe more than how many steps separate two vertices. Effective resistance, for example, measures how well two vertices are connected. This paper studies a related quantity called biharmonic distance, asking what it reveals about a graph’s overall structure and how that information can support practical graph analysis.

The authors prove results supporting the interpretation that biharmonic distance measures an edge’s importance to global topology. Their analysis connects this distance with established connectivity quantities, including total resistance and sparsity. These connections give mathematical support to using the distance as a structural signal, beyond simply treating it as another numerical measure of separation.

Building on the theory, the paper introduces two clustering algorithms based on biharmonic distance. It also defines a broader family called k-harmonic distance and empirically investigates both measures for edge centrality and graph clustering. The contribution combines an interpretation of what these distances capture with concrete ways to use them when identifying important edges and organizing vertices into groups.
summary.tldr: The paper connects biharmonic graph distance to global edge importance and develops clustering methods and higher-order distance variants.

title: Biharmonic Distance of Graphs and its Higher-Order Variants: Theoretical Properties with Applications to Centrality and Clustering

abstract: Differential privacy (DP) offers a theoretical upper bound on the potential privacy leakage of an algorithm, while empirical auditing establishes a practical lower bound. Auditing techniques exist for DP training algorithms. However machine learning can also be made private at inference. We propose the first framework for auditing private prediction where we instantiate adversaries with varying poisoning and query capabilities. This enables us to study the privacy leakage of four private prediction algorithms: PATE (Papernot et al., 2016), CaPC (Choquette-Choo et al., 2020), PromptPATE (Duan et al., 2023), and Private-kNN (Zhu et al., 2020). To conduct our audit, we introduce novel techniques to empirically evaluate privacy leakage in terms of Renyi DP. Our experiments show that (i) the privacy analysis of private prediction can be improved, (ii) algorithms which are easier to poison lead to much higher privacy leakage, and (iii) the privacy leakage is significantly lower for adversaries without query control than those with full control.

paragraphs: Differential privacy provides an upper bound on how much information an algorithm could reveal, while an empirical audit establishes a lower bound on leakage demonstrated in practice. This paper brings auditing to private prediction, where privacy protection operates when a model answers queries. That extends the focus beyond existing audits of private training algorithms.

The framework constructs adversaries with different abilities to poison data and control prediction queries. It studies four private prediction methods: PATE, CaPC, PromptPATE, and Private-kNN. The authors also introduce techniques for measuring empirical leakage in terms of Rényi differential privacy, connecting their experiments to a formal privacy accounting framework.

The experiments indicate that the privacy analysis of private prediction can be improved. They also find substantially greater leakage in algorithms that are easier to poison, and significantly less leakage when adversaries lack query control. Together, these results show why an audit’s adversary capabilities matter: the practical leakage demonstrated by an attack depends on both the prediction mechanism and the access available to the attacker.
summary.tldr: A framework for auditing private prediction shows how poisoning and query control affect experimentally demonstrated privacy leakage.

title: Auditing Private Prediction

abstract: Scribble-supervised semantic segmentation presents a cost-effective training method that utilizes annotations generated through scribbling. It is valued in attaining high performance while minimizing annotation costs, which has made it highly regarded among researchers. Scribble supervision propagates information from labeled pixels to the surrounding unlabeled pixels, enabling semantic segmentation for the entire image. However, existing methods often ignore the features of classified pixels during feature propagation. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a prototype-based feature augmentation method that leverages feature prototypes to augment scribble supervision. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset in scribble-supervised semantic segmentation tasks. The code is available at https://github.com/TranquilChan/PFA.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns a category to every pixel in an image. Scribble supervision reduces annotation effort by asking for marks on only some pixels, then using those labels to help classify the rest. The central learning challenge is to extend the sparse supervision across the image while making effective use of the available visual features.

This paper identifies a weakness in existing propagation methods: they often overlook features of pixels that have already been classified. The proposed method uses feature prototypes to augment scribble supervision. These prototypes provide representative feature information that can contribute to the propagation process, incorporating information beyond the original sparse marks.

The approach matters because it targets how limited annotations are used, which is central to the appeal of scribble-based training. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance for scribble-supervised semantic segmentation on PASCAL VOC 2012. The stated finding supports prototype-based feature augmentation as an effective way to improve full-image segmentation from sparse labels within that evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: Feature prototypes improve the use of sparse scribble annotations, achieving state-of-the-art segmentation results on PASCAL VOC 2012.

title: Scribble-Supervised Semantic Segmentation with Prototype-based Feature Augmentation

abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) can convert any model’s output into prediction sets guaranteed to include the true label with any user-specified probability. However, same as the model itself, CP is vulnerable to adversarial test examples (evasion) and perturbed calibration data (poisoning). We derive provably robust sets by bounding the worst-case change in conformity scores. Our tighter bounds lead to more efficient sets. We cover both continuous and discrete (sparse) data and our guarantees work both for evasion and poisoning attacks (on both features and labels).
originalAbstract: Conformal prediction (CP) can convert any model’s output into prediction sets guaranteed to include the true label with any user-specified probability. However, same as the model itself, CP is vulnerable to adversarial test examples (evasion) and perturbed calibration data (poisoning). We derive provably robust sets by bounding the worst-case change in conformity scores. Our tighter bounds lead to more efficient sets. We cover both continuous and discrete (sparse) data and our guarantees work both for evasion and poisoning attacks (on both features and labels).

paragraphs: Conformal prediction turns a model's output into a set of possible labels, targeting a user-chosen probability that the true label is included. The paper examines how this protection can be undermined by manipulated data. It considers both evasion, where an adversary changes a test example, and poisoning, where the calibration data used to construct prediction sets are perturbed.

The authors derive robust sets by bounding how much conformity scores can change in the worst case. Those scores determine how candidate labels are judged when building a prediction set. Accounting for their possible movement provides a route to mathematical robustness guarantees. Tighter bounds also produce more efficient sets, reducing the conservatism needed to accommodate the considered perturbations.

The framework covers continuous data and discrete sparse data. Its guarantees address evasion and poisoning, including changes to features and labels. The contribution connects robustness with the usefulness of the resulting prediction sets: controlling score uncertainty more precisely allows the method to retain protection while avoiding unnecessarily broad sets under the analyzed attacks.
summary.tldr: Tighter worst-case bounds on conformity scores yield provably robust and more efficient prediction sets under evasion and poisoning attacks.

title: Robust Yet Efficient Conformal Prediction Sets

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has significantly advanced the field of combinatorial optimization (CO). However, its practicality is hindered by the necessity for a large number of reward evaluations, especially in scenarios involving computationally intensive function assessments. To enhance the sample efficiency, we propose a simple but effective method, called symmetric replay training (SRT), which can be easily integrated into various DRL methods. Our method leverages high-reward samples to encourage exploration of the under-explored symmetric regions without additional online interactions - free. Through replay training, the policy is trained to maximize the likelihood of the symmetric trajectories of discovered high-rewarded samples. Experimental results demonstrate the consistent improvement of our method in sample efficiency across diverse DRL methods applied to real-world tasks, such as molecular optimization and hardware design.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning can solve combinatorial optimization problems, but learning often requires many reward evaluations. That becomes costly when assessing a candidate solution is computationally intensive. Symmetric replay training aims to extract more training value from high-reward samples that have already been discovered.

The method uses symmetric trajectories associated with those successful samples. During replay, the policy is trained to increase the likelihood of these trajectories, encouraging exploration of symmetric regions that have received less attention. This process does not require additional online interactions. The claimed free exploration refers to that interaction saving, while the method still performs replay training.

SRT is designed as a simple addition that can be integrated into different deep reinforcement-learning methods. Experiments report consistent sample-efficiency improvements across diverse methods on tasks including molecular optimization and hardware design. The findings support using symmetry to extend the usefulness of existing successful experience, particularly when obtaining another reward evaluation is a major part of the cost of learning.
summary.tldr: Symmetric replay training reuses successful trajectories to improve exploration and sample efficiency without additional online interactions.

title: Symmetric Replay Training: Enhancing Sample Efficiency in Deep Reinforcement Learning for Combinatorial Optimization

abstract: Generative models have the potential to accelerate key steps in the discovery of novel molecular therapeutics and materials. Diffusion models have recently emerged as a powerful approach, excelling at unconditional sample generation and, with data-driven guidance, conditional generation within their training domain. Reliably sampling from high-value regions beyond the training data, however, remains an open challenge—with current methods predominantly focusing on modifying the diffusion process itself. In this paper, we develop context-guided diffusion (CGD), a simple plug-and-play method that leverages unlabeled data and smoothness constraints to improve the out-of-distribution generalization of guided diffusion models. We demonstrate that this approach leads to substantial performance gains across various settings, including continuous, discrete, and graph-structured diffusion processes with applications across drug discovery, materials science, and protein design.

paragraphs: Generating plausible molecules is different from reliably generating valuable candidates beyond the examples used for training. The paper focuses on this second challenge. Although diffusion models perform well at unconditional generation and guided generation within their training domain, directing them toward high-value regions outside that domain remains difficult.

Context-guided diffusion, or CGD, uses unlabeled data and smoothness constraints to improve the generalization of guided diffusion models. The method is designed as a simple, plug-and-play addition. Its central idea is to bring additional contextual information and smoothness requirements into the effort to guide generation beyond the training distribution.

The authors report substantial performance improvements across continuous, discrete, and graph-structured diffusion settings, with applications in drug discovery, materials science, and protein design. This range matters because the approach is demonstrated across several forms of generated data. The findings support context-guided diffusion as a way to improve out-of-distribution design in the evaluated settings, while reliable sampling of high-value candidates beyond training data remains the broader challenge motivating the work.
summary.tldr: Context-guided diffusion uses unlabeled data and smoothness constraints to improve molecular and protein generation beyond the training distribution.

title: Context-Guided Diffusion for Out-of-Distribution Molecular and Protein Design

abstract: Federated Learning is widely employed to tackle distributed sensitive data. Existing methods primarily focus on addressing in-federation data heterogeneity. However, we observed that they suffer from significant performance degradation when applied to unseen clients for out-of-federation (OOF) generalization. The recent attempts to address generalization to unseen clients generally struggle to scale up to large-scale distributed settings due to high communication or computation costs. Moreover, methods that scale well often demonstrate poor generalization capability. To achieve OOF-resiliency in a scalable manner, we propose Topology-aware Federated Learning (TFL) that leverages client topology - a graph representing client relationships - to effectively train robust models against OOF data. We formulate a novel optimization problem for TFL, consisting of two key modules: Client Topology Learning, which infers the client relationships in a privacy-preserving manner, and Learning on Client Topology, which leverages the learned topology to identify influential clients and harness this information into the FL optimization process to efficiently build robust models. Empirical evaluation on a variety of real-world datasets verifies TFL’s superior OOF robustness and scalability.

The recent attempts to address generalization to unseen clients generally struggle to scale up to large-scale distributed settings due to high communication or computation costs. To achieve OOF-resiliency in a scalable manner, we propose Topology-aware Federated Learning (TFL) that leverages client topology - a graph representing client relationships - to effectively train robust models against OOF data. Empirical evaluation on a variety of real-world datasets verifies TFL’s superior OOF robustness and scalability.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains models across distributed clients holding sensitive data. Much of its research addresses differences among participating clients, but this paper focuses on a different challenge: performance on clients that never joined training. The authors observe substantial degradation on these unseen clients and identify a tension between generalization and the communication or computation costs of existing approaches.

Their method, Topology-aware Federated Learning, represents relationships among clients as a graph. One module learns those relationships in a privacy-preserving way. A second module uses the resulting graph to identify influential clients and incorporates that information into the training optimization. Client relationships therefore become an explicit input to how the shared model is learned.

Evaluations across several real-world datasets support improved robustness on unseen clients alongside scalability. The contribution is a way to use the structure of the participating population to help models generalize beyond it. The reported evidence connects those two objectives, rather than treating robustness and distributed training efficiency as separate problems.
summary.tldr: Topology-aware Federated Learning uses learned client relationships to improve generalization to unseen clients while supporting scalable training.

title: Beyond the Federation: Topology-aware Federated Learning for Generalization to Unseen Clients

abstract: Machine learning on graphs, especially using graph neural networks (GNNs), has seen a surge in interest due to the wide availability of graph data across a broad spectrum of disciplines, from life to social and engineering sciences. Despite their practical success, our theoretical understanding of the properties of GNNs remains highly incomplete. Recent theoretical advancements primarily focus on elucidating the coarse-grained expressive power of GNNs, predominantly employing combinatorial techniques. However, these studies do not perfectly align with practice, particularly in understanding the generalization behavior of GNNs when trained with stochastic first-order optimization techniques. In this position paper, we argue that the graph machine learning community needs to shift its attention to developing a balanced theory of graph machine learning, focusing on a more thorough understanding of the interplay of expressive power, generalization, and optimization.

Despite their practical success, our theoretical understanding of the properties of GNNs remains highly incomplete. Recent theoretical advancements primarily focus on elucidating the coarse-grained expressive power of GNNs, predominantly employing combinatorial techniques. However, these studies do not perfectly align with practice, particularly in understanding the generalization behavior of GNNs when trained with stochastic first-order optimization techniques. In this position paper, we argue that the graph machine learning community needs to shift its attention to developing a balanced theory of graph machine learning, focusing on a more thorough understanding of the interplay of expressive power, generalization, and optimization.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks are used across disciplines with graph-structured data, including life sciences, social sciences, and engineering. Their practical success has outpaced the theory explaining their behavior. This position paper identifies an imbalance in that theory and argues for a broader research agenda.

Much recent theoretical work studies expressive power: what kinds of distinctions or functions a graph neural network can represent. The authors describe this work as largely combinatorial and coarse-grained. Such results do not fully explain what happens when networks are actually trained, especially how models learned through stochastic first-order optimization generalize beyond their training data.

The proposed direction is a balanced theory connecting expressiveness, generalization, and optimization. These questions concern different parts of the same learning process: available representational capacity, behavior on unseen examples, and the procedure used to fit the model. The paper’s contribution is an argument for studying their interaction, with the aim of bringing theoretical analysis into closer contact with the behavior of trained graph learning systems.
summary.tldr: This position paper calls for graph-learning theory that jointly studies expressiveness, generalization, and optimization to better explain trained models.

title: Position: Future Directions in the Theory of Graph Machine Learning

abstract: The diversity of contexts in which large language models (LLMs) are deployed requires the ability to modify or customize default model behaviors to incorporate nuanced requirements and preferences. A convenient interface to specify such model adjustments is high-level verbal feedback, such as “Don’t use emojis when drafting emails to my boss.” However, while writing high-level feedback is far simpler than collecting annotations for reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), we find that simply prompting a model with such feedback leads to $\textbf{overgeneralization}$–applying feedback in contexts where it is not relevant. We propose a new method Contextualized Critiques with Constrained Preference Optimization (C3PO) to learn from high-level verbal feedback while reducing overgeneralization compared to current work. C3PO uses a piece of high-level feedback to generate a small synthetic preference dataset to specify when and how the feedback should (and should not) be applied. It then fine-tunes the model in accordance with the synthetic preference data while minimizing the divergence from the original model for prompts where the feedback does not apply. Our experimental results indicate that our approach effectively applies verbal feedback to relevant scenarios while preserving existing behaviors for other contexts more than current methods. For both human- and GPT-4-generated high-level feedback, C3PO effectively adheres to the given feedback comparably to in-context baselines while reducing overgeneralization by 30%.

paragraphs: Verbal feedback offers a convenient way to customize a language model, but a contextual preference can spread too broadly. An instruction about tone in one kind of message may change behavior in unrelated situations. This paper finds that simply adding high-level feedback to a prompt can cause such overgeneralization.

The proposed method, Contextualized Critiques with Constrained Preference Optimization, or C3PO, turns feedback into a small synthetic preference dataset. The examples specify both how the preference should apply and where it should leave behavior unchanged. Fine-tuning then follows those preferences while minimizing divergence from the original model on prompts outside the feedback’s scope.

Experiments use high-level feedback written by humans and generated by GPT-4. C3PO follows the requested feedback comparably to in-context baselines while reducing overgeneralization by 30%. It also preserves behavior in unrelated contexts better than the compared methods. The contribution is a way to learn the boundary of a preference alongside the preference itself, making model customization more sensitive to the context in which a user intended it.
summary.tldr: C3PO learns contextual verbal preferences through synthetic examples and constrained fine-tuning, reducing reported overgeneralization by 30%.

title: RLVF: Learning from Verbal Feedback without Overgeneralization

abstract: Transformer has shown promise in reinforcement learning to model time-varying features for obtaining generalized low-level robot policies on diverse robotics datasets in embodied learning. However, it still suffers from the issues of low data efficiency and high inference latency. In this paper, we propose to investigate the task from a new perspective of the frequency domain. We first observe that the energy density in the frequency domain of a robot’s trajectory is mainly concentrated in the low-frequency part. Then, we present the Fourier Controller Network (FCNet), a new network that uses Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) to extract and encode time-varying features through frequency domain interpolation. In order to do real-time decision-making, we further adopt FFT and Sliding DFT methods in the model architecture to achieve parallel training and efficient recurrent inference. Extensive results in both simulated (e.g., D4RL) and real-world environments (e.g., robot locomotion) demonstrate FCNet’s substantial efficiency and effectiveness over existing methods such as Transformer, e.g., FCNet outperforms Transformer on multi-environmental robotics datasets of all types of sizes (from 1.9M to 120M). The project page and code can be found https://thkkk.github.io/fcnet.

paragraphs: Learning robot control from diverse trajectories requires a model to understand how movement changes over time. Transformers can model these changing features, but the paper identifies data efficiency and inference latency as obstacles. The authors start from an observation about robot trajectories: much of their frequency-domain energy lies in the low-frequency components.

Their Fourier Controller Network, FCNet, builds on that observation by representing temporal features in the frequency domain. It uses the Short-Time Fourier Transform to extract those features and frequency-domain interpolation to encode them. The architecture also incorporates the Fast Fourier Transform and Sliding Discrete Fourier Transform, supporting parallel training alongside efficient recurrent inference for real-time decisions.

Experiments in simulated environments and real-world robot locomotion report strong efficiency and effectiveness relative to existing methods. FCNet outperforms a Transformer on the evaluated multi-environment robotics datasets across sizes from 1.9 million to 120 million. The findings support frequency-based temporal modeling as a useful control architecture across the tested data scales and environments.
summary.tldr: FCNet models robot trajectories in the frequency domain to support efficient training and real-time control, outperforming Transformers across the evaluated dataset sizes.

title: Fourier Controller Networks for Real-Time Decision-Making in Embodied Learning

abstract: Aligning text-to-image diffusion model (T2I) with preference has been gaining increasing research attention. While prior works exist on directly optimizing T2I by preference data, these methods are developed under the bandit assumption of a latent reward on the entire diffusion reverse chain, while ignoring the sequential nature of the generation process. This may harm the efficacy and efficiency of preference alignment. In this paper, we take on a finer dense reward perspective and derive a tractable alignment objective that emphasizes the initial steps of the T2I reverse chain. In particular, we introduce temporal discounting into DPO-style explicit-reward-free objectives, to break the temporal symmetry therein and suit the T2I generation hierarchy. In experiments on single and multiple prompt generation, our method is competitive with strong relevant baselines, both quantitatively and qualitatively. Further investigations are conducted to illustrate the insight of our approach. Source code is available at https://github.com/Shentao-YANG/Dense_Reward_T2I .

paragraphs: This paper studies how to make text-to-image diffusion models better reflect preferences. Earlier approaches treat the entire image-generation trajectory as receiving one overall reward. The authors argue that this treatment overlooks the sequence of decisions involved in generation and may reduce the effectiveness and efficiency of preference alignment.

Their alternative considers rewards at a finer temporal level and derives a practical training objective that places greater emphasis on the initial steps of reverse diffusion. They introduce temporal discounting into objectives resembling Direct Preference Optimization, while retaining the ability to train without an explicit reward model. This changes how different generation steps contribute to the alignment objective.

Experiments involving both individual prompts and multiple prompts show results competitive with strong relevant baselines in quantitative assessments and qualitative comparisons. The stated finding is competitiveness, rather than consistent superiority. The contribution is a way to account for the generation process’s temporal structure when learning from preferences, supported by further investigations into the approach.
summary.tldr: A temporally discounted preference objective emphasizes early diffusion steps and achieves competitive text-to-image alignment results.

title: A Dense Reward View on Aligning Text-to-Image Diffusion with Preference

abstract: Both text and video data are abundant on the internet and support large-scale self-supervised learning through next token or frame prediction. However, they have not been equally leveraged: language models have had significant real-world impact, whereas video generation has remained largely limited to media entertainment. Yet video data captures important information about the physical world that is difficult to express in language. To address this gap, we discuss an under-appreciated opportunity to extend video generation to solve tasks in the real world. We observe how, akin to language, video can serve as a unified interface that can absorb internet knowledge and represent diverse tasks. Moreover, we demonstrate how, like language models, video generation can serve as planners, agents, compute engines, and environment simulators through techniques such as in-context learning, planning and reinforcement learning. We identify major impact opportunities in domains such as robotics, self-driving, and science, supported by recent work that demonstrates how such advanced capabilities in video generation are plausibly within reach. Lastly, we identify key challenges in video generation that mitigate progress. Addressing these challenges will enable video generation models to demonstrate unique value alongside language models in a wider array of AI applications.

paragraphs: Video records information about the physical world that can be difficult to express in words. This position paper argues that video generation has an underused role in real-world decision making. Although both text and video support large-scale self-supervised prediction, video generation has largely been applied to media entertainment rather than the broader range of tasks associated with language models.

The authors present video as a possible unified interface for absorbing internet knowledge and representing diverse tasks. They discuss and demonstrate how video generation can take roles such as planning, acting, computation, and environment simulation. Techniques including in-context learning, planning, and reinforcement learning connect these roles to approaches already used with language models.

Robotics, self-driving, and science are identified as major opportunities. Recent work supports the plausibility of advanced video-generation capabilities, while the paper also identifies challenges that impede progress. The argument concerns a research direction with promising evidence: overcoming those challenges could allow video models to contribute distinctive capabilities alongside language models in a wider range of applications.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that video generation could become a general interface for planning, simulation, and real-world decision making alongside language models.

title: Position: Video as the New Language for Real-World Decision Making

abstract: Transformers with linear attention allow for efficient parallel training but can simultaneously be formulated as an RNN with 2D (matrix-valued) hidden states, thus enjoying linear-time inference complexity. However, linear attention generally underperforms ordinary softmax attention. Moreover, current implementations of linear attention lack I/O-awareness and are thus slower than highly optimized implementations of softmax attention. This work describes a hardware-efficient algorithm for linear attention that trades off memory movement against parallelizability. The resulting implementation, dubbed FlashLinearAttention, is faster than FlashAttention-2 as a standalone layer even on short sequence lengths (e.g., 1K). We then generalize this algorithm to a more expressive variant of linear attention with data-dependent gates. When used as a replacement for the standard attention layer in Transformers, the resulting gated linear attention (GLA) Transformer is found to perform competitively against the LLaMA-architecture Transformer as well recent linear-time-inference baselines such as RetNet and Mamba on moderate-scale language modeling experiments. GLA Transformer is especially effective at length generalization, enabling a model trained on 2K to generalize to sequences longer than 20K without significant perplexity degradations. For training speed, the GLA Transformer has higher throughput than a similarly-sized Mamba model.

paragraphs: Linear attention supports parallel training and a recurrent formulation with matrix-valued hidden states, enabling linear-time inference. Yet its theoretical efficiency does not automatically produce fast implementations, and its modeling performance often trails ordinary softmax attention. The paper addresses both the hardware execution problem and the expressiveness of the attention mechanism.

FlashLinearAttention balances memory movement against parallel execution. As a standalone layer, it runs faster than FlashAttention-2 even at sequence lengths such as 1K. The authors extend this algorithm with data-dependent gates to create gated linear attention, or GLA. These gates make the attention variant more expressive while retaining an implementation designed around hardware efficiency.

In moderate-scale language modeling experiments, GLA Transformers are competitive with a LLaMA-architecture Transformer, RetNet, and Mamba. A model trained on 2K sequences generalizes beyond 20K without significant perplexity degradation, and training throughput exceeds that of a similarly sized Mamba model. These findings jointly support the approach's modeling quality, length generalization, and speed within the reported experimental scope.
summary.tldr: Hardware-aware linear attention with data-dependent gates combines competitive language modeling, strong length generalization, and efficient training in moderate-scale experiments.

title: Gated Linear Attention Transformers with Hardware-Efficient Training

abstract: Understanding cellular responses to stimuli is crucial for biological discovery and drug development. Transcriptomics provides interpretable, gene-level insights, while microscopy imaging offers rich predictive features but is harder to interpret. Weakly paired datasets, where samples share biological states, enable multimodal learning but are scarce, limiting their utility for training and multimodal inference. We propose a framework to enhance transcriptomics by distilling knowledge from microscopy images. Using weakly paired data, our method aligns and binds modalities, enriching gene expression representations with morphological information. To address data scarcity, we introduce (1) Semi-Clipped, an adaptation of CLIP for cross-modal distillation using pretrained foundation models, achieving state-of-the-art results, and (2) PEA (Perturbation Embedding Augmentation), a novel augmentation technique that enhances transcriptomics data while preserving inherent biological information. These strategies improve the predictive power and retain the interpretability of transcriptomics, enabling rich unimodal representations for complex biological tasks.

paragraphs: Gene expression measurements and microscopy images reveal different aspects of how cells respond to a stimulus. Transcriptomics offers interpretable information about individual genes, while images capture useful features of cellular appearance. This paper asks whether information from images can improve representations of gene expression while preserving their biological interpretability.

The framework transfers knowledge between these modalities using weakly paired samples: observations that share biological states. It aligns their representations so that morphological information can enrich the transcriptomics representation. Because suitable paired data are scarce, the authors introduce two complementary techniques. Semi-Clipped adapts CLIP for knowledge transfer using pretrained foundation models, while Perturbation Embedding Augmentation, or PEA, augments transcriptomics data while preserving its underlying biological information.

The authors report state-of-the-art results for Semi-Clipped and improved predictive power from the proposed strategies. The intended result is a richer representation usable with transcriptomics alone, carrying information learned from microscopy. This matters because the benefits of combining modalities can remain useful when subsequent biological tasks rely on a single measurement type.
summary.tldr: The framework transfers microscopy knowledge into interpretable transcriptomics representations using cross-modal distillation and biologically preserving data augmentation.

title: A Cross Modal Knowledge Distillation & Data Augmentation Recipe for Improving Transcriptomics Representations through Morphological Features

abstract: We study learning-augmented binary search trees (BSTs) via Treaps with carefully designed priorities. The result is a simple search tree in which the depth of each item $x$ is determined by its predicted weight $w_x$. Specifically, each item $x$ is assigned a composite priority of $-\lfloor\log\log(1/w_x)\rfloor + U(0, 1)$ where $U(0, 1)$ is the uniform random variable. By choosing $w_x$ as the relative frequency of $x$, the resulting search trees achieve static optimality. This approach generalizes the recent learning-augmented BSTs [Lin-Luo-Woodruff ICML‘22], which only work for Zipfian distributions, by extending them to arbitrary input distributions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method can be generalized to a B-Tree data structure using the B-Treap approach [Golovin ICALP’09]. Our search trees are also capable of leveraging localities in the access sequence through online self-reorganization, thereby achieving the working-set property. Additionally, they are robust to prediction errors and support dynamic operations, such as insertions, deletions, and prediction updates. We complement our analysis with an empirical study, demonstrating that our method outperforms prior work and classic data structures.

paragraphs: This paper develops search trees that use predicted item weights to decide how deeply items should sit in the tree. It builds on treaps, assigning each item a priority that combines a transformed predicted weight with uniform randomness. The design connects access predictions to tree organization through a simple priority rule.

When weights equal relative access frequencies, the resulting trees achieve static optimality. The analysis covers arbitrary input distributions, extending earlier learning-augmented search-tree results restricted to Zipfian distributions. The authors also generalize the approach to B-trees through a B-treap construction, carrying the central weighting idea into another search-tree structure.

The trees can reorganize online to exploit locality in access sequences and achieve the working-set property. They also support insertion, deletion, and prediction updates, and the authors establish robustness to prediction errors. An empirical study reports improvements over prior methods and classic structures. Together, these results address both the value of accurate predictions and the practical need for a tree to keep functioning as access patterns, stored items, and predictions change.
summary.tldr: Prediction-weighted treap priorities yield robust, dynamic search trees with optimality guarantees extending to arbitrary access distributions.

title: On the Power of Learning-Augmented Search Trees

abstract: Our ability to continuously acquire, organize, and leverage knowledge is a key feature of human intelligence that AI systems must approximate to unlock their full potential. Given the challenges in continual learning with large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has become the dominant way to introduce new information. However, its reliance on vector retrieval hinders its ability to mimic the dynamic and interconnected nature of human long-term memory. Recent RAG approaches augment vector embeddings with various structures like knowledge graphs to address some of these gaps, namely sense-making and associativity. However, their performance on more basic factual memory tasks drops considerably below standard RAG. We address this unintended deterioration and propose HippoRAG 2, a framework that outperforms standard RAG comprehensively on factual, sense-making, and associative memory tasks. HippoRAG 2 builds upon the Personalized PageRank algorithm used in HippoRAG and enhances it with deeper passage integration and more effective online use of an LLM. This combination pushes this RAG system closer to the effectiveness of human long-term memory, achieving a 7% improvement in associative memory tasks over the state-of-the-art embedding model while also exhibiting superior factual knowledge and sense-making memory capabilities. This work paves the way for non-parametric continual learning for LLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/HippoRAG.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation gives language models access to new information through retrieval. The paper asks how this approach can better support interconnected memory. It identifies a tradeoff in recent structured retrieval systems: adding mechanisms for associations and sense-making can come at the expense of simpler factual recall, where standard RAG remains stronger.

HippoRAG 2 aims to improve all three capabilities together. It builds on the Personalized PageRank algorithm used in HippoRAG, adding deeper integration of passages and more effective use of a language model during online operation. The proposed combination strengthens the relationship between retrieved text and the system's structured retrieval process.

The authors report that HippoRAG 2 outperforms standard RAG across factual, sense-making, and associative memory tasks. On associative tasks, they report a 7% improvement over the state-of-the-art embedding model, alongside stronger factual and sense-making capabilities. These results support retrieval as a route toward non-parametric continual learning, with improved organization and use of external knowledge rather than merely adding more information to retrieve.
summary.tldr: HippoRAG 2 improves factual, associative, and sense-making retrieval by combining Personalized PageRank with deeper passage integration and online LLM use.

title: From RAG to Memory: Non-Parametric Continual Learning for Large Language Models

abstract: Deep neural networks trained as image denoisers are widely used as priors for solving imaging inverse problems. We introduce Stochastic deep Restoration Priors (ShaRP), a novel framework that stochastically leverages an ensemble of deep restoration models beyond denoisers to regularize inverse problems. By using generalized restoration models trained on a broad range of degradations beyond simple Gaussian noise, ShaRP effectively addresses structured artifacts and enables self-supervised training without fully sampled data. We prove that ShaRP minimizes an objective function involving a regularizer derived from the score functions of minimum mean square error (MMSE) restoration operators. We also provide theoretical guarantees for learning restoration operators from incomplete measurements. ShaRP achieves state-of-the-art performance on tasks such as magnetic resonance imaging reconstruction and single-image super-resolution, surpassing both denoiser- and diffusion-model-based methods without requiring retraining.
