paragraphs: Reconstructing an image from incomplete or degraded measurements requires guidance about which images are plausible. Neural networks trained to remove noise often provide that guidance. ShaRP expands this approach by stochastically using an ensemble of restoration models trained on a broader range of degradations, including problems beyond simple Gaussian noise.

This broader restoration knowledge helps address structured artifacts and enables self-supervised training without fully sampled data. The authors also establish an optimization interpretation: ShaRP minimizes an objective with a regularizer derived from score functions of minimum-mean-square-error restoration operators. Additional theoretical guarantees address learning those restoration operators from incomplete measurements, connecting the reconstruction method to its training setting.

The reported experiments include magnetic resonance imaging reconstruction and single-image super-resolution. ShaRP achieves state-of-the-art performance, exceeding both denoiser-based and diffusion-based methods without requiring retraining. The contribution combines a more varied source of restoration knowledge with mathematical support for how it regularizes reconstruction, while demonstrating its usefulness across the stated imaging tasks.
summary.tldr: ShaRP uses an ensemble of restoration models to improve image reconstruction, with theoretical support and strong results without retraining.

title: Stochastic Deep Restoration Priors for Imaging Inverse Problems

abstract: This study considers multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) through the information gain of the Pareto-frontier. To calculate the information gain, a predictive distribution conditioned on the Pareto-frontier plays a key role, which is defined as a distribution truncated by the Pareto-frontier. However, it is usually impossible to obtain the entire Pareto-frontier in a continuous domain, and therefore, the complete truncation cannot be known. We consider an approximation of the truncated distribution by using a mixture distribution consisting of two possible approximate truncations obtainable from a subset of the Pareto-frontier, which we call over- and under-truncation. Since the optimal balance of the mixture is unknown beforehand, we propose optimizing the balancing coefficient through the variational lower bound maximization framework, by which the approximation error of the information gain can be minimized. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method particularly when the number of objective functions is large.

However, it is usually impossible to obtain the entire Pareto-frontier in a continuous domain, and therefore, the complete truncation cannot be known. We consider an approximation of the truncated distribution by using a mixture distribution consisting of two possible approximate truncations obtainable from a subset of the Pareto-frontier, which we call over- and under-truncation. paragraphs: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization searches for good tradeoffs between competing objectives. One strategy chooses evaluations based on how much they are expected to reveal about the Pareto frontier, the set of tradeoffs that cannot be improved in one objective without worsening another. Computing this information gain requires a predictive distribution conditioned on that frontier.

The conditioning truncates the predictive distribution, but the complete frontier is usually unavailable in a continuous domain. The paper approximates the required distribution using a mixture of two truncations that can be constructed from a partial frontier. These over- and under-truncations provide different approximations, and their best relative weighting is not known beforehand.

The authors learn the mixture balance by maximizing a variational lower bound, providing a way to minimize approximation error in the information-gain calculation. Empirical evaluation supports the method's effectiveness, particularly with many objectives. The contribution is therefore a tractable way to improve the information used for choosing evaluations when only part of the frontier is available.
summary.tldr: An optimized mixture of approximate truncations improves Pareto-frontier information-gain estimation, especially in optimization problems with many objectives.

title: Pareto-frontier Entropy Search with Variational Lower Bound Maximization

abstract: Answering questions with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) has significantly enhanced the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet its impact on Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) still lacks a systematic assessment and in-depth investigation. In this paper, we introduce MME-CoT, a specialized benchmark evaluating the CoT reasoning performance of LMMs, spanning six domains: math, science, OCR, logic, space-time, and general scenes. As the first comprehensive study in this area, we propose a thorough evaluation suite incorporating three novel metrics that assess the reasoning quality, robustness, and efficiency at a fine-grained level. Leveraging curated high-quality data and a unique evaluation strategy, we conduct an in-depth analysis of state-of-the-art LMMs, uncovering several key insights: 1) Models with reflection mechanism demonstrate a superior CoT quality, with Kimi k1.5 outperforming GPT-4o and demonstrating the highest quality results; 2) CoT prompting often degrades LMM performance on perception-heavy tasks, suggesting a potentially harmful overthinking behavior; and 3) Although the CoT quality is high, LMMs with reflection exhibit significant inefficiency in both normal response and self-correction phases. We hope MME-CoT serves as a foundation for advancing multimodal reasoning in LMMs.

paragraphs: MME-CoT evaluates how chain-of-thought reasoning affects large multimodal models, where answering can depend on both visual perception and reasoning. The benchmark spans mathematics, science, optical character recognition, logic, space-time, and general scenes. Its evaluation suite introduces three metrics covering reasoning quality, robustness, and efficiency, allowing the analysis to go beyond whether a final answer is correct.

The evaluated models with reflection mechanisms show stronger chain-of-thought quality. Kimi k1.5 achieves the highest quality results in the study and outperforms GPT-4o on that measure. However, chain-of-thought prompting often reduces performance on tasks dominated by perception, suggesting that additional reasoning can sometimes introduce harmful overthinking rather than improve visual interpretation.

The study also finds substantial inefficiency in reflective models during both ordinary responses and self-correction. This means high-quality reasoning and efficient reasoning are separate evaluation concerns. By examining quality, robustness, and efficiency together, MME-CoT provides evidence about where extended reasoning helps multimodal models and where its use carries performance or computational costs.
summary.tldr: MME-CoT finds that reflection improves multimodal reasoning quality but can be inefficient, while chain-of-thought prompting often hurts perception-heavy tasks.

title: MME-CoT: Benchmarking Chain-of-Thought in Large Multimodal Models for Reasoning Quality, Robustness, and Efficiency

abstract: Offline Opponent Modeling (OOM) aims to learn an adaptive autonomous agent policy that dynamically adapts to opponents using an offline dataset from multi-agent games. Previous work assumes that the dataset is optimal. However, this assumption is difficult to satisfy in the real world. When the dataset is suboptimal, existing approaches struggle to work. To tackle this issue, we propose a simple and general algorithmic improvement framework, Truncated Q-driven Instant Policy Refinement (TIPR), to handle the suboptimality of OOM algorithms induced by datasets. The TIPR framework is plug-and-play in nature. Compared to original OOM algorithms, it requires only two extra steps: (1) Learn a horizon-truncated in-context action-value function, namely Truncated Q, using the offline dataset. The Truncated Q estimates the expected return within a fixed, truncated horizon and is conditioned on opponent information. (2) Use the learned Truncated Q to instantly decide whether to perform policy refinement and to generate policy after refinement during testing. Theoretically, we analyze the rationale of Truncated Q from the perspective of No Maximization Bias probability. Empirically, we conduct extensive comparison and ablation experiments in four representative competitive environments. TIPR effectively improves various OOM algorithms pretrained with suboptimal datasets.

paragraphs: Offline opponent modeling trains an agent from previously collected multi-agent game data so it can adapt to opponents. Existing methods can struggle when those data contain suboptimal behavior rather than optimal decisions. Truncated Q-driven Instant Policy Refinement, or TIPR, is a plug-and-play framework intended to improve such pretrained agents without requiring the offline dataset to be optimal.

TIPR adds two steps. First, it learns an action-value function from the offline data that accounts for opponent information and estimates expected return over a fixed, truncated horizon. Second, during testing, it uses this learned Truncated Q function to decide whether refinement is warranted and to produce a refined policy when needed.

The theoretical analysis explains the role of Truncated Q through the probability of avoiding maximization bias. Experiments and ablations in four competitive environments show improvements across multiple opponent-modeling algorithms trained on suboptimal datasets. The contribution is an additional refinement mechanism that uses opponent-conditioned value estimates to improve decisions at test time, addressing shortcomings inherited from the training data.
summary.tldr: TIPR uses opponent-conditioned, truncated-horizon value estimates to refine offline-trained policies at test time when their training data are suboptimal.

title: Offline Opponent Modeling with Truncated Q-driven Instant Policy Refinement

abstract: Recent advances in diffusion-based generative modeling have demonstrated significant promise in tackling long-horizon, sparse-reward tasks by leveraging offline datasets. While these approaches have achieved promising results, their reliability remains inconsistent due to the inherent stochastic risk of producing infeasible trajectories, limiting their applicability in safety-critical applications. We identify that the primary cause of these failures is inaccurate guidance during the sampling procedure, and demonstrate the existence of manifold deviation by deriving a lower bound on the guidance gap. To address this challenge, we propose Local Manifold Approximation and Projection (LoMAP), a training-free method that projects the guided sample onto a low-rank subspace approximated from offline datasets, preventing infeasible trajectory generation. We validate our approach on standard offline reinforcement learning benchmarks that involve challenging long-horizon planning. Furthermore, we show that, as a standalone module, LoMAP can be incorporated into the hierarchical diffusion planner, providing further performance enhancements.

paragraphs: Diffusion planners can use offline datasets to tackle tasks with long horizons and sparse rewards, yet their generated trajectories can be infeasible. This paper investigates why that happens. The authors identify inaccurate sampling guidance as the primary cause and derive a lower bound on the guidance gap to demonstrate deviation from the trajectory manifold.

Their proposed method, Local Manifold Approximation and Projection, or LoMAP, operates without additional training. It approximates a low-rank subspace from offline data and projects guided samples onto that subspace. This makes the geometry represented by the dataset directly influence sampling, addressing guidance that would otherwise move a generated trajectory away from feasible behavior.

The authors validate LoMAP on standard offline reinforcement-learning benchmarks involving difficult long-horizon planning. They also incorporate it as a standalone module into a hierarchical diffusion planner and report further performance improvements. The contribution combines a theoretical explanation of guidance-related failures with a sampling intervention that can be added to an existing planner, making it relevant to reliability as well as planning performance.
summary.tldr: LoMAP projects guided diffusion samples onto a data-derived subspace to address infeasible trajectories without additional training.

title: Local Manifold Approximation and Projection for Manifold-Aware Diffusion Planning

abstract: Recent advancements in Large Vision-Language Models built upon Large Language Models have established aligning visual features with LLM representations as the dominant paradigm. However, inherited LLM architectural designs introduce suboptimal characteristics for multimodal processing. First, LVLMs exhibit a bimodal distribution in attention allocation, leading to the progressive neglect of middle visual content as context expands. Second, conventional positional encoding schemes fail to preserve vital 2D structural relationships when processing dynamic high-resolution images. To address these limitations, we propose CoMemo - a dual-path architecture that combines a Context image path with an image Memory path for visual processing, effectively alleviating visual information neglect. Additionally, we introduce RoPE-DHR, a novel positional encoding mechanism that employs thumbnail-based positional aggregation to maintain 2D spatial awareness while mitigating remote decay in extended sequences. Evaluations across seven benchmarks,including long-context comprehension, multi-image reasoning, and visual question answering, demonstrate CoMemo’s superior performance compared to conventional LVLM architectures. Project page is available at https://lalbj.github.io/projects/CoMemo/.

paragraphs: Vision-language models often adapt language-model architectures by aligning visual features with language representations. The paper identifies two problems with this design. As context grows, attention increasingly neglects visual content in the middle. Conventional positional encodings also fail to retain important two-dimensional relationships when handling images at dynamic high resolutions.

CoMemo introduces two paths for processing images: a context image path and an image memory path. This arrangement alleviates the neglect of visual information. A complementary positional encoding, RoPE-DHR, aggregates positions using thumbnails to preserve spatial awareness while reducing the weakening of relationships across distant positions in long sequences.

Evaluations cover seven benchmarks spanning long-context comprehension, reasoning across multiple images, and visual question answering. CoMemo performs better than conventional vision-language architectures in these tests. The results support addressing both how visual information remains available and how its spatial layout is represented. These are related but distinct architectural issues that become especially relevant as image content and context length increase.
summary.tldr: CoMemo combines image context, image memory, and spatial positional encoding to improve vision-language processing.

title: CoMemo: LVLMs Need Image Context with Image Memory

abstract: Graph neural networks use relational information as an inductive bias to enhance prediction performance. Not rarely, task-relevant relations are unknown and graph structure learning approaches have been proposed to learn them from data. Given their latent nature, no graph observations are available to provide a direct training signal to the learnable relations. Therefore, graph topologies are typically learned on the prediction task alongside the other graph neural network parameters. In this paper, we demonstrate that minimizing point-prediction losses does not guarantee proper learning of the latent relational information and its associated uncertainty. Conversely, we prove that suitable loss functions on the stochastic model outputs simultaneously grant solving two tasks: (i) learning the unknown distribution of the latent graph and (ii) achieving optimal predictions of the target variable. Finally, we propose a sampling-based method that solves this joint learning task. Empirical results validate our theoretical claims and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks use relationships between entities to improve predictions, but the relevant relationships may be unknown. In that case, graph structure learning infers them alongside the network’s other parameters. Because the graph is latent, there are no directly observed graphs to tell the model whether its inferred relationships are correct.

The paper demonstrates that minimizing a loss for point predictions does not guarantee recovery of either the latent relational information or its uncertainty. A training objective can therefore be useful for predicting the target without guaranteeing that the graph representation is learned properly. This distinction matters when the learned relationships themselves are part of the intended output.

The authors prove that suitable losses on stochastic model outputs can support both objectives simultaneously: learning the unknown distribution over graphs and achieving optimal target predictions. They then propose a sampling-based method for this joint task. Empirical results support the theoretical claims and the method’s effectiveness. The contribution identifies a route to learning predictive behavior and uncertainty about the underlying relationships together.
summary.tldr: Suitable losses on stochastic outputs can jointly learn latent graph uncertainty and optimal predictions, where point-prediction losses provide no such guarantee.

title: Learning Latent Graph Structures and their Uncertainty

abstract: We describe HypotheSAEs, a general method to hypothesize interpretable relationships between text data (e.g., headlines) and a target variable (e.g., clicks). HypotheSAEs has three steps: (1) train a sparse autoencoder on text embeddings to produce interpretable features describing the data distribution, (2) select features that predict the target variable, and (3) generate a natural language interpretation of each feature (e.g., mentions being surprised or shocked) using an LLM. Each interpretation serves as a hypothesis about what predicts the target variable. Compared to baselines, our method better identifies reference hypotheses on synthetic datasets (at least +0.06 in F1) and produces more predictive hypotheses on real datasets ( twice as many significant findings), despite requiring 1-2 orders of magnitude less compute than recent LLM-based methods. HypotheSAEs also produces novel discoveries on two well-studied tasks: explaining partisan differences in Congressional speeches and identifying drivers of engagement with online headlines.

paragraphs: HypotheSAEs generates interpretable hypotheses about relationships between text and a target variable, such as headline content and clicks. The aim is to find patterns that both predict an outcome and can be expressed in ordinary language, making them useful candidates for further investigation.

The method has three stages. A sparse autoencoder learns interpretable features from text embeddings. Features that predict the target variable are then selected. Finally, a language model describes each selected feature in natural language. Those descriptions become hypotheses about what predicts the target, connecting statistical feature selection with human-readable explanations.

On synthetic datasets, the method improves recovery of reference hypotheses by at least 0.06 F1 over baselines. On real datasets, it produces twice as many significant findings while using one to two orders of magnitude less compute than recent LLM-based approaches. The authors also report new discoveries concerning partisan differences in Congressional speeches and engagement with online headlines. These are hypotheses about predictive relationships; the method’s stated goal is to identify interpretable associations.
summary.tldr: HypotheSAEs turns predictive sparse-autoencoder features into readable hypotheses, reporting stronger discoveries with much less compute than recent LLM-based methods.

title: Sparse Autoencoders for Hypothesis Generation

abstract: There is growing interest in extending average treatment effect (ATE) estimation to incorporate non-tabular data, such as images and text, which may act as sources of confounding. Neglecting these effects risks biased results and flawed scientific conclusions. However, incorporating non-tabular data necessitates sophisticated feature extractors, often in combination with ideas of transfer learning. In this work, we investigate how latent features from pre-trained neural networks can be leveraged to adjust for sources of confounding. We formalize conditions under which these latent features enable valid adjustment and statistical inference in ATE estimation, demonstrating results along the example of double machine learning. We discuss critical challenges inherent to latent feature learning and downstream parameter estimation arising from the high dimensionality and non-identifiability of representations. Common structural assumptions for obtaining fast convergence rates with additive or sparse linear models are shown to be unrealistic for latent features. We argue, however, that neural networks are largely insensitive to these issues. In particular, we show that neural networks can achieve fast convergence rates by adapting to intrinsic notions of sparsity and dimension of the learning problem.

paragraphs: Images and text can contain information that confounds estimates of a treatment's average effect. Ignoring that information can produce biased conclusions, but incorporating it requires turning complex inputs into usable features. This paper examines when representations from pretrained neural networks can support valid adjustment for these sources of confounding.

The authors formalize conditions under which those features permit valid treatment-effect estimation and statistical inference, using double machine learning as an example. They also examine difficulties caused by high-dimensional representations and by the fact that their coordinates are not uniquely determined. Assumptions that make additive or sparse linear models converge quickly can be unrealistic for such learned features.

The paper argues that neural networks are largely insensitive to these representation issues. In particular, it shows that they can achieve fast convergence by adapting to the learning problem's intrinsic sparsity and dimension. The contribution therefore concerns both when pretrained features preserve the information needed for causal adjustment and which downstream estimators can use those features effectively.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditions for causal adjustment with pretrained features and explains why neural networks can handle their representation challenges.

title: Adjustment for Confounding using Pre-Trained Representations

abstract: Recent advances in large multimodal models (LMMs) have recognized fine-grained grounding as an imperative factor of visual understanding and dialogue. However, the benefits of such representation in LMMs are limited to the natural image domain, and these models perform poorly for remote sensing (RS). The distinct overhead viewpoint, scale variation, and presence of small objects in high-resolution RS imagery present a unique challenge in region-level comprehension. Moreover, the development of the grounding conversation capability of LMMs within RS is hindered by the lack of granular, RS domain-specific grounded data. Addressing these limitations, we propose GeoPixel - the first end-to-end high-resolution RS-LMM that supports pixel-level grounding. This capability allows fine-grained visual perception by generating interleaved masks in conversation. GeoPixel supports up to 4K HD resolution in any aspect ratio, ideal for high-precision RS image analysis. To support the grounded conversation generation (GCG) in RS imagery, we curate a visually grounded dataset GeoPixelD through a semi-automated pipeline that utilizes set-of-marks prompting and spatial priors tailored for RS data to methodically control the data generation process. GeoPixel demonstrates superior performance in pixel-level comprehension, surpassing existing LMMs in both single-target and multi-target segmentation tasks. Our methodological ablation studies validate the effectiveness of each component in the overall architecture. Our code and data will be publicly released.

paragraphs: Remote-sensing images pose challenges that ordinary photographs do not: overhead views, large changes in scale, and small objects within high-resolution scenes. Multimodal models also lack enough detailed, domain-specific examples connecting conversation to image regions. GeoPixel addresses these issues by linking conversational outputs to precise pixel masks in remote-sensing imagery.

The model supports images up to 4K resolution with arbitrary aspect ratios and can interleave segmentation masks with conversation. This gives its responses an explicit visual reference at the pixel level. The authors also construct GeoPixelD, a grounded conversation dataset, using a semi-automated process that combines set-of-marks prompting with spatial information tailored to remote sensing.

GeoPixel outperforms the existing multimodal models evaluated on segmentation involving both single and multiple targets. Component-removal studies also support the usefulness of the architecture’s individual parts. The contribution combines a model capable of detailed visual grounding with training data built for the same setting, addressing both the representation and data challenges behind remote-sensing conversation.
summary.tldr: GeoPixel combines high-resolution remote-sensing conversation with pixel masks and a domain-specific grounded dataset.

title: GeoPixel: Pixel Grounding Large Multimodal Model in Remote Sensing

abstract: Retrosynthesis, the process of breaking down a target molecule into simpler precursors through a series of valid reactions, stands at the core of organic chemistry and drug development. Although recent machine learning (ML) research has advanced single-step retrosynthetic modeling and subsequent route searches, these solutions remain restricted by the extensive combinatorial space of possible pathways. Concurrently, large language models (LLMs) have exhibited remarkable chemical knowledge, hinting at their potential to tackle complex decision-making tasks in chemistry. In this work, we explore whether LLMs can successfully navigate the highly constrained, multi-step retrosynthesis planning problem. We introduce an efficient scheme for encoding reaction pathways and present a new route-level search strategy, moving beyond the conventional step-by-step reactant prediction. Through comprehensive evaluations, we show that our LLM-augmented approach excels at retrosynthesis planning and extends naturally to the broader challenge of synthesizable molecular design.

paragraphs: Retrosynthesis plans how to make a target molecule by working backward through valid reactions to simpler precursors. Even when a model can predict useful individual reaction steps, searching for a complete route remains difficult because the number of possible pathways grows rapidly. This paper investigates whether language models’ chemical knowledge can help with that constrained, multistep planning problem.

The authors introduce an efficient way to encode reaction pathways and a search strategy that operates at the route level. This changes the unit of decision-making from individual reactant predictions to synthesis pathways. The approach uses language models to augment the planning process, aiming to navigate the large space of possible routes more effectively.

Comprehensive evaluations are reported to show strong retrosynthesis-planning performance. The method also extends to synthesizable molecular design, connecting the choice of a molecule with the question of how it could be made. The contribution is therefore a way to organize chemical knowledge and route search together, with demonstrated applicability to both planning synthesis and designing molecules around synthesis considerations.
summary.tldr: An LLM-augmented route-level search approach supports multistep retrosynthesis planning and extends to synthesizable molecular design.

title: LLM-Augmented Chemical Synthesis and Design Decision Programs

abstract: We study online learning in Bayesian Stackelberg games, where a leader repeatedly interacts with a follower whose unknown private type is independently drawn at each round from an unknown probability distribution. The goal is to design algorithms that minimize the leader’s regret with respect to always playing an optimal commitment computed with knowledge of the game. We consider, for the first time to the best of our knowledge, the most realistic case in which the leader does not know anything about follower’s types, i.e., the possible follower’s payoffs. This raises considerable additional challenges compared to the usually addressed case in which follower’s payoffs are known. First, we prove a strong negative result: no-regret is unattainable under action feedback, i.e., when the leader only observes the follower’s best response at the end of each round. Thus, we focus on the easier type feedback model, where the follower’s type is also revealed. In such a setting, we propose an algorithm that achieves a regret of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$, ignoring the dependence on other parameters.

paragraphs: In the repeated game studied here, a leader commits to a strategy and a follower responds according to a private type. Each round draws that type independently from an unknown distribution. The leader also lacks knowledge of the possible follower payoffs, making the learning problem more demanding than settings where those payoffs are supplied.

The objective is to limit regret relative to repeatedly using an optimal commitment chosen with full knowledge of the game. The paper first shows that no-regret learning is impossible when the leader sees only the follower’s chosen best response. Observing actions alone therefore provides insufficient feedback for this objective in the unknown-type setting.

The authors then consider richer feedback that reveals the follower’s type after each round as well. Under this feedback model, they propose an algorithm with regret of approximately square-root order in the number of rounds, suppressing logarithmic factors and dependence on other parameters. The contrast identifies feedback about private types as a decisive ingredient separating an impossibility result from a positive learning guarantee.
summary.tldr: With unknown follower payoffs, no-regret Stackelberg learning is impossible from action feedback alone but achievable with revealed types.

title: Learning in Bayesian Stackelberg Games With Unknown Follower’s Types

abstract: Survival analysis is a cornerstone of clinical research by modeling time-to-event outcomes such as metastasis, disease relapse, or patient death. Unlike standard tabular data, survival data often come with incomplete event information due to dropout, or loss to follow-up. This poses unique challenges for synthetic data generation, where it is crucial for clinical research to faithfully reproduce both the event-time distribution and the censoring mechanism. In this paper, we propose SurvDiff, an end-to-end diffusion model specifically designed for generating synthetic data in survival analysis. SurvDiff is tailored to capture the data-generating mechanism by jointly generating mixed-type covariates, event times, and right-censoring, guided by a survival-tailored loss function. The loss encodes the time-to-event structure and directly optimizes for downstream survival tasks, which ensures that SurvDiff (i) reproduces realistic event-time distributions and (ii) preserves the censoring mechanism. Across multiple datasets, we show that SurvDiff outperforms state-of-the-art generative baselines in both distributional fidelity and survival model evaluation metrics across multiple medical datasets. To the best of our knowledge, SurvDiff is the first end-to-end diffusion model explicitly designed for generating synthetic survival data.

This poses unique challenges for synthetic data generation, where it is crucial for clinical research to faithfully reproduce both the event-time distribution and the censoring mechanism. SurvDiff is tailored to capture the data-generating mechanism by jointly generating mixed-type covariates, event times, and right-censoring, guided by a survival-tailored loss function. The loss encodes the time-to-event structure and directly optimizes for downstream survival tasks, which ensures that SurvDiff (i) reproduces realistic event-time distributions and (ii) preserves the censoring mechanism. Across multiple datasets, we show that SurvDiff outperforms state-of-the-art generative baselines in both distributional fidelity and survival model evaluation metrics across multiple medical datasets. To the best of our knowledge, SurvDiff is the first end-to-end diffusion model explicitly designed for generating synthetic survival data.

paragraphs: Survival data record how long it takes for an event to occur, but observation can end before the event is seen. This right-censoring makes synthetic survival data more complicated than ordinary tables: a generator must reproduce both event timing and the process that leaves some outcomes incomplete. SurvDiff is a diffusion model designed around that joint requirement.

The model generates mixed-type covariates, event times, and right-censoring together. Its survival-specific loss encodes time-to-event structure and directly optimizes for downstream survival tasks. This connects the generation objective to how the resulting records will be used, while targeting realistic event-time distributions and preservation of the censoring mechanism.

Across multiple medical datasets, SurvDiff outperforms state-of-the-art generative baselines on both distributional fidelity and survival-model evaluation metrics. Those two forms of evaluation address complementary goals: resembling the source data and retaining information useful for survival analysis. The authors present it, to their knowledge, as the first end-to-end diffusion model explicitly developed for synthetic survival data, emphasizing the value of incorporating the task's incomplete-observation structure.
summary.tldr: SurvDiff jointly generates patient covariates, event times, and censoring to improve synthetic survival data fidelity and downstream usefulness.

title: SurvDiff: A Diffusion Model for Generating Synthetic Data in Survival Analysis

abstract: Spectrally sparse signal reconstruction arises in a wide range of applications and can be formulated as a low-rank Hankel matrix completion problem. We develop a Jacobi-preconditioned gradient descent method that preserves the low per-iteration complexity of first-order algorithms while achieving linear convergence at a rate independent of the condition number. By introducing a generator that maps factor-based iterates to matrix space, we establish equivalence with manifold-based methods, enabling direct convergence analysis while avoiding the need to define distances under complex-symmetric factorization ambiguity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both iteration count and computational time across a broad range of problem settings.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a spectrally sparse signal can be expressed as completing a low-rank Hankel matrix. This formulation turns signal recovery into a structured matrix problem. The paper develops a gradient descent method designed to keep each iteration inexpensive while reducing the number of iterations needed to reach an accurate reconstruction.

The method uses Jacobi preconditioning and achieves linear convergence at a rate independent of the condition number. For its analysis, the authors introduce a generator mapping factor-based iterates into matrix space. This establishes an equivalence with manifold-based methods and allows convergence to be studied directly, avoiding the need to define distances amid ambiguities in complex-symmetric factorization.

The contribution brings together an efficient update rule and an analysis that handles the factorization's representational ambiguity. Its reported benefit is therefore both theoretical, through the convergence rate, and practical, through the observed reduction in reconstruction time.
summary.tldr: Jacobi-preconditioned gradient descent accelerates spectrally sparse signal reconstruction with inexpensive iterations and a condition-number-independent linear convergence rate.

title: Fast Spectrally Sparse Signal Reconstruction via Jacobi-Preconditioned Gradient Descent

abstract: Assistive agents should not only take actions on behalf of a human, but also step out of the way and cede control when there are important decisions to be made. However, current methods for building assistive agents, whether via mimicking expert humans or via RL finetuning on an inferred reward, often encourage agents to complete tasks on their own rather than truly assisting the human achieve her objectives. We propose a new approach to tuning assistive language models based on maximizing the human’s empowerment, their ability to effect desired changes in the environment. Our empowerment-maximizing method, Empower, only requires offline examples of human-written text, providing a self-supervised method for fine-tuning language models to better assist humans. To study the efficacy of our approach, we conducted an 18-person user study comparing our empowerment assistant with a strong baseline. Participants preferred our assistant 78% of the time (p=0.015), with a 31% higher acceptance rate. With this empowerment objective, we provide a framework for useful aligned AI agents without the need for human feedback or verifiable rewards.

paragraphs: An assistive agent should help a person achieve their objectives while leaving them control over important decisions. The paper argues that imitation and reward-based fine-tuning can encourage agents to complete tasks independently. It proposes human empowerment as a training objective, defined as the person’s ability to bring about desired changes in the environment.

The resulting method, Empower, fine-tunes language models using only offline examples of human-written text. The paper offers empowerment maximization as a framework for training useful assistants around human agency, supported by the reported user preferences.
summary.tldr: Empower fine-tunes assistants to support human agency using offline text, earning 78% preference in an 18-person comparison study.

title: Training LLM Agents to Empower Humans

abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown remarkable abilities by integrating large language models with visual inputs. However, they often rely on textual shortcuts rather than adequately using visual evidence during reasoning. Although reinforcement learning (RL) can align models with desired behaviors, its application to VLMs has been hindered by the lack of scalable and reliable rewards. To overcome this challenge, we propose SSL4RL, a novel framework that leverages self-supervised learning (SSL) tasks as a source of verifiable rewards for RL. Our approach reformulates SSL objectives like rotation prediction and patch reconstruction into dense automatic rewards, removing the need for human preferences or AI evaluators. Experiments show that SSL4RL substantially improves performance on both vision-centric and vision-language reasoning benchmarks, with encouraging potentials on open-ended scenarios and stronger resilience to visual corruptions. Through systematic ablations, we identify key factors influencing SSL4RL, including data volume, model scale, model choice, task combination, and task difficulty, thereby offering new design principles for future work. Our implementation is open-sourced at https://github.com/PKU-ML/SSL4RL, with models hosted on Huggingface collection https://huggingface.co/collections/PKU-ML/ssl4rl.

Reinforcement learning could encourage better visual reasoning, but it requires reliable rewards that can be produced at scale. SSL4RL uses self-supervised visual tasks to supply those rewards automatically, without human preference labels or AI evaluators.

The framework turns objectives such as predicting image rotation and reconstructing patches into dense, verifiable reward signals. This connects reinforcement learning to tasks whose supervision comes from the visual learning setup itself. The approach makes the reward source a central design choice, using visual tasks to encourage capabilities relevant to interpreting images.

Experiments report substantial improvements on vision-centric and vision-language reasoning benchmarks, along with greater resilience to visual corruption. Results in open-ended scenarios are described as encouraging potential. Ablations examine data volume, model size and choice, task combinations, and task difficulty. Those analyses help identify which design decisions influence the approach, beyond establishing that self-supervised rewards can improve the tested models.
summary.tldr: SSL4RL converts self-supervised visual tasks into automatic reinforcement-learning rewards, improving visual reasoning and resilience to image corruption.

title: SSL4RL: Revisiting Self-supervised Learning as Intrinsic Reward for Visual-Language Reasoning

abstract: Diffusion Transformer models can generate images with remarkable fidelity and detail, yet training them at ultra-high resolutions remains extremely costly due to the self-attention mechanism’s quadratic scaling with the number of image tokens. In this paper, we introduce Dynamic Position Extrapolation (DyPE), a novel, training-free method that enables pre-trained diffusion transformers to synthesize images at resolutions far beyond their training data, with no additional sampling cost. DyPE takes advantage of the spectral progression inherent to the diffusion process, where low-frequency structures converge early, while high-frequencies take more steps to resolve. Specifically, DyPE dynamically adjusts the model’s positional encoding at each diffusion step, matching their frequency spectrum with the current stage of the generative process. This approach allows us to generate images at resolutions that exceed the training resolution dramatically, e.g., 16 million pixels using FLUX. On multiple benchmarks, DyPE consistently improves performance and achieves state-of-the-art fidelity in ultra-high-resolution image generation, with gains becoming even more pronounced at higher resolutions.

paragraphs: Diffusion Transformers can generate detailed images, but training at very high resolutions is expensive because attention costs grow quadratically with the number of image tokens. DyPE addresses the challenge of using an already trained model at resolutions far beyond those encountered during training, without additional training or sampling cost.

Its central observation concerns how diffusion resolves an image over time. Broad, low-frequency structures settle earlier, while fine, high-frequency details require more steps. DyPE changes positional encodings at each diffusion step so that their frequency spectrum matches the current stage of image formation. Position information therefore adapts as generation moves from coarse structure toward finer detail.

The authors report generating images with 16 million pixels using FLUX. Across multiple benchmarks, DyPE consistently improves performance and achieves state-of-the-art fidelity for ultra-high-resolution generation, with larger gains at higher resolutions. The stated result shows that adapting position representations during sampling can extend a pretrained model’s usable resolution range, without requiring the costly high-resolution training that motivates the work.
summary.tldr: DyPE dynamically adjusts positional encodings during diffusion to improve generation far beyond training resolution without additional training or sampling cost.

title: DyPE: Dynamic Position Extrapolation for Ultra High Resolution Diffusion

abstract: Recent multi-bit watermarking methods for large language models (LLMs) prioritize capacity over reliability, often conflating decoding with detection. Our analysis reveals that existing ECC-based extractors suffer from catastrophic false positive rates (FPR), and applying rejection thresholds merely collapses detection sensitivity (TPR) to random guessing. To resolve this structural limitation, we propose BREW (Block-wise Reliable Embedding for Watermarking), a framework shifting the paradigm to designated verification. BREW employs a two-stage mechanism: (i) blind message estimation via independent block voting, followed by (ii) window-shifting verification that rigorously validates the payload against local edits. Experiments demonstrate that BREW achieves a TPR of 0.965 with an FPR of 0.02 under 10% synonym substitution, demonstrating that the high-FPR issue is not an inherent trade-off of multi-bit watermarking, but a solvable structural flaw of prior decoding-centric designs. Our framework is model-agnostic and theoretically grounded, providing a scalable solution for reliable forensic deployment.

paragraphs: Multi-bit text watermarks embed a recoverable message in generated text. Recovering a candidate message, however, is different from establishing that a watermark is actually present. The paper finds that existing extractors based on error-correcting codes can confuse these tasks, producing extremely high false-positive rates. Adding rejection thresholds can then reduce detection sensitivity to chance levels.

BREW separates the process into message estimation and designated verification. Independent votes from text blocks first produce a candidate payload without knowing it in advance. A second stage shifts verification windows to check that payload while accounting for local edits. This gives the method a distinct step for validating evidence of a watermark.

Under 10% synonym substitution, the reported true-positive rate is 0.965 at a false-positive rate of 0.02. This result supports the authors’ claim that unreliable detection is a fixable structural problem in the evaluated decoding-centered designs, rather than an unavoidable consequence of carrying multiple bits. The framework is model-agnostic and combines theoretical grounding with empirical evidence for more reliable watermark verification.
summary.tldr: BREW separates watermark-message recovery from verification to improve reliable detection after local text edits.

title: Block-wise Codeword Embedding for Reliable Multi-bit Text Watermarking

abstract: Recently, machine learning Hamiltonian (MLH) models have gained traction as fast approximations of electronic structures such as orbitals and electron densities, while also enabling direct evaluation of energies and forces from their predictions. However, despite their physical grounding, existing Hamiltonian models are evaluated mainly by reconstruction metrics, leaving it unclear how well they perform as energy–force predictors. We address this gap with a benchmark that computes energies and forces directly from predicted Hamiltonians. Within this framework, we propose QHFlow2, a state-of-the-art Hamiltonian model with an SO(2)-equivariant backbone and a two-stage edge update. QHFlow2 achieves $40%$ lower Hamiltonian error than the previous best model with fewer parameters. Under direct evaluation on MD17/rMD17, it is the first Hamiltonian model to reach NequIP-level force accuracy while achieving up to $20\times$ lower energy MAE. On QH9, QHFlow2 reduces energy error by up to $20\times$ compared to MACE. Finally, we demonstrate that QHFlow2 exhibits consistent scaling behavior with respect to model capacity and data, and that improvements in Hamiltonian accuracy effectively translate into more accurate energy and force computations.

paragraphs: Machine-learning Hamiltonian models approximate electronic structure and allow energies and forces to be computed from their predictions. Yet evaluating how closely they reconstruct a Hamiltonian does not directly establish their usefulness for those physical quantities. This paper introduces a benchmark that evaluates energies and forces obtained from predicted Hamiltonians themselves.

Within that framework, the authors propose QHFlow2, using an SO(2)-equivariant backbone and a two-stage edge update. It reduces Hamiltonian error by 40% relative to the previous best model while using fewer parameters. The architecture is assessed both on its intermediate electronic-structure prediction and on the resulting energy and force calculations.

The authors also observe consistent scaling with model capacity and data, with improvements in Hamiltonian accuracy translating into better energy and force estimates. These findings support evaluating learned Hamiltonians as practical physical predictors, beyond reconstruction quality alone.
summary.tldr: QHFlow2 improves Hamiltonian prediction and demonstrates that those gains translate into highly accurate direct energy and force calculations.

title: Machine Learning Hamiltonians are Accurate Energy-Force Predictors

abstract: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is an important technique for ensuring the trustworthiness of LLMs, given their tendency to hallucinate. Existing state-of-the-art UQ approaches for free-form generation rely heavily on sampling, which incurs high computational cost and variance. In this work, we propose the first gradient-based UQ method for free-form generation, SemGrad, which is sampling-free and computationally efficient. Unlike prior gradient-based methods developed for classification tasks that operates in parameter space, we propose to consider gradients in semantic space. Our method builds on the key intuition that a confident LLM should maintain stable output distributions under semantically equivalent input perturbations. We interpret the stability as the gradients in semantic space and introduce a Semantic Preservation Score (SPS) to identify embeddings that best capture semantics, with respect to which gradients are computed. We further propose HybridGrad, which combines the strengths of SemGrad and parameter gradients. Experiments demonstrate that both of our methods provide efficient and effective uncertainty estimates, achieving superior performance than state-of-the-art methods, particularly in settings with multiple valid responses.

paragraphs: Estimating uncertainty in freely generated language often requires sampling several responses, which adds computation and variability. SemGrad instead measures uncertainty through gradients, avoiding repeated response sampling. Its guiding intuition is that a confident model should produce stable output distributions when the input changes in ways that preserve its meaning.

The method computes gradients with respect to semantic representations rather than relying only on changes in model parameters. A Semantic Preservation Score identifies embeddings that best retain meaning, providing the space in which sensitivity is measured. The paper also introduces HybridGrad, which combines the semantic-gradient approach with parameter gradients.

Experiments report efficient uncertainty estimates and better performance than leading alternatives, particularly when a prompt admits multiple valid responses. That setting matters because variation among acceptable answers need not indicate unreliable reasoning. By examining sensitivity in a meaning-preserving space, the method seeks a confidence signal aligned with semantic stability. The results support this signal as a practical alternative to uncertainty estimation dominated by response sampling.
summary.tldr: SemGrad estimates language-model uncertainty without sampling by measuring sensitivity in embeddings chosen to preserve meaning.

title: Gradients with Respect to Semantics Preserving Embeddings Tell the Uncertainty of Large Language Models

abstract: Latent Factorization-of-Tensors (LFT) models are an effective approach for relation analysis. Existing LFT models assume each mode of the target tensor corresponds to an entity set and the relationships between entity sets are bipartite graphs to explore the relationships among entities within a mode. However, when the topological structure of entities in a mode is known, for example, entities are ordered physical quantities, such as time or coordinates, the relations between such modes forms a more complicated structure, i.e., aligned bipartite networks, and existing LFT models cannot accurately capture this structure. This work is the first to recognize and analyze this issue, and proposes an Asymmetric Latent Factorization-of-Tensors (ALFT) model to address it. ALFT can model aligned bipartite networks in mode pairs of a tensor by imposing constraints between particular mode pairs in the tensor network. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the existence of this issue and confirm that the proposed ALFT model can effectively resolve it.

paragraphs: Tensor factorization represents relationships across several sets of entities through compact latent factors. Existing models commonly treat each tensor dimension, or mode, as an entity set and describe relationships between sets using bipartite graphs. This paper examines what happens when entities within a mode also have a known structure.

For ordered physical quantities such as time or coordinates, entities are not simply interchangeable items in a set. Their organization creates what the authors call aligned bipartite networks between modes. The paper argues that existing latent tensor factorization models cannot accurately represent this richer arrangement and presents an analysis of the resulting mismatch.

The proposed Asymmetric Latent Factorization-of-Tensors model, ALFT, adds constraints between selected pairs of modes in the tensor network. Those constraints let it model their alignment explicitly. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the identified problem and support ALFT’s ability to address it. The contribution is therefore a structural change to relation modeling: known organization within entity sets becomes part of the factorization rather than being omitted from its assumptions.
summary.tldr: ALFT adds constraints between tensor modes to capture relationships shaped by known ordering or topology within entity sets.

title: An Asymmetric Latent Factorization-of-Tensors Model for Relation Analysis

abstract: While Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) achieves remarkable success, hallucinations remain a significant barrier to their reliable deployment. Recent studies primarily attribute these defects to cross-modal attention imbalances, with most solutions focusing on re-weighting visual tokens or suppressing language priors. Such approaches often overlook the spectral characteristics of the visual information flow and frequently rely on Contrastive Decoding (CD), which doubles the inference time. Instead of following conventional approaches, we identify two distinct hallucination patterns—Perceptual-Semantic Dissociation and Localized Fixation—and accordingly develop FLASH (Frequency-Localized Attention SHaping), a training-free and CD-free framework. FLASH utilizes a Spectral Vortex Score to detect visual heads within multi-head attention layers, applying adaptive spectral modulation to rectify the visual information flow during the decoding phase. Empirical results demonstrate that FLASH offers a superior balance between performance and efficiency compared to SOTA methods.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can produce descriptions that do not match the visual evidence. Existing remedies often adjust how much attention goes to images versus language, or use contrastive decoding, which the abstract identifies as doubling inference time. This paper examines another aspect of the problem: the spectral structure of visual information as it flows through attention.

The authors identify two hallucination patterns, called Perceptual-Semantic Dissociation and Localized Fixation. They develop FLASH, a method that changes attention during decoding without additional training or contrastive decoding. A Spectral Vortex Score identifies visual attention heads, and adaptive spectral modulation then adjusts the information flowing through those heads.

The approach matters because it changes the structure of visual processing rather than relying solely on the total attention assigned to visual tokens. The experiments report a better balance between performance and efficiency than the compared state-of-the-art methods. This supports spectral modulation as a practical intervention for reducing hallucinations while avoiding the particular inference overhead associated with contrastive decoding.
summary.tldr: FLASH reduces vision-language hallucinations by modifying the spectral structure of visual attention during decoding, without training or contrastive decoding.

title: Beyond Attention Imbalance: Mitigating Hallucinations via Spectral Surgery

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success across complex decision-making tasks, especially with the advent of deep neural networks. However, the resulting models are often opaque, making their deployment in safety-critical domains challenging. Explainable AI aims to address this issue, but most specific efforts for deep RL remain limited either to post-hoc explanation methods or to imitation learning and distillation procedures. These latter approaches rely on pre-trained black-box agents and are typically restricted to environments with discrete action spaces, limiting their scalability and interpretability. In this paper, we introduce ProtoSAC, a novel deep RL architecture that integrates a prototype-based actor into the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm, enabling intrinsic interpretability in continuous action spaces. Our method learns a set of prototypes that represent interpretable state clusters, each associated with a Gaussian action distribution. Actions are generated as a similarity-weighted mixture over these prototypes, providing more inspectable and decomposable decision-making without sacrificing performance compared to standard SAC. We evaluate ProtoSAC on continuous control environments and show that it matches the performance of the original SAC while offering enhanced interpretability.

Explainable AI aims to address this issue, but most specific efforts for deep RL remain limited either to post-hoc explanation methods or to imitation learning and distillation procedures. These latter approaches rely on pre-trained black-box agents and are typically restricted to environments with discrete action spaces, limiting their scalability and interpretability. In this paper, we introduce ProtoSAC, a novel deep RL architecture that integrates a prototype-based actor into the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm, enabling intrinsic interpretability in continuous action spaces. Our method learns a set of prototypes that represent interpretable state clusters, each associated with a Gaussian action distribution. Actions are generated as a similarity-weighted mixture over these prototypes, providing more inspectable and decomposable decision-making without sacrificing performance compared to standard SAC. We evaluate ProtoSAC on continuous control environments and show that it matches the performance of the original SAC while offering enhanced interpretability.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning agents can make effective decisions while offering little insight into how those decisions arise. This paper introduces ProtoSAC, which builds an inspectable decision process into Soft Actor-Critic. It targets continuous action spaces, where approaches based on explaining or copying a pretrained black-box agent have faced limitations.

ProtoSAC learns prototypes representing interpretable clusters of states. Each prototype has an associated Gaussian action distribution. For a new state, the actor generates actions through a mixture weighted by similarity to these prototypes. A decision can therefore be examined through the states it resembles and the contributions of their associated action distributions.

This structure makes interpretability part of the actor’s computation and allows its decisions to be decomposed into prototype contributions. In the evaluated continuous-control environments, ProtoSAC matches standard SAC performance while improving interpretability. The result supports prototype-based action generation as a way to expose the basis of continuous decisions without the performance loss that might otherwise make such an architecture difficult to adopt.
summary.tldr: ProtoSAC makes continuous-control decisions inspectable through learned state prototypes while matching standard SAC performance in the tested environments.

title: This State Looks Like That: Self-Interpretable Reinforcement Learning Agents using Prototype Soft Actor-Critic

abstract: Analogy is a central faculty of human intelligence, enabling abstract patterns discovered in one domain to be applied to another. However, the mechanisms underlying analogical reasoning in Transformers remain poorly understood. In this work, inspired by the notion of functors in category theory, we formalize analogical reasoning as the inference of correspondences between entities across categories. Based on this formulation, we introduce synthetic tasks that evaluate the emergence of analogical reasoning under controlled settings. We find that the emergence of analogical reasoning is highly sensitive to data characteristics, optimization choices, and model scale. Through mechanistic analysis, we show that analogical reasoning in Transformers decomposes into two key components: (1) geometric alignment of relational structure in the embedding space, and (2) the application of a functor within the Transformer. These mechanisms enable models to transfer relational structure from one category to another, realizing analogy. Finally, we quantify these effects and find that the same trends are observed in pretrained LLMs. In doing so, we move analogy from an abstract cognitive notion to a concrete, mechanistically grounded phenomenon in modern neural networks.

abstract: Continual learning for visual question answering (VQA) is typically implemented by training one expert per task and routing each query using task-ID supervision. Yet continual VQA tasks overlap substantially: on the VQA-v2 task stream, a non-native expert outperforms the task’s own expert on $49.9%$ of queries, so hard routing both wastes transferable knowledge and can be confidently wrong when mismatched. We propose a calibrated Bayesian mixture-of-experts that trains parameter-efficient per-task adapters, learns routing by directly maximizing expected VQA utility, and marginalizes expert identity at inference via Bayesian aggregation in a unified answer space; an entropy penalty prevents the utility objective from collapsing to one-hot routing, enabling evidence pooling across plausible experts. We reach $64.16$ accuracy with $0.63$ forgetting on VQA-v2 CL-LS ($+5.74%$ accuracy, $-2.99$ forgetting vs. the strongest prior method), $78.81$ with $0.40$ forgetting on TDIUC CL-LS ($+3.10$, $-1.74$), and $83.41$ with $3.21$ forgetting on TDIUC CL-VS ($+1.58$, $-0.82$). Calibration also improves on VQA-v2, reducing ECE from $0.15$ to $0.07$.

summary.tldr: A calibrated Bayesian mixture combines knowledge across task experts to improve continual visual question answering and reduce forgetting.

title: Calibrated Knowledge Aggregation in Bayesian Mixture-of-Experts for Continual VQA

abstract: What formal languages can a recurrent neural language model recognize? Formal results in the literature conflict: some authors report Turing-completeness, while others show equivalence to regular languages. The reason for this discrepancy is that the underlying arithmetic model differs. The paper develops a unified algebraic account of the expressivity of recurrent neural networks, starting with a formal account of various arithmetic models. This account reduces expressivity to an algebraic question, e.g., whether a network’s syntactic monoid divides a certain wreath product. As a case study, the paper revisits diagonal state-space models: the same architecture cannot implement an even-modulus counter once floating-point recurrences are enforced, yet realizes every even-modulus counter under unsigned-integer quantization.

This paper attributes the discrepancy to different assumptions about the arithmetic used inside the recurrence. Those assumptions change what the model can represent and compute.

One such question concerns a relationship between a language's syntactic monoid and a wreath product. The result shows why expressivity claims need to identify the numerical rules as well as the network architecture.
summary.tldr: An algebraic framework explains how arithmetic choices can fundamentally change a recurrent model's computational expressivity.

title: An Algebraic View of the Expressivity of Recurrent Language Models

abstract: Audio large language models (Audio LLMs) demonstrate strong performance on speech understanding tasks, yet their ability to understand paralinguistic information remains limited. To systematically quantify this issue, we introduce VoxParadox, an adversarial benchmark with 2,000 verified examples, spanning 10 paralinguistic tasks, created with controlled speech synthesis to intentionally mismatch transcript claims and speaking style, enabling direct measurement of speech paralinguistic understanding. Evaluation of a diverse set of Audio LLMs reveals consistently low accuracy on acoustic ground truth and a strong tendency to follow language-implied (incorrect) answers. To understand the cause of this gap, we perform layer-wise probing and find that (i) paralinguistic cues can degrade in deeper encoder layers and at the encoder–LLM interface, and (ii) even when such cues are available in audio tokens, the language model frequently ignores them. To address these problems, we propose Prompt-Conditioned Layer Mixer (PCLM), which adaptively combines information from multiple audio layers based on the input prompt, and pair it with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to explicitly prefer acoustically supported options over language-implied alternatives. These methods substantially improve Audio LLM paralinguistic understanding, improving Audio Flamingo 3 from 17.40% to 65.20% on VoxParadox, and from 37.74% to 54.78% on MMSU paralinguistic subset. Our project page is available at https://voxparadox.github.io/.

title: Do Audio LLMs Listen or Read? Analyzing and Mitigating Paralinguistic Failures with VoxParadox

abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight draft model to propose candidate tokens that are then verified in parallel by the target model. The speedup is significantly determined by the acceptance rate, yet standard training minimizes Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence as a proxy objective. While KL divergence and acceptance rate share the same global optimum, small draft models, having limited capacity, typically converge to suboptimal solutions where minimizing KL does not guarantee maximizing acceptance rate. To address this issue, we propose LK losses, special training objectives that directly target acceptance rate. Comprehensive experiments across four draft architectures and six target models, ranging from 8B to 685B parameters, demonstrate consistent improvements in acceptance metrics across all configurations compared to the standard KL-based training. We evaluate our approach on general, coding and math domains and report gains of up to 8-10% in average acceptance length. LK losses are easy to implement, introduce no computational overhead and can be directly integrated into any existing speculator training framework, making them a compelling alternative to the existing draft training objectives.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding speeds up language generation by letting a small model propose tokens that a larger target model verifies in parallel. Its effectiveness depends strongly on how many proposed tokens are accepted. Draft models are commonly trained using Kullback-Leibler divergence, but this objective only serves as a proxy for the acceptance behavior that determines useful progress.

The paper explains why the proxy can fall short: KL divergence and acceptance rate share a global optimum, yet small draft models have limited capacity and usually reach suboptimal solutions. The authors describe the losses as easy to implement, free of additional computational overhead, and compatible with existing speculator training frameworks.
summary.tldr: LK losses train speculative draft models directly for token acceptance, improving acceptance metrics over KL-based training in every tested configuration.

title: LK Losses: Direct Acceptance Rate Optimization for Speculative Decoding

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising avenue for scientific discovery, yet their application to symbolic regression is often constrained by inefficient search strategies and coarse feedback signals. Current methods typically guide LLMs using scalar metrics (e.g., global Mean Squared Error), which fail to identify which components of a proposed equation are driving performance or causing error. We introduce Influence-Guided Symbolic Regression (IGSR), a method that frames equation discovery as an iterative two-step process combining diverse term generation with rigorous selection: an LLM generates candidate basis functions $\psi_j(\mathbf{x})$ for a linear model, which are then evaluated using granular influence scores $\Delta_j$. These scores quantify each term’s marginal contribution to generalization accuracy, enabling an influence-guided pruning process that systematically refines the model structure. Integrating this mechanism into a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) enables navigating the combinatorial search space while balancing exploration of novel functional forms with exploitation of high-influence components. We demonstrate IGSR’s effectiveness on a diverse suite of benchmarks, including LLM-SRBench, pharmacological PKPD models, an epidemiological simulation, and real-world genomic data. Notably, we validate the framework’s capacity for genuine discovery in a case study using a high-dimensional biological dataset, in which IGSR identified a novel relationship between DNA methylation and RNA Polymerase II pausing; a hypothesis that was subsequently supported via wet-lab experimentation.

When a language model proposes an equation and receives only an overall error score, it gets little guidance about which terms help. Influence-Guided Symbolic Regression addresses this problem by providing feedback on individual components of a candidate equation.

The method alternates between generating diverse basis functions and selecting useful ones. A language model proposes the functions for a linear combination, and influence scores measure each term's marginal contribution to generalization accuracy. These scores guide pruning. summary.tldr: IGSR guides language-model equation search with term-level influence scores and reports a biological hypothesis supported by wet-lab experiments.

title: Influence-Guided Symbolic Regression: Scientific Discovery via LLM-Driven Equation Search with Granular Feedback

abstract: Scaling inference methods such as Markov chain Monte Carlo to high-dimensional models remains a central challenge in Bayesian deep learning. A promising recent proposal, microcanonical Langevin Monte Carlo, has shown state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of problems. However, its reliance on full-dataset gradients makes it prohibitively expensive for large-scale problems. This paper addresses a fundamental question: Can microcanonical dynamics effectively leverage mini-batch gradient noise? We provide the first systematic study of this problem, establishing a novel continuous-time theoretical analysis of stochastic-gradient microcanonical dynamics. We reveal two critical failure modes: a theoretically derived bias due to anisotropic gradient noise and numerical instabilities in complex high-dimensional posteriors. To tackle these issues, we propose a principled gradient noise preconditioning scheme shown to significantly reduce this bias and develop a novel, energy-variance-based adaptive tuner that automates step size selection and dynamically informs numerical guardrails. The resulting algorithm is a robust and scalable microcanonical Monte Carlo sampler that achieves state-of-the-art performance on challenging high-dimensional inference tasks like Bayesian neural networks. Combined with recent ensemble techniques, our work unlocks a new class of stochastic microcanonical Langevin ensemble (SMILE) samplers for large-scale Bayesian inference.

This paper investigates whether gradients from smaller batches can make the method practical. The central issue is whether the noise introduced by batching can be accommodated without undermining sampling behavior.

summary.tldr: Noise preconditioning and adaptive numerical tuning make mini-batch microcanonical sampling more robust for large-scale Bayesian inference.

title: Can Microcanonical Langevin Dynamics Leverage Mini-Batch Gradient Noise?

abstract: Generative Reward Models (GRMs) have demonstrated strong performance in reward modeling, due to their interpretability and potential for refinement through reinforcement learning (RL). However, widely used pairwise GRMs create a computational bottleneck in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), when calibrating or aggregating preference signals over $n$ candidates, often incurring $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ pairwise judgments. To address this issue, we propose Intergroup Relative Preference Modeling (IRPM), an RL-based method that extends the Bradley-Terry preference-learning paradigm via intergroup comparisons to train pointwise GRMs from pairwise preference data. IRPM derives a pointwise reward for each response by contrasting groups of chosen vs. rejected samples, enabling pointwise scores comparable across candidate sets and $\mathcal{O}(n)$ reward evaluation for a variable number of candidates during RL training, while preserving interpretability and scalability. Experiments show that IRPM achieves state-of-the-art performance among pointwise GRMs on JudgeBench and RewardBench, and approaches the performance of leading pairwise GRMs. In addition, IRPM achieves substantial gains in post-training evaluations, demonstrating its effectiveness. Our models and code are available at https://github.com/XINGYUN-AI-LAB/IRPM.

paragraphs: IRPM addresses the cost of evaluating candidate responses with generative reward models. Pairwise models judge responses against one another, and calibrating or aggregating preferences across n candidates often requires O(n²) judgments. A pointwise model instead assigns each response its own score, offering a more scalable route to reward evaluation.

The challenge is learning scores that remain comparable across different candidate sets while starting from pairwise preference data. IRPM extends the Bradley–Terry preference-learning framework through comparisons between groups of chosen and rejected samples. This reinforcement-learning approach derives an individual reward for each response while retaining the interpretability associated with generative reward models.

During reinforcement-learning training, the resulting model evaluates variable-sized candidate sets in O(n) reward evaluations. On JudgeBench and RewardBench, IRPM achieves state-of-the-art results among pointwise generative reward models and approaches leading pairwise models. The authors also report substantial post-training gains. Together, these results support intergroup training as a way to preserve useful preference information while reducing evaluation cost.
summary.tldr: IRPM learns comparable per-response rewards from grouped preference comparisons, enabling linear-cost evaluation of candidate sets.

title: IRPM: Intergroup Relative Preference Modeling for Pointwise Generative Reward Models

abstract: Research on adversarial robustness in language models is currently fragmented across applications and attacks, obscuring shared vulnerabilities. In this work, we propose unifying the study of adversarial robustness in text scoring models spanning dense retrievers, rerankers, and reward models. This motivates adapting both attacks and adversarial training methods across model roles. Unlike open-ended generation, text scoring failures are directly testable: an attack succeeds when an irrelevant or rejected text outscores a relevant or chosen one. Using this principled lens of text scoring, we demonstrate that current adversarial training formulations for language models are often short-sighted, failing to effectively generalize across attacks. To address this, we introduce multiple adversarial training methods for text scoring models and show that combining complementary training methods can yield strong robustness while also improving task effectiveness. We also highlight the practical value of our approach for RLHF, showing that our adversarially trained reward models mitigate reward hacking and support the training of better-aligned LLMs. We provide our code and models for further study.

This paper uses that shared structure to unify adversarial robustness research across these roles. An attack has a directly testable outcome when irrelevant or rejected text receives a higher score than relevant or preferred text.

The authors find that current training formulations often generalize poorly beyond the attacks they address. They introduce multiple training methods and show that combining complementary approaches can provide strong robustness while also improving ordinary task effectiveness.

The paper also examines reward models used in reinforcement learning from human feedback.
