These findings connect robust text scoring to both retrieval quality and the reliability of learning signals, showing practical value in studying vulnerabilities across model roles through one evaluation lens.
summary.tldr: A unified text-scoring perspective enables complementary adversarial training methods that improve robustness, task effectiveness, and resistance to reward hacking.

title: Unifying Adversarial Robustness and Training Across Text Scoring Models

abstract: In this paper, we introduce a model of evolution and learning in robots that co-optimizes a distribution of latent design vectors (genotypes) and a mixture of control experts (neural modules), which are gated by the latent coordinates of each decoded design (phenotype). This provides a scalable alternative to co-design algorithms that either train an individual policy for every robot, which is inefficient, or a monolithic universal controller for all robots, which results in overly conservative structures and behaviors. Our approach lies somewhere between these two extremes, preserving ancestral knowledge in a unified yet modular framework in which different body plans activate and deactivate different combinations of learned sensorimotor circuits for goal-directed behavior. This allows one part of the controller to be overhauled to better suit new species of designs as they emerge without disrupting the hard-earned knowledge contained within other expert modules. It also allows pretrained expert policies to be directly plugged into the mixture, which can steer evolution into otherwise unexplored areas of latent space containing desired morphological traits. We refer to this process as "evo by demo" and explore how it may be used to guide freeform evolution toward canonical structures defined by the pretrained model. Videos and code can be found at: https://eco-moe.github.io.

paragraphs: Robot co-design optimizes both a body and the controller that makes it useful. Training a separate controller for every design is inefficient, while one universal controller can encourage overly conservative bodies and behaviors. ECo-MoE takes an intermediate approach: it jointly optimizes a distribution of latent robot designs and a modular collection of control experts.

Each decoded body uses its latent design coordinates to determine which experts contribute to control. Different body plans can therefore activate different combinations of learned sensorimotor modules. This arrangement preserves shared knowledge while allowing part of the controller to change for newly emerging designs without disrupting knowledge stored in other experts.

The framework also allows pretrained expert policies to be inserted directly into the mixture. These policies can steer evolution toward previously unexplored design regions with desired morphological traits. The authors call this process evo by demo and explore its potential to guide freeform evolution toward structures represented by the pretrained model. The contribution is a mechanism for combining inherited control knowledge, modular adaptation, and directed exploration of robot designs.
summary.tldr: ECo-MoE jointly evolves robot designs and modular controllers, using body-dependent expert selection to preserve knowledge and potentially steer evolution with pretrained policies.

title: ECo-MoE: Embodiment-Conditioned Mixture of Experts Increases the Evolvability of Robots

abstract: While enabling effective collaboration on complex tasks, LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) face critical security challenges due to vulnerabilities at the agent and interaction levels. Most existing MAS security defenses are built upon two core assumptions: semantically-explicit malicious attacks and explicit graph-based modeling of the MAS topology and agent-level interactions. In practice, real-world attacks are becoming more semantically stealthy, while MAS execution is typically asynchronous without the temporal alignment assumed by graph-based propagation models. To address these limitations, we propose AcMAS, an activation-based framework for malicious-behavior detection in MAS. By analyzing internal reasoning states in the activation space of local agents, AcMAS detects even stealthy attacks in a synchronization-robust fashion, without relying on explicit interaction graphs. Moreover, our activation analysis provides critical signals to guide AcMAS in restoring the functionality of compromised agents, rather than the disruptive agent isolation commonly used by the state-of-the-art methods. Comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that AcMAS significantly outperforms graph-based baselines against stealthy attacks, by +0.22 F1 in synchronous settings (0.94 vs. 0.72) and by +0.55 F1 in asynchronous settings (0.93 vs. 0.38), with generalization across diverse open-source LLM backbones, attack intensity, and MAS scale.

paragraphs: Multi-agent language-model systems can face attacks that hide malicious intent in seemingly ordinary interactions. Defenses based on explicit attack language and synchronized interaction graphs can struggle when attacks are subtle or agents execute asynchronously. AcMAS instead examines internal activations within individual agents to detect malicious behavior.

The framework analyzes local reasoning states without requiring an explicit graph of agent interactions. This makes its detection mechanism robust to synchronization differences in the evaluated settings. Its activation analysis also provides signals for restoring compromised agents' functionality, offering a recovery mechanism beyond removing agents from the collaboration.

Against stealthy attacks, evaluations report an F1 score of 0.94 versus 0.72 for graph-based baselines in synchronous settings, and 0.93 versus 0.38 in asynchronous settings. The method also generalizes across the tested open-source model backbones, attack intensities, and system scales. These results support internal activation signals as a useful basis for detecting subtle compromise while maintaining the functioning of a collaborating agent system.
summary.tldr: AcMAS detects stealthy malicious agent behavior through internal activations and uses those signals to guide recovery.

title: When Agents Go Rogue: Activation-Based Detection of Malicious Behaviors in Multi-Agent Systems

abstract: Tertiary structure-based RNA design aims to generate RNA sequences that can fold into desired 3D structures, but remains a challenging problem due to the scarcity of annotated data, structural noise, and the intrinsic complexity of RNA topology. Existing structure-to-sequence frameworks largely rely on static k-nearest neighbor graphs and rigid message passing schemes, which fail to capture the flexible and heterogeneous nature of RNA geometry. To address these issues, we propose a unified framework, ATL-FGD, that integrates Adaptive Topology Learning (ATL) and FiLM-Guided Distillation (FGD) for robust RNA design. ATL introduces a differentiable edge gating mechanism to jointly learn topology and representation, enabling the model to construct data-driven, layer-adaptive graphs that better reflect structural dynamics and biochemical consistency. On top of this, FGD bridges structural and sequence representations via feature-wise linear modulation, softly transferring the semantic knowledge from RNA foundation models without relying on them during inference. Extensive experiments on tertiary structure-based RNA design benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves significant improvements in both sequence recovery and structural fidelity.

Existing structure-to-sequence frameworks largely rely on static k-nearest neighbor graphs and rigid message passing schemes, which fail to capture the flexible and heterogeneous nature of RNA geometry. ATL introduces a differentiable edge gating mechanism to jointly learn topology and representation, enabling the model to construct data-driven, layer-adaptive graphs that better reflect structural dynamics and biochemical consistency. paragraphs: Structure-based RNA design seeks sequences that can fold into a specified three-dimensional shape. The paper identifies scarce annotations, noisy structures, and complex RNA geometry as major challenges. It also argues that fixed nearest-neighbor graphs and rigid information-passing rules inadequately represent the flexible, heterogeneous relationships within RNA structures.

ATL-FGD addresses representation and knowledge transfer together. Adaptive Topology Learning uses differentiable gates on graph edges, allowing connections and features to be learned jointly. The resulting graph can change across layers according to the data. FiLM-Guided Distillation then uses feature-wise linear modulation to connect structural and sequence representations, transferring knowledge from RNA foundation models.

The foundation models provide knowledge during learning without being required at inference. This makes their sequence information available to the design framework without adding that dependency when generating sequences. Experiments report significant improvements in sequence recovery and structural fidelity. Together, these findings support combining learned structural relationships with transferred sequence knowledge for more robust RNA design.
summary.tldr: ATL-FGD combines adaptive structural graphs with distilled RNA foundation-model knowledge to improve sequence recovery and structural fidelity.

title: Learning Adaptive Topology with FiLM-Guided Distillation for Tertiary Structure-Based RNA Design

abstract: Despite progress of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in biomedical visual question answering (VQA), existing benchmarks provide limited assessment of their scientific reasoning capabilities. Most datasets adopt single-image question construction and outcome-oriented evaluation, where correctness is judged by answer plausibility rather than alignment with experimental evidence. Such formulations fail to capture the evidence-constrained, multi-step nature of biomedical reasoning, and obscure whether models can derive conclusions through causal interpretation of experimental observations. To address these critical gaps in reasoning evaluation, we propose a principled benchmark construction framework that reconstructs scientific reasoning paths directly from biomedical literature. By jointly modeling clusters of experimentally related images together with their captions and context, the framework generates tightly coupled question–reasoning–answer triples that require multi-image integration and explicit evidence-driven inference. Based on this framework, we introduce SORBE (Scientific Observation & Reasoning for Biomedical Evaluation), a large-scale multi-image pathology-derived biomedical VQA benchmark designed to evaluate evidence alignment and multi-step experimental reasoning. Under a process-oriented evaluation metric, state-of-the-art biomedical-specialized MLLMs exhibit substantial performance degradation, revealing systematic limitations in evidence grounding and causal reasoning that are not reflected by existing benchmarks. Data and code are available at: https://github.com/UniverseOfUniverse/SORBE.git.

paragraphs: A biomedical model can give a plausible answer without correctly connecting that answer to experimental evidence. This paper argues that common visual question answering benchmarks make this distinction difficult to detect because they often use single images and judge the final answer. The authors instead build an evaluation around the steps connecting observations to scientific conclusions.

Their framework reconstructs reasoning paths from biomedical literature. It groups experimentally related images with their captions and surrounding context, then creates linked questions, reasoning sequences, and answers. The resulting benchmark, SORBE, uses multiple pathology-derived images to test whether models can combine observations and make explicit inferences supported by the evidence.

The evaluation examines the reasoning process as well as its outcome. Under this metric, leading biomedical-specialized multimodal models show substantial performance degradation. The stated finding is that existing evaluations can overlook systematic weaknesses in evidence grounding and causal reasoning. SORBE makes those weaknesses more visible by requiring conclusions to follow an experimentally supported path.
summary.tldr: SORBE tests biomedical models on evidence-linked reasoning across multiple images, exposing weaknesses that answer-focused benchmarks can miss.

title: Benchmarking the Scientific Mind: A Pathology-Derived Biomedical VQA Benchmark for Complex Scientific Reasoning

abstract: Proper accounting of the energy requirements and environmental impact of artificial intelligence (AI) systems is necessary for researchers, developers, policy makers, and users to assess the barriers to building systems at scale. With the growing complexity of pipelines and underlying infrastructure needed to develop and deploy AI systems, previous approaches for evaluating AI efficiency which focus on the costs of a single training run or an individual inference prediction are no longer sufficient. In this position paper, we enunciate the need for applying life cycle assessment to evaluate the costs of the machine learning model development and deployment pipeline to properly account for the required resources and downstream impact. Life cycle assessments enable the incorporation of costs across the full life cycle of an AI system and its underlying infrastructure, from the embodied costs associated with the physical computing hardware through the operational costs in training and inference.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that evaluating AI resource use requires accounting for the full life cycle of a model and its supporting infrastructure. Measurements of one training run or one prediction cover only parts of that process. As development and deployment pipelines become more complex, the authors regard those narrow measurements as insufficient.

Their proposed approach is life cycle assessment, which brings costs from different parts of the system into a shared accounting scope. This includes embodied costs associated with physical computing hardware as well as operational costs from training and inference. The underlying infrastructure therefore belongs in the assessment alongside the computations performed by the model.

The motivation is practical: researchers, developers, policy makers, and users need adequate information about energy requirements and environmental consequences to assess barriers to building AI at scale. The paper's contribution is a position on what such evaluations must include. It argues that resource and impact assessments should reflect the entire development and deployment pipeline, extending beyond isolated measures of computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: AI resource assessments should include hardware and operational costs across the full model development and deployment life cycle.

abstract: POMDPs are the models of choice for reinforcement learning (RL) tasks where the environment cannot be observed directly. In many applications we need to learn the POMDP structure and parameters from experience and this is considered to be a difficult problem. In this paper we address this issue by modeling the hidden environment with a novel class of models that are less expressive, but easier to learn and plan with than POMDPs. We call these models {\em deterministic Markov models} (DMMs), which are deterministic-probabilistic finite automata from learning theory, extended with actions to the sequential (rather than i.i.d.) setting. Conceptually, we extend the Utile Suffix Memory method of McCallum to handle long term memory. We describe DMMs, give Bayesian algorithms for learning and planning with them and also present experimental results for some standard POMDP tasks and tasks to illustrate its efficacy.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning becomes harder when the agent cannot directly observe the environment's underlying state. Partially observable Markov decision processes provide a model for this situation, but learning their structure and parameters from experience is difficult. This paper proposes a simpler model class to make both learning and planning more manageable.

The proposed deterministic Markov models extend deterministic-probabilistic finite automata with actions. This brings the models into a sequential decision setting, where experience arrives through an ongoing interaction rather than as independent examples. Conceptually, the approach extends the Utile Suffix Memory method to accommodate long-term memory, addressing the need to represent information from earlier experience.

The authors provide Bayesian algorithms for learning these models and planning with them, alongside experiments on standard POMDP tasks and illustrative tasks. The central tradeoff is explicit: deterministic Markov models are less expressive than POMDPs but easier to learn and use for planning. Their purpose is to offer a tractable way to construct useful hidden-state models.
summary.tldr: Deterministic Markov models offer a less expressive but more manageable alternative to POMDPs for learning and planning with hidden state.

title: Constructing States for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: It is usually expected that, when labeled data are limited, the learning performance can be improved by exploiting unlabeled data. In many cases, however, the performances of current semi-supervised learning approaches may be even worse than purely using the limited labeled data.It is desired to have \textit{safe} semi-supervised learning approaches which never degenerate learning performance by using unlabeled data. In this paper, we focus on semi-supervised support vector machines (S3VMs) and propose S4VMs, i.e., safe S3VMs. Unlike S3VMs which typically aim at approaching an optimal low-density separator, S4VMs try to exploit the candidate low-density separators simultaneously to reduce the risk of identifying a poor separator with unlabeled data. We describe two implementations of S4VMs, and our comprehensive experiments show that the overall performance of S4VMs are highly competitive to S3VMs, while in contrast to S3VMs which degenerate performance in many cases, S4VMs are never significantly inferior to inductive SVMs.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning aims to improve prediction by supplementing limited labeled examples with unlabeled data. The paper begins from a practical problem: using those extra examples can sometimes make performance worse than learning only from the labels. It focuses on reducing this risk for semi-supervised support vector machines.

The proposed S4VM approach considers multiple candidate low-density separators simultaneously. Conventional semi-supervised SVMs typically seek a single optimal separator in a low-density region. Considering several candidates is intended to reduce the chance that unlabeled data steers learning toward a poor choice. The authors describe two implementations of this strategy.

Across their experiments, S4VMs achieve overall performance highly competitive with semi-supervised SVMs while never being significantly inferior to inductive SVMs. The latter comparison is the evidence for the method's safety motivation: the supervised alternative provides the reference point for avoiding harm. The reported finding is empirical and qualified by significance; it does not establish that unlabeled data can never reduce performance on any possible dataset.
summary.tldr: S4VMs consider multiple separators to reduce harm from unlabeled data and are never significantly worse than supervised SVMs in the reported experiments.

title: Towards Making Unlabeled Data Never Hurt

abstract: This paper is dedicated to the improvement of model learning in multi-class LogitBoost for classification. Motivated by statistical view, LogitBoost can be seen as additive tree regression. Important facts in such a setting are 1) coupled classifier output as sum-to-zero constraint and 2) dense Hessian matrix arising in tree node split gain and node values fitting. On the one hand, the setting is too complicated for a tractable model learning algorithm; On the other hand, too aggressive simplification of the setting may lead to degraded performance. For example, the original LogitBoost is outperformed by ABC-LogitBoost due to the later's more careful treatment for the above two key points in problem settings. In this paper we propose improved methods to address the challenge: we adopt 1) vector tree (i.e. node value is vector) that enforces sum-to-zero constraint and 2) adaptive block coordinate descent exploiting dense Hessian when computing tree split gain and node values. Higher classification accuracy and faster convergence rate are observed for a range of public data sets when comparing to both original and ABC LogitBoost.

paragraphs: Multi-class LogitBoost can be viewed as building a classifier through additive tree regression. Its outputs are coupled by a sum-to-zero constraint, and its optimization involves a dense Hessian matrix. These features make learning complicated, but simplifying them too aggressively can sacrifice predictive performance.

AOSO-LogitBoost addresses both features directly. It uses vector-valued trees, so each node carries multiple output values and can enforce the sum-to-zero constraint. It also uses adaptive block coordinate descent to exploit the dense Hessian when choosing tree splits and fitting node values. The aim is to preserve important interactions among class outputs within a tractable learning procedure.

The authors compare the method with original LogitBoost and ABC-LogitBoost across a range of public datasets. They observe higher classification accuracy and faster convergence than both alternatives. These results support the value of handling the output constraint and optimization structure more carefully. The improvement is an empirical finding from the reported comparisons, rather than a claim that the method wins on every classification problem.
summary.tldr: AOSO-LogitBoost handles coupled class outputs with vector trees and adaptive optimization, improving accuracy and convergence in reported comparisons.

title: AOSO-LogitBoost: Adaptive One-Vs-One LogitBoost for Multi-Class Problem
